The first result in that direction pertains to the case in which 𝒮\mathcal{S} and 𝒞\mathcal{C} are respectively given by the full set of quantum states and channels on some separable, possibly infinite dimensional Hilbert space (Theorem 5.1). The key insight for the proof is to compose the original channel 𝒩\mathcal{N} with a particular choice of generalised depolarising channel. We then show the resulting channel ℳ\mathcal{M} has a unique fixed point state σ\sigma which is close to the original state ρ.\rho. Notably, the new state depends on both the original state ρ\rho and channel 𝒩\mathcal{N} in a highly non-linear way. The same proof technique can also be applied in the classical case where the state and channel can respectively be represented by a probability distribution and a stochastic mapping on some countable alphabet (see Theorem 5.2). The scaling of the approximation functions found in Theorems 5.1 and 5.2 is essentially optimal as we show in Remark 5.4.

Additionally, we establish in the finite dimensional case rapid fixability for a range of other interesting choices for 𝒮\mathcal{S} and 𝒞\mathcal{C}. Specifically, for 𝒮\mathcal{S} being the full set of quantum states and 𝒞\mathcal{C} being the set of 1) unitary channels, 2) mixed-unitary channels or 3) unital channels (see Theorems 6.10, 6.11 and 6.13). Furthermore, we consider the setting of bipartite systems with 𝒮\mathcal{S} being the set of pure bipartite states, and 𝒞\mathcal{C} the set of local channels which act trivially on the first system (Theorem 6.17). All of these results follow by similar proof techniques, which include the application of what we call spectral clustering techniques, rotation lemmas and the generalised depolarising trick. Here, spectral clustering techniques are used to define the new state σ\sigma and the latter two methods are used to define the new channel ℳ,\mathcal{M}, which fix the corresponding approximate fixed point equation. Interestingly, in contrast to the above-mentioned case of general states and channels, here the new fixed-point state is independent of the original channel.

Lastly, we provide an example of 𝒮\mathcal{S} and 𝒞\mathcal{C} where rapid fixability of approximate fixed points is impossible (Corollary 7.3): We consider bipartite quantum systems with 𝒮=𝔖⁡(ℋA​B)\mathcal{S}=\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}_{AB}) being the set of general mixed states and 𝒞=idA⊗CPTP⁡(ℋB)\mathcal{C}={\rm{id}}_{A}\otimes{\rm{CPTP}}(\mathcal{H}_{B}) being once again the set of local channels which act trivially on the first system. In that case we provide an explicit counterexample for which the corresponding approximate fixed point equation can only be fixed with poor control on the respective approximation functions ff and g.g. In particular they cannot be written in the form of f⁡(d,ε)=c​db​εaf(d,\varepsilon)=c\,d^{b}\varepsilon^{a}, and similarly for g⁡(d,ε)g(d,\varepsilon), for some constants a>0,a>0, b,c≥0b,c\geq 0 independent of dd and ε.\varepsilon. This shows, by contrasting with the statement of Theorem 6.17 for pure states and local channels in the bipartite setting mentioned above, that the situation dramatically changes when widening the set 𝒮\mathcal{S} from pure states on ℋA​B\mathcal{H}_{AB} to the set of general mixed states. Interestingly, the mentioned counterexample is essentially classical and therefore also disproves the possibility of rapid fixability in the corresponding classical case.

To prove this result we naturally extend the question of (rapid) fixability of approximate fixed points to the situation of multiple approximate fixed point equations. Here, we consider multiple states and one channel, which all satisfy an approximate fixed point equation, and we ask whether there exist close-by new states and one universal channel which satisfies fixed point equations for all of the states. We then provide a concrete counter example showing that already in the case of two approximate fixed point equations rapid fixability is not possible in general (Theorems 7.1 and 7.2). This example is then encoded into the bipartite setting proving the above-mentioned Corollary 7.3.

Outline of the rest of the paper
In Section 2 we provide some basic notations and facts which are need for the derivations of the results of this paper. In Section 3 we give formal definitions for the fixability and rapid fixability of approximate fixed points (Definitions 3.1 and 3.2) and discuss some elementary examples and observations. In Section 4 we show that for general closed sets 𝒮⊆𝔖⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{S}\subseteq\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}) and 𝒞⊆CPTP⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{C}\subseteq{\rm{CPTP}}(\mathcal{H}) such that a fixed point pair exists, approximate fixed point equations are fixable in the sense of Definition 3.1 (Proposition 4.1). We then review, as a motivating example for studying the fixability of approximate fixed points, the robustness theory of quantum Markov chains. We apply Proposition 4.1 in this context and obtain a robustness result for approximate quantum Markov chains of the form (1.5) in Proposition 4.2. In Section 5 we prove rapid fixability of approximate fixed points in the sense of Definition 3.2 for general quantum states and quantum channels, i.e. for the choice 𝒮=𝔖⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{S}=\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}) and 𝒞=CPTP⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{C}={\rm{CPTP}}(\mathcal{H}) (Theorem 5.1) and for classical states and classical channels, i.e. for the choice 𝒮=Prob⁡(𝒳)\mathcal{S}={\rm{Prob}}({\cal X}) and 𝒞=Stoch⁡(𝒳)\mathcal{C}={\rm{Stoch}}({\cal X}) (Theorem 5.2).

In Section 6 we show rapid fixability of approximate fixed points for a variety of different natural choices of 𝒮\mathcal{S} and 𝒞,\mathcal{C}, which are all strict subsets of the full sets of states and channels. In particular, we consider 𝒮=𝔖⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{S}=\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}) together with 𝒞\mathcal{C} being the set of unitary channels (Theorem 6.13), mixed-unitary channels (Theorem 6.11) and unital channels (Theorem 6.13). All of these results rely on what we call spectral clustering techniques and rotation lemmas studied in Sections 6.1 and 6.2 respectively. We then end this section by proving rapid fixability in the bipartite setting with Hilbert space ℋA​B=ℋA⊗ℋB,\mathcal{H}_{AB}=\mathcal{H}_{A}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{B}, 𝒮\mathcal{S} being the set of pure states on ℋA​B\mathcal{H}_{AB} and 𝒞=idA⊗CPTP⁡(ℋA​B)\mathcal{C}={\rm{id}}_{A}\otimes{\rm{CPTP}}(\mathcal{H}_{AB}) the set of local channels (Theorem 6.17). This result relies on similar proof techniques as the others in this section. In particular we again make use of the rotation lemmas mentioned above.

In Section 7 we show the impossibility of rapid fixability of approximate fixed points in the bipartite setting for the pairs of sets 𝒮=𝔖⁡(ℋA​B)\mathcal{S}=\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}_{AB}) and 𝒞=idA⊗CPTP⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{C}={\rm{id}}_{A}\otimes{\rm{CPTP}}(\mathcal{H}) and also 𝒮=Prob⁡(𝒳×𝒴)\mathcal{S}={\rm{Prob}}({\cal X}\times\mathcal{Y}) and 𝒞=id𝒳⊗Stoch⁡(𝒴)\mathcal{C}={\rm{id}}_{\cal X}\otimes{\rm{Stoch}}(\mathcal{Y}) (Corollary 7.3).

We then end the paper with a summary of the results and a discussion of open problems for interesting future research in Section 8.

2 Preliminaries

In this section we recall some well-known definitions and facts which are used for the derivations of this paper.

Basic notation: For n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} we denote the set [n]≔{1,⋯,n}.[n]\coloneqq\{1,\cdots,n\}. The set of non-negative real numbers is written as ℝ+.\mathbbm{R}_{+}. In this thesis, if not explicitly stated otherwise, log\log denotes the natural logarithm with base e.e.

2.1 States and channels

In this section we review some basic facts about quantum states and channels on some separable Hilbert space ℋ,\mathcal{H}, for a reference consider [Hol01, Wil13, Wol12, Wat18, KW20, RS80]. Here and in the rest of the thesis we focus on quantum channels in the so-called Schrödinger picture.

We denote by ℬ⁡(ℋ){\mathcal{B}}(\mathcal{H}) the set of bounded linear operators and by 𝒯⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{T}(\mathcal{H}) the set of trace class operators on ℋ.\mathcal{H}. We say an operator ρ∈𝒯⁡(ℋ)\rho\in\mathcal{T}(\mathcal{H}) is a quantum state (or often simply state in the following) if ρ≥0\rho\geq 0 and it has unit trace Tr⁡(ρ)=1.\mathrm{Tr}(\rho)=1. We denote the set of states on ℋ\mathcal{H} by 𝔖⁡(ℋ).\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}).

We say a state ρ\rho is pure if it is a rank-1 projection and can hence be written as ρ=|ψ⟩​⟨ψ|\rho=|\psi\rangle\!\langle\psi| for some normalised |ψ⟩∈ℋ.|\psi\rangle\in\mathcal{H}. The set of pure states on ℋ\mathcal{H} is denoted by Pure⁡(ℋ).\operatorname{Pure}(\mathcal{H}). We refer to the vectors corresponding to pure states (i.e. |ψ⟩∈ℋ|\psi\rangle\in\mathcal{H} such that ⟨ψ|ψ⟩=1\langle\psi|\psi\rangle=1) as state vectors. On the other hand, we call states ρ,\rho, which are not pure, mixed.

We can write any state vector |ψ⟩A​B|\psi\rangle_{AB} on some bipartite Hilbert space ℋA​B=ℋA⊗ℋB\mathcal{H}_{AB}=\mathcal{H}_{A}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{B} in Schmidt decomposition as

|ψ⟩A​B=∑i=1d∗λi​|ei⟩A​|fi⟩B\displaystyle|\psi\rangle_{AB}=\sum_{i=1}^{d_{*}}\sqrt{\lambda_{i}}|e_{i}\rangle_{A}|f_{i}\rangle_{B}

with d∗=min⁡{dim(ℋA),dim(ℋB)}d_{*}=\min\{\dim(\mathcal{H}_{A}),\dim(\mathcal{H}_{B})\} (and dim(ℋA),dim(ℋB)=∞\dim(\mathcal{H}_{A}),\dim(\mathcal{H}_{B})=\infty if the underlying Hilbert spaces are infinite dimensional), (λi)i=1d∗\left(\lambda_{i}\right)_{i=1}^{d_{*}} being a probability distribution which we refer to as Schmidt coefficients and (|ei⟩A)i=1d∗\left(|e_{i}\rangle_{A}\right)_{i=1}^{d_{*}} and (|fi⟩B)i=1d∗\left(|f_{i}\rangle_{B}\right)_{i=1}^{d_{*}} being orthonormal systems on ℋA\mathcal{H}_{A} and ℋB\mathcal{H}_{B} respectively which we refer to as Schmidt vectors.

For ρ\rho and σ\sigma being states, we denote the trace distance by 12​‖ρ−σ‖1∈[0,1],\frac{1}{2}\left\|\rho-\sigma\right\|_{1}\in[0,1], where the trace norm is given by ‖x‖1≔Tr​|x|=Tr​x∗​x\left\|x\right\|_{1}\coloneqq\mathrm{Tr}|x|=\mathrm{Tr}\sqrt{x^{*}x} for x∈ℬ⁡(ℋ)x\in{\mathcal{B}}(\mathcal{H}). For a hermitian operator A∈𝒯⁡(ℋ)A\in\mathcal{T}(\mathcal{H}) with Tr⁡(A)=0\mathrm{Tr}(A)=0 we have the variational expression

12​‖A‖1=sup0≤Λ≤𝟙Tr⁡(Λ​A)=Tr⁡(π+​A),\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left\|A\right\|_{1}=\sup_{0\leq\Lambda\leq\mathbbm{1}}\mathrm{Tr}\left(\Lambda A\right)=\mathrm{Tr}\left(\pi_{+}A\right), (2.1)

where we denoted the orthogonal projection onto the support of the positive part of AA by π+.\pi_{+}. This in particular implies the following variational expression of the trace distance of two states ρ\rho and σ\sigma

12​‖ρ−σ‖1=sup0≤Λ≤𝟙Tr⁡(Λ⁡(ρ−σ)).\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left\|\rho-\sigma\right\|_{1}=\sup_{0\leq\Lambda\leq\mathbbm{1}}\mathrm{Tr}\left(\Lambda\left(\rho-\sigma\right)\right). (2.2)

Moreover, for two pure states |ψ⟩​⟨ψ||\psi\rangle\!\langle\psi| and |φ⟩​⟨φ||\varphi\rangle\!\langle\varphi| the trace distance has the form

12​‖|ϕ⟩​⟨ϕ|−|ψ⟩​⟨ψ|‖1=1−|⟨ψ,φ⟩|2.\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left\||\phi\rangle\!\langle\phi|-|\psi\rangle\!\langle\psi|\right\|_{1}=\sqrt{1-|\langle\psi,\varphi\rangle|^{2}}. (2.3)

We say a linear map 𝒩:𝒯⁡(ℋ)→𝒯⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{N}:\mathcal{T}(\mathcal{H})\to\mathcal{T}(\mathcal{H}) is a quantum channel, or often also just channel for simplicity, if it is completely positive and trace preserving. The set of quantum channels on ℋ\mathcal{H}55 5 Here and henceforth we often refer to a channel 𝒩\mathcal{N} on some Hilbert space ℋ\mathcal{H}, although strictly speaking it is linear map on 𝒯⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{T}(\mathcal{H}) the set of trace class operators on ℋ\mathcal{H}. is denoted by CPTP⁡(ℋ).{\rm{CPTP}}(\mathcal{H}).

Every 𝒩∈CPTP⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{N}\in{\rm{CPTP}}(\mathcal{H}) can by Stinespring’s dilation theorem be written in the form

𝒩⁡(x)=TrE​(V​x​V∗),\displaystyle\mathcal{N}(x)=\mathrm{Tr}_{E}\left(VxV^{*}\right),

for some isometry V:ℋ→ℋ⊗ℋE,V:\mathcal{H}\to\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{E}, which we henceforth call the Stinespring isometry of 𝒩,\mathcal{N}, ℋE\mathcal{H}_{E} being some environment Hilbert space and TrE\mathrm{Tr}_{E} denoting the partial trace on ℋE\mathcal{H}_{E}.

For a bounded linear map 𝒩:𝒯⁡(ℋ)→𝒯⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{N}:\mathcal{T}(\mathcal{H})\to\mathcal{T}(\mathcal{H}) we can define the diamond norm by

‖𝒩‖⋄≔supd∈ℕ,x∈𝒯⁡(ℋ⊗ℂd)​‖x‖1=1‖(𝒩⊗idd)​(x)‖1.\displaystyle\left\|\mathcal{N}\right\|_{\diamond}\coloneqq\sup_{d\in\mathbb{N},x\in\mathcal{T}(\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathbb{C}^{d})\,\|x\|_{1}=1}\left\|(\mathcal{N}\otimes{\rm{id}}_{d})(x)\right\|_{1}.

Classical states and channels

In the following we discuss so-called classical states and channels, which are a special case of quantum states and channels discussed previously. We focus on the case of discrete classical alphabets here as this is all we need for the remainder of this paper.

Consider for some countable set 𝒳,{\cal X}, refered to as classical alphabet in the following, the Banach space l1​(𝒳)l^{1}({\cal X}) consisting of absolutely summable sequences s≡(sx)x∈𝒳s\equiv\left(s_{x}\right)_{x\in{\cal X}} with norm

‖s‖1≔∑x∈𝒳|sx|.\displaystyle\left\|s\right\|_{1}\coloneqq\sum_{x\in{\cal X}}|s_{x}|. (2.4)

We say s∈l1​(𝒳)s\in l^{1}({\cal X}) is positive semi-definite if ss is non-negative component wise. A classical state is hence a positive semi-definite sequence P∈l1​(𝒳)P\in l^{1}({\cal X}) which sums to 1 or, in other words, a probability distribution over 𝒳.{\cal X}. The set of probability distributions on 𝒳{\cal X} is denoted by Prob⁡(𝒳).{\rm{Prob}}({\cal X}). Furthermore, we refer to probability distributions on a finite classical alphabet 𝒳{\cal X} as probability vectors.

A classical channel is a linear map 𝒩:l1​(𝒳)→l1​(𝒳)\mathcal{N}:l^{1}({\cal X})\to l^{1}({\cal X}) which maps probability distributions to probability distributions. Denoting the matrix elements T≡(Tx​y)x,y∈𝒳≔(𝒩​(δy)x)x,y∈𝒳T\equiv\left(T_{xy}\right)_{x,y\in{\cal X}}\coloneqq\left(\mathcal{N}(\delta_{y})_{x}\right)_{x,y\in{\cal X}} with δy\delta_{y} being the delta distribution with yt​hy^{th} element equal to 1 and all other elements equal to zero, 𝒩\mathcal{N} is a classical channel if and only if TT is a stochastic mapping, i.e. Tx​y≥0T_{xy}\geq 0 for all x,y∈𝒳x,y\in{\cal X} and

∑x∈𝒳Tx​y=1\displaystyle\sum_{x\in{\cal X}}T_{xy}=1 (2.5)

for all y∈𝒳.y\in{\cal X}. Furthermore, we call a stochastic mapping on a finite classical alphabet |𝒳|<∞|{\cal X}|<\infty a stochastic matrix. We denote the set of classical channels or stochastic mappings on 𝒳{\cal X} by Stoch⁡(𝒳).{\rm{Stoch}}({\cal X}).

Note that l1​(𝒳)l^{1}({\cal X}) can be embedded into 𝒯⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{T}(\mathcal{H}) for ℋ\mathcal{H} being a separable Hilbert space, which can be taken to have finite dimension if |𝒳|<∞|{\cal X}|<\infty. For that we fix an orthonormal basis (|x⟩)x∈𝒳\left(|x\rangle\right)_{x\in{\cal X}} of ℋ\mathcal{H} and consider the map

l1​(𝒳)\displaystyle l^{1}({\cal X}) →𝒯⁡(ℋ)\displaystyle\to\mathcal{T}(\mathcal{H})
s\displaystyle s ↦∑x∈𝒳sx​|x⟩​⟨x|.\displaystyle\mapsto\sum_{x\in{\cal X}}s_{x}|x\rangle\!\langle x|.

Classical states can hence be seen as states on ℋ\mathcal{H} which are diagonal in the fixed basis, in particulur we introduce for P=(px)x∈𝒳∈Prob⁡(𝒳)P=\left(p_{x}\right)_{x\in{\cal X}}\in{\rm{Prob}}({\cal X}) the notation ρP∈𝔖⁡(ℋ)\rho_{P}\in\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}) with

ρP≔∑x∈𝒳px​|x⟩​⟨x|.\displaystyle\rho_{P}\coloneqq\sum_{x\in{\cal X}}p_{x}|x\rangle\!\langle x|. (2.6)

Furthermore, for T∈Stoch⁡(𝒳)T\in{\rm{Stoch}}({\cal X}) we can define the channel on ℋ\mathcal{H} by

𝒩T≔∑x,y∈𝒳Tx​y​|x⟩​⟨x|​⟨y|(⋅)|y⟩.\displaystyle\mathcal{N}_{T}\coloneqq\sum_{x,y\in{\cal X}}T_{xy}|x\rangle\!\langle x|\langle y|(\,\cdot\,)|y\rangle. (2.7)

Note for two stochastic mappings TT and SS we have the relation for the diamond norm

‖𝒩T−𝒩S‖⋄=‖T−S‖≔supy∈𝒴∑x∈𝒳|Tx​y−Sx​y|.\displaystyle\left\|\mathcal{N}_{T}-\mathcal{N}_{S}\right\|_{\diamond}=\|T-S\|\coloneqq\sup_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\sum_{x\in{\cal X}}\left|T_{xy}-S_{xy}\right|. (2.8)

If the fixed basis (|x⟩)x∈𝒳\left(|x\rangle\right)_{x\in{\cal X}} is clear from the context, we interchangeably refer to states on ℋ\mathcal{H} of the form (2.6) and elements of Prob⁡(𝒳){\rm{Prob}}({\cal X}) as classical states and to channels on ℋ\mathcal{H} of the form (2.7) and elements in Stoch⁡(𝒳){\rm{Stoch}}({\cal X}) as classical channels.

2.2 Fixed points of channels

In this section we review some basic facts about fixed points of quantum channels. In fact, the following section applies to all positive and trace preserving maps 𝒩:𝒯⁡(ℋ)→𝒯⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{N}:\mathcal{T}(\mathcal{H})\to\mathcal{T}(\mathcal{H}) without requiring complete positivity. For a more complete overview including also several facts which exclusively hold for quantum channels, consider [Wol12, BCG+13, Wat18].

The space of fixed points of 𝒩\mathcal{N} is denoted by

ℱ⁡(𝒩)≔{x∈𝒯⁡(ℋ)|𝒩⁡(x)=x}=ker⁡(id−𝒩).\displaystyle{\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{N})\coloneqq\left\{x\in\mathcal{T}(\mathcal{H})\Big|\,\mathcal{N}(x)=x\right\}=\ker\left({\rm{id}}-\mathcal{N}\right).

Furthermore, we can define the Cesàro mean of 𝒩\mathcal{N} by

An=1n​∑k=1n𝒩k.\displaystyle A_{n}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathcal{N}^{k}. (2.9)

If the limit P≔limn→∞AnP\coloneqq\lim_{n\to\infty}A_{n} exists, PP given by the projection onto the fixed point space ℱ⁡(𝒩){\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{N}) and for 𝒩∈CPTP⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{N}\in{\rm{CPTP}}(\mathcal{H}) we also have P∈CPTP⁡(ℋ).P\in{\rm{CPTP}}(\mathcal{H}).

First, note that on a finite dimensional Hilbert space, the fixed point space of a positive and trace preserving map 𝒩\mathcal{N} is non-trivial. This is a direct consequence of the fact that 𝒩\mathcal{N} maps the convex and compact set of states on ℋ\mathcal{H} onto itself and therefore there exists, by Brouwer’s fixed point theorem, a fixed point state

ρ∈𝔖⁡(ℋ)∩ℱ⁡(𝒩).\displaystyle\rho\in\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H})\cap{\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{N}). (2.10)

Again, in finite dimensions, the limit of the Cesàro mean AnA_{n} as n→∞n\to\infty always exists by a standard compactness argument.

For infinite dimensional separable Hilbert spaces ℋ\mathcal{H} these arguments based on compactness break down. In fact, one can consider as an example the shift channel 𝒩shift\mathcal{N}_{\text{shift}} which, for (|i⟩)i∈ℕ\left(|i\rangle\right)_{i\in\mathbb{N}} being an orthonormal basis of ℋ\mathcal{H}, is defined by

𝒩shift​(x)=∑i=1∞⟨i|x⁡|i⟩|i+1⟩​⟨i+1|\displaystyle\mathcal{N}_{\text{shift}}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\langle i|x|i\rangle|i+1\rangle\!\langle i+1|

for all x∈𝒯⁡(ℋ).x\in\mathcal{T}(\mathcal{H}). Assuming 𝒩shift​(x)=x\mathcal{N}_{\text{shift}}(x)=x immediately gives ⟨i|x|j⟩=0\langle i|x|j\rangle=0 for all i≠ji\neq j and furthermore ⟨i|x|i⟩=⟨i+1|x|i+1⟩\langle i|x|i\rangle=\langle i+1|x|i+1\rangle for all i∈ℕ.i\in\mathbb{N}. This already shows that x=c​𝟙x=c\mathbbm{1} for some c∈ℂc\in\mathbb{C} and as xx is supposed to be a trace class operator, we have c=0.c=0. Therefore, 𝒩shift\mathcal{N}_{\text{shift}} cannot have any non-trivial fixed points, i.e.

ℱ⁡(𝒩shift)={0}.\displaystyle{\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{N}_{\text{shift}})=\{0\}.

However, we still have that 11 is in the spectrum of 𝒩shift\mathcal{N}_{\text{shift}} which follows as the pure state |1⟩​⟨1||1\rangle\!\langle 1| does not lie in the image of id−𝒩shift.{\rm{id}}-\mathcal{N}_{\text{shift}}.

Another useful fact for 𝒩:𝒯⁡(ℋ)→𝒯⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{N}:\mathcal{T}(\mathcal{H})\to\mathcal{T}(\mathcal{H}) being a positive and trace preserving is that for any fixed point A∈ℱ⁡(𝒩)A\in{\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{N}) we have that also the corresponding real- and imaginary- and furthermore their respective positive- and negative parts are fixed points as well66 6 Here, we introduced the notation ℜ⁡(A)≔A+A∗2\Re(A)\coloneqq\frac{A+A^{*}}{2} and ℑ⁡(A)≔A−A∗2​i\Im(A)\coloneqq\frac{A-A^{*}}{2i} for real and imaginary part of an operator A∈ℬ⁡(ℋ).A\in{\mathcal{B}}(\mathcal{H}). And furthermore the positive and negative parts [A]+≔|A|+A2[A]_{+}\coloneqq\frac{|A|+A}{2} and [A]−≔|A|−A2[A]_{-}\coloneqq\frac{|A|-A}{2} which are positive semi-definite for AA self-adjoint.

[ℜ⁡(A)]+,[ℜ⁡(A)]−,[ℑ⁡(A)]+,[ℑ⁡(A)]−∈ℱ⁡(𝒩).\displaystyle[\Re(A)]_{+},[\Re(A)]_{-},[\Im(A)]_{+},[\Im(A)]_{-}\in{\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{N}). (2.11)

An approximate version of this result, which includes (2.11) as a special case, is shown in Lemma 6.14 below.

Lastly, for any non-zero and positive semi-definite operator ρ∈ℱ⁡(𝒩)\rho\in{\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{N}), its support is an invariant subspace of 𝒩.\mathcal{N}. More precisely, denoting by π\pi the orthogonal projection onto the support of ρ,\rho, we have

Tr⁡((𝟙−π)​𝒩​(π))=0.\displaystyle\ \mathrm{Tr}((\mathbbm{1}-\pi)\mathcal{N}(\pi))=0. (2.12)

Furthermore, for any state σ\sigma with support in ran⁡(π),\operatorname{ran}(\pi), also the image 𝒩⁡(σ)\mathcal{N}(\sigma) has support in ran⁡(π),\operatorname{ran}(\pi), which gives 𝒩⁡(σ)≤π.\mathcal{N}(\sigma)\leq\pi. Interestingly, unlike the fact (2.11), (2.12) is not robust77 7 With that we mean that 12​‖𝒩⁡(ρ)−ρ‖1≤ε\frac{1}{2}\left\|\mathcal{N}(\rho)-\rho\right\|_{1}\leq\varepsilon does not imply Tr⁡((𝟙−π)​𝒩​(π))=f⁡(ε)\mathrm{Tr}((\mathbbm{1}-\pi)\mathcal{N}(\pi))=f(\varepsilon) for some function f⁡(ε)→ε→00.f(\varepsilon)\xrightarrow[\varepsilon\to 0]{}0. against introducing small errors in the fixed point equations, i.e. when only demanding 12​‖𝒩⁡(ρ)−ρ‖1≤ε\frac{1}{2}\left\|\mathcal{N}(\rho)-\rho\right\|_{1}\leq\varepsilon for some small ε>0.\varepsilon>0. A construction where exactly this non-robustness is employed can be found in Section 7.

2.3 Notation for approximate equality

In the following we introduce some notation for approximate equality between elements of normed vector spaces. Here, the meaning of the approximate equality, denoted by ≈\approx, depends on the context as follows: Let ε≥0.\varepsilon\geq 0. For two quantum or classical states ρ\rho and σ\sigma we write

ρ≈εσif12‖ρ−σ‖1≤ε.\displaystyle\rho\approx^{\varepsilon}\sigma\quad\text{if}\quad\frac{1}{2}\left\|\rho-\sigma\right\|_{1}\leq\varepsilon. (2.13)

Similarly, we write for two quantum channels 𝒩\mathcal{N} and ℳ\mathcal{M}

𝒩≈εℳif12‖𝒩−ℳ‖⋄≤ε.\displaystyle\mathcal{N}\approx^{\varepsilon}\mathcal{M}\quad\text{if}\quad\frac{1}{2}\left\|\mathcal{N}-\mathcal{M}\right\|_{\diamond}\leq\varepsilon. (2.14)

For two stochastic mappings TT and SS we write

T≈εSif12‖T−S‖≤ε,\displaystyle T\approx^{\varepsilon}S\quad\text{if}\quad\frac{1}{2}\left\|T-S\right\|\leq\varepsilon, (2.15)

with corresponding norm being defined in (2.8). For two unitaries UU and VV on ℋ\mathcal{H} we write

U≈εVif‖U−V‖≤ε,\displaystyle U\approx^{\varepsilon}V\quad\text{if}\quad\left\|U-V\right\|\leq\varepsilon, (2.16)

and similarly for two orthogonal projections EE and FF

E≈εFif‖E−F‖≤ε,\displaystyle E\approx^{\varepsilon}F\quad\text{if}\quad\left\|E-F\right\|\leq\varepsilon, (2.17)

with the norm being the operator norm in both cases. For two Hilbert space vectors ψ,φ∈ℋ\psi,\varphi\in\mathcal{H} we write

ψ≈εφif‖ψ−φ‖≤ε.\displaystyle\psi\approx^{\varepsilon}\varphi\quad\text{if}\quad\left\|\psi-\varphi\right\|\leq\varepsilon. (2.18)

with norm being the usual Hilbert space norm. Lastly, we write for two complex numbers z1,z2∈ℂz_{1},z_{2}\in\mathbb{C}

z1≈εz2if|z1−z2|≤ε.\displaystyle z_{1}\approx^{\varepsilon}z_{2}\quad\text{if}\quad|z_{1}-z_{2}|\leq\varepsilon. (2.19)

3 Fixability of approximate fixed point equations

As explained in the Introduction, in this paper we adress the following question:

Given a quantum channel and a quantum state which almost satisfy a fixed point equation, can we find a new channel and a new state, which are respectively close to the original ones, such that they satisfy an exact fixed point equation?

This question can be asked under many interesting constraints in which the original channel and state are assumed to have certain structures which the new channel and state are supposed to satisfy as well.

In precise mathematical terms we consider, on some separable Hilbert space ℋ\mathcal{H}, subsets of states 𝒮⊆𝔖⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{S}\subseteq\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}) and subsets of channels 𝒞⊆CPTP⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{C}\subseteq{\rm{CPTP}}(\mathcal{H}) which correspond to certain structures of interest. For example 𝒮\mathcal{S} could be the set of pure states, general mixed states, or, on a bipartite Hilbert space ℋA​B=ℋA⊗ℋB,\mathcal{H}_{AB}=\mathcal{H}_{A}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{B}, the set of entangled states. Similarly, 𝒞\mathcal{C} could for example be the set of general quantum channels, classical channels, unitary channels, unital channels or, on a bipartite Hilbert space ℋ≡ℋA⊗ℋB\mathcal{H}\equiv\mathcal{H}_{A}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{B}, local channels of the form 𝒩A​B≡idA⊗𝒩B.\mathcal{N}_{AB}\equiv{\rm{id}}_{A}\otimes\mathcal{N}_{B}.

For error parameter ε≥0,\varepsilon\geq 0, ρ∈𝒮\rho\in\mathcal{S} and 𝒩∈𝒞\mathcal{N}\in\mathcal{C} we say ρ\rho is an approximate fixed point of 𝒩\mathcal{N} if

𝒩(ρ)≈ερ.\displaystyle\mathcal{N}(\rho)\approx^{\varepsilon}\rho. (3.1)

For a given pair (𝒮,𝒞)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C}) we are hence concerned with whether approximate fixed point equations like (3.1) can be fixed in the sense of the following definition:

Definition 3.1 (Fixability of approximate fixed points)

We say approximate fixed point equations88 8 In the following we often interchangeably refer to an approximate fixed point being fixable meaning fixability of the corresponding approximate fixed point equation. are fixable for the pair 𝒮⊆𝔖⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{S}\subseteq\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}) and 𝒞⊆CPTP⁡(ℋ),\mathcal{C}\subseteq{\rm{CPTP}}(\mathcal{H}), with ℋ\mathcal{H} being some separable Hilbert space, if the following holds true: There exist approximation functions f,g:ℝ+→ℝ+f,\,g:\mathbbm{R}_{+}\to\mathbbm{R}_{+} such that we have

limε→0f⁡(ε)=limε→0g⁡(ε)=0\displaystyle\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}f(\varepsilon)=\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}g(\varepsilon)=0 (3.2)

and for all ρ∈𝒮,𝒩∈𝒞\rho\in\mathcal{S},\,\mathcal{N}\in\mathcal{C} and ε≥0\varepsilon\geq 0 such that 𝒩(ρ)≈ερ\mathcal{N}(\rho)\approx^{\varepsilon}\rho, we can find a new state and a channel of the same structure

σ∈𝒮andℳ∈𝒞,\displaystyle\sigma\in\mathcal{S}\quad\quad\text{and}\quad\quad\mathcal{M}\in\mathcal{C},\quad (3.3)

which are close to original ones, i.e.

σ≈f⁡(ε)ρandℳ≈g⁡(ε)𝒩,\displaystyle\sigma\approx^{f(\varepsilon)}\rho\quad\quad\text{and}\quad\quad\mathcal{M}\approx^{g(\varepsilon)}\mathcal{N}, (3.4)

and which are a fixed point pair, i.e. they satisfy the fixed point equation99 9 Putting this differently, approximate fixed point equations are fixable for the pair (𝒮,𝒞)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C}) if and only if we have for the worst case error sup(ρ,𝒩)∈𝒮×𝒞𝒩(ρ)≈ερinf(σ,ℳ)∈𝒮×𝒞ℳ⁡(σ)=σmax⁡{‖ρ−σ‖1,‖𝒩−ℳ‖⋄}→ε→00.\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}(\rho,\mathcal{N})\in\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{C}\\ \mathcal{N}(\rho)\approx^{\varepsilon}\rho\end{subarray}}\inf_{\begin{subarray}{c}(\sigma,\mathcal{M})\in\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{C}\\ \mathcal{M}(\sigma)=\sigma\end{subarray}}\max\{\|\rho-\sigma\|_{1},\|\mathcal{N}-\mathcal{M}\|_{\diamond}\}\xrightarrow[\varepsilon\to 0]{}0.

ℳ⁡(σ)=σ.\displaystyle\mathcal{M}(\sigma)=\sigma. (3.5)

It is important to note that the functional form of ff and gg in the above definition solely depends on the sets 𝒮\mathcal{S} and 𝒞\mathcal{C} (and hence also on the underlying Hilbert space ℋ\mathcal{H}), but not on the specific ρ∈𝒮,\rho\in\mathcal{S}, 𝒩∈𝒞\mathcal{N}\in\mathcal{C} and ε≥0.\varepsilon\geq 0. Note also that for finite dimensional Hilbert spaces with dimension d,d, the approximation functions ff and gg can hence implicitly depend on d,d, i.e. f⁡(d,ε)≡f⁡(ε)f(d,\varepsilon)\equiv f(\varepsilon) and g⁡(d,ε)≡g⁡(ε)g(d,\varepsilon)\equiv g(\varepsilon) as denoted in the Introduction.

To illustrate Definition 3.1 we first note that for general sets 𝒮\mathcal{S} and 𝒞,\mathcal{C}, approximate fixed point equations might not be fixable, and hence the above is not trivially true in general. For that we could consider sets with just one element 𝒮={ρ}\mathcal{S}=\{\rho\} and 𝒞={𝒩}\mathcal{C}=\{\mathcal{N}\} such that 𝒩⁡(ρ)≠ρ.\mathcal{N}(\rho)\neq\rho. In that case approximate fixed point equations are not fixable, simply as there exists no pair (σ,ℳ)∈𝒮×𝒞(\sigma,\mathcal{M})\in\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{C} satisfying an exact fixed point equation. More interesting counterexamples occur when one or both of the sets are non-closed. For example, take as Hilbert space ℋ=ℂ2\mathcal{H}=\mathbb{C}^{2}, and then the convex but open set 𝒮={(1−ε)​|0⟩​⟨0|+ε|1⟩​⟨1|| 0<ε<1}\mathcal{S}=\{(1-\varepsilon)|0\rangle\!\langle 0|+\varepsilon|1\rangle\!\langle 1|\ \big|\ 0<\varepsilon<1\} and furthermore 𝒞={Tr⁡(⋅)​|0⟩​⟨0|,Tr⁡(⋅)​𝟙/2}.\mathcal{C}=\{\mathrm{Tr}(\,\cdot\,)|0\rangle\!\langle 0|,\mathrm{Tr}(\,\cdot\,)\mathbbm{1}/2\}. First of all, as σ=𝟙/2∈𝒮\sigma=\mathbbm{1}/2\in\mathcal{S} and ℳ=Tr⁡(⋅)​𝟙/2∈𝒞,\mathcal{M}=\mathrm{Tr}(\,\cdot\,)\mathbbm{1}/2\in\mathcal{C}, we have, unlike in the previously mentioned counterexample, a pair of state and channel satisfying ℳ⁡(σ)=σ.\mathcal{M}(\sigma)=\sigma. However, for every ε>0\varepsilon>0 there exists ρ∈𝒮\rho\in\mathcal{S} such that for 𝒩=Tr⁡(⋅)​|0⟩​⟨0|∈𝒞\mathcal{N}=\mathrm{Tr}(\,\cdot\,)|0\rangle\!\langle 0|\in\mathcal{C} we have

𝒩(ρ)≈ερ.\displaystyle\mathcal{N}(\rho)\approx^{\varepsilon}\rho. (3.6)

As 12​‖𝒩−Tr⁡(⋅)​𝟙/2‖⋄=1/2\frac{1}{2}\|\mathcal{N}-\mathrm{Tr}(\,\cdot\,)\mathbbm{1}/2\|_{\diamond}=1/2 and the unique fixed point state of 𝒩\mathcal{N} given by |0⟩​⟨0||0\rangle\!\langle 0| is not contained in 𝒮,\mathcal{S}, the approximate fixed point equation (3.6) can not be fixed in this setup.

It turns out that in the finite dimensional case the above counterexamples illustrate the only two situations in which approximate fixed point equations might not be fixable, i.e. non-existence of a fixed point pair or non-closedness of the sets 𝒮\mathcal{S} and 𝒞.\mathcal{C}. In fact, in Proposition 4.1 below we show by a compactness argument that for 𝒮\mathcal{S} and 𝒞\mathcal{C} being closed and such that a fixed point pair exists, approximate fixed point equations are always fixable.

Under the named assumptions of Proposition 4.1, the existence of approximation functions ff and gg satisfying Definition 3.1 is merely ensured by compactness and their precise form is rather implicit. Our focus therefore lies in providing good control of the functions ff and gg for concrete examples of 𝒮\mathcal{S} and 𝒞.\mathcal{C}. Especially, we are interested in cases where the interplay of the dimension dd and ε\varepsilon in f⁡(d,ε)≡f⁡(ε)f(d,\varepsilon)\equiv f(\varepsilon) and g⁡(d,ε)≡g⁡(ε)g(d,\varepsilon)\equiv g(\varepsilon) is rather mild, and the convergence in limε→0f⁡(d,ε)=limε→0g⁡(d,ε)\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}f(d,\varepsilon)=\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}g(d,\varepsilon) happens rather fast and we therefore have good approximation by the fixed point pair in (3.4). To make this more precise, we consider 𝒮=(𝒮d)d∈ℕ\mathcal{S}=\left(\mathcal{S}_{d}\right)_{d\in\mathbb{N}} and 𝒞=(𝒞d)d∈ℕ\mathcal{C}=\left(\mathcal{C}_{d}\right)_{d\in\mathbb{N}} to be sequences of sets with 𝒮d⊆𝔖⁡(ℋd)\mathcal{S}_{d}\subseteq\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}_{d}) and 𝒞d⊆CPTP⁡(ℋd)\mathcal{C}_{d}\subseteq{\rm{CPTP}}(\mathcal{H}_{d}) and ℋd≅ℂd.\mathcal{H}_{d}\cong\mathbb{C}^{d}. These could, for example, consist of the full set of quantum states and channels or alternatively unitary channels on Hilbert spaces for different dimensions. We are then interested in whether approximate fixed point equations are rapidly fixable for a pair (𝒮,𝒞)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C}) in the sense of the following definition:

Definition 3.2 (Rapid fixability of approximate fixed points)

Let 𝒮=(𝒮d)d∈ℕ\mathcal{S}=\left(\mathcal{S}_{d}\right)_{d\in\mathbb{N}} and 𝒞=(𝒞d)d∈ℕ\mathcal{C}=\left(\mathcal{C}_{d}\right)_{d\in\mathbb{N}} with 𝒮d⊆𝔖⁡(ℋd)\mathcal{S}_{d}\subseteq\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}_{d}) and 𝒞d⊆CPTP⁡(ℋd)\mathcal{C}_{d}\subseteq{\rm{CPTP}}(\mathcal{H}_{d}) and ℋd\mathcal{H}_{d} being a dd-dimensional Hilbert space. We say approximate fixed point equations are rapidly fixable for the pair (𝒮,𝒞)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C}) if for all d∈ℕd\in\mathbb{N} they are fixable for (𝒮d,𝒞d)(\mathcal{S}_{d},\mathcal{C}_{d}) in the sense of Definition 3.1 with corresponding approximation functions ff and gg satisfying

f⁡(d,ε)=c​db​εaandg⁡(d,ε)=c′​db′​εa′,\displaystyle f(d,\varepsilon)=c\,d^{b}\varepsilon^{a}\quad\quad\text{and}\quad\quad g(d,\varepsilon)=c^{\prime}d^{b^{\prime}}\varepsilon^{a^{\prime}}, (3.7)

for some a,a′>0a,a^{\prime}>0 (and typically a,a′≤1a,a^{\prime}\leq 1) and b′,b′,c,c′≥0b^{\prime},b^{\prime},c,c^{\prime}\geq 0 all independent of dd and ε.\varepsilon.

In the following, we often drop for simplicity the difference between the sequences 𝒮=(𝒮d)d∈ℕ\mathcal{S}=\left(\mathcal{S}_{d}\right)_{d\in\mathbb{N}} and 𝒞=(𝒞d)d∈ℕ\mathcal{C}=\left(\mathcal{C}_{d}\right)_{d\in\mathbb{N}} and the corresponding sets 𝒮d\mathcal{S}_{d} and 𝒞d\mathcal{C}_{d} when the full sequence is clear from the context.

For the majority of the remainder of this paper we are concerned with proving that for certain examples of 𝒮\mathcal{S} and 𝒞\mathcal{C} approximate fixed point equations are rapidly fixable and to provide concrete numerical values for a,a′,b′,b′,ca,a^{\prime},b^{\prime},b^{\prime},c and c′.c^{\prime}. In particular we show that approximate fixed point equations are rapidly fixable for 𝒮=𝔖⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{S}=\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}) being the full set of quantum states on ℋ\mathcal{H} and

  1. 1.

    𝒞=CPTP⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{C}={\rm{CPTP}}(\mathcal{H}) being the full set of quantum channels (Theorem 5.1),

  2. 2.

    𝒞\mathcal{C} being the set of unitary channels (Theorem 6.10),

  3. 3.

    𝒞\mathcal{C} being the set of mixed-unitary channels (Theorem 6.11),

  4. 4.

    𝒞\mathcal{C} being the set of unital channels (Theorem 6.13).

Furthermore, we also show rapid fixabilitity of approximate fixed point equations in the following cases:

  1. 5.

    𝒮=Prob⁡(𝒳)\mathcal{S}={\rm{Prob}}({\cal X}) being the set of classical states, i.e. probability vectors, and 𝒞=Stoch⁡(𝒳)\mathcal{C}={\rm{Stoch}}({\cal X}) being the set of classical channels, i.e. stochastic matrices, on some finite classical alphabet 𝒳{\cal X} (Theorem 5.2),

  2. 6.

    𝒮\mathcal{S} being the set of pure states on a bipartite Hilbert space ℋA​B=ℋA⊗ℋB\mathcal{H}_{AB}=\mathcal{H}_{A}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{B} and 𝒞=idA⊗CPTP⁡(ℋB)≔{idA⊗𝒩B|𝒩B∈CPTP⁡(ℋB)},\mathcal{C}={\rm{id}}_{A}\otimes{\rm{CPTP}}(\mathcal{H}_{B})\coloneqq\left\{{\rm{id}}_{A}\otimes\mathcal{N}_{B}\,\big|\,\mathcal{N}_{B}\in{\rm{CPTP}}(\mathcal{H}_{B})\right\}, which we call local channels in the following (Theorem 6.17).

On the other hand, by providing a concrete counterexample, we show that approximate fixed points for 𝒮=𝔖⁡(ℋA​B)\mathcal{S}=\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}_{AB}) being the full set of quantum states on a bipartite Hilbert space and the set of local channels 𝒞=idA⊗CPTP⁡(ℋB)\mathcal{C}={\rm{id}}_{A}\otimes{\rm{CPTP}}(\mathcal{H}_{B}) are not rapidly fixable (Corollary 7.3). In fact, this counterexample already rules out rapid fixability of approximate fixed points in the corresponding classical case with 𝒮=Prob⁡(𝒳×𝒴)\mathcal{S}={\rm{Prob}}({\cal X}\times\mathcal{Y}) and 𝒞=idX⊗Stoch⁡(𝒴)≔{idX⊗TY|TY∈Stoch⁡(𝒴)}\mathcal{C}={\rm{id}}_{X}\otimes{\rm{Stoch}}(\mathcal{Y})\coloneqq\left\{{\rm{id}}_{X}\otimes T_{Y}\,\big|\,T_{Y}\in{\rm{Stoch}}(\mathcal{Y})\right\}\,

To illustrate the above question of fixability of approximate fixed points further, let us discuss the following variant: Instead of allowing to change both state ρ\rho to σ\sigma and channel 𝒩\mathcal{N} to ℳ\mathcal{M} in (3.4), one could ask whether the approximate fixed point equation 𝒩(ρ)≈ερ\mathcal{N}(\rho)\approx^{\varepsilon}\rho can be fixed by only changing one of them. The following example shows that this is not possible in general:

Example 3.3 (Necessity to change both state and channel)

We take 𝒮=𝔖⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{S}=\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}) and 𝒞=CPTP⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{C}={\rm{CPTP}}(\mathcal{H}) the full set of quantum states and channels on some finite-dimensional Hilbert space ℋ.\mathcal{H}. Consider first ℋ1=ℂ2\mathcal{H}_{1}=\mathbb{C}^{2} with orthonormal basis {|0⟩,|1⟩}\left\{|0\rangle,|1\rangle\right\}, ρ1=|0⟩​⟨0|\rho_{1}=|0\rangle\!\langle 0| and for ε>0\varepsilon>0 the quantum channel

𝒩1,ε=(1−ε)​id+ε​Tr​(⋅)​|1⟩​⟨1|.\displaystyle\mathcal{N}_{1,\varepsilon}=(1-\varepsilon){\rm{id}}+\varepsilon\mathrm{Tr}(\,\cdot\,)\,|1\rangle\!\langle 1|.

This pair of state and channel surely satisfies the approximate fixed point equation

𝒩1,ε(ρ1)≈ερ1.\displaystyle\mathcal{N}_{1,\varepsilon}(\rho_{1})\approx^{\varepsilon}\rho_{1}. (3.8)

However, ρ1\rho_{1} is far from the fixed point space of 𝒩1,ε\mathcal{N}_{1,\varepsilon} given by ℱ⁡(𝒩1,ε)=span⁡{|1⟩​⟨1|},{\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{N}_{1,\varepsilon})={\rm{span}}\left\{|1\rangle\!\langle 1|\right\}, i.e.

minx∈ℱ⁡(𝒩1,ε)⁡‖ρ1−x‖1=‖|0⟩​⟨0|‖1=1\displaystyle\min_{x\in{\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{N}_{1,\varepsilon})}\left\|\rho_{1}-x\right\|_{1}=\left\||0\rangle\!\langle 0|\right\|_{1}=1

Therefore, the approximate fixed point equation (3.8) cannot be fixed in the sense of (3.4) and (3.5) by solely changing the state ρ1\rho_{1} but not the channel 𝒩1,ε.\mathcal{N}_{1,\varepsilon}.1010 10 Another interesting example where this phenomenon occurs is taking 𝒩1,ε\mathcal{N}_{1,\varepsilon} to be a unitary channel U⁡(⋅)​U∗U(\,\cdot\,)U^{*} for some unitary UU satisfying 0<‖U−𝟙‖≤ε0<\|U-\mathbbm{1}\|\leq\varepsilon but with eigenbasis given by |+⟩|+\rangle and |−⟩|-\rangle and therefore ρ1=|0⟩​⟨0|\rho_{1}=|0\rangle\!\langle 0| being far from the fixed point space ℱ(𝒩1,ε)==span{|+⟩⟨+|,|−⟩⟨−|}.{\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{N}_{1,\varepsilon})={\rm={span}}\{|+\rangle\!\langle+|,|-\rangle\!\langle-|\}. However, it is possible to fix the approximate fixed point equation (3.8) by only changing the channel, as we can simply take σ=ρ1\sigma=\rho_{1} and ℳ=id≈ε𝒩1,ε.\mathcal{M}={\rm{id}}\approx^{\varepsilon}\mathcal{N}_{1,\varepsilon}.

An example where the opposite occurs is given by the following: Take as Hilbert space ℋ2=ℂ3\mathcal{H}_{2}=\mathbb{C}^{3} and the unitary channel 𝒩2=U⁡(⋅)​U∗\mathcal{N}_{2}=U(\,\cdot\,)U^{*} with unitary

U=σx⊕1=(010100001),\displaystyle U=\sigma_{x}\oplus 1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\ 1&0&0\\ 0&0&1\end{pmatrix},

where we denoted by σx\sigma_{x} the Pauli-xx matrix. Then take for every ε>0\varepsilon>0 the state

ρ2,ε=ε⁡|0⟩​⟨0|+(1−ε)|2⟩​⟨2|=(ε 000 000 01−ε).\displaystyle\rho_{2,\varepsilon}=\varepsilon|0\rangle\!\langle 0|+(1-\varepsilon)|2\rangle\!\langle 2|=\begin{pmatrix}\varepsilon&\ \ 0&0\\ 0&\ \ 0&0\\ 0&\ \ 0&1-\varepsilon\end{pmatrix}.

Clearly, we have the approximate fixed point equation

𝒩2(ρ2,ε)=ε|1⟩⟨1|+(1−ε)|2⟩⟨2|≈ερ2.\displaystyle\mathcal{N}_{2}(\rho_{2,\varepsilon})=\varepsilon|1\rangle\!\langle 1|+(1-\varepsilon)|2\rangle\!\langle 2|\approx^{\varepsilon}\rho_{2}. (3.9)

Assume now there exist a function g:ℝ+→ℝ+g:\mathbbm{R}_{+}\to\mathbbm{R}_{+} such that limε→0g⁡(ε)=0\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}g(\varepsilon)=0, and, for all ε≥0\varepsilon\geq 0, a channel1111 11 Note that we only used linearity and positivity of ℳε\mathcal{M}_{\varepsilon} showing that in fact the approximate fixed point equation cannot be fixed by only changing 𝒩2\mathcal{N}_{2} to ℳε\mathcal{M}_{\varepsilon} even if we allow for the wider class of all positive maps. ℳε\mathcal{M}_{\varepsilon} approximating 𝒩2,\mathcal{N}_{2}, i.e.

ℳε≈g⁡(ε)𝒩2\displaystyle\mathcal{M}_{\varepsilon}\approx^{g(\varepsilon)}\mathcal{N}_{2} (3.10)

and satisfying the exact fixed point equation

ℳε​(ρ2,ε)=ρ2,ε.\displaystyle\mathcal{M}_{\varepsilon}(\rho_{2,\varepsilon})=\rho_{2,\varepsilon}. (3.11)

From (3.10) we however already see

⟨1|ℳε​(|0⟩​⟨0|)|1⟩≥1−g⁡(ε)>0\displaystyle\langle 1|\mathcal{M}_{\varepsilon}(|0\rangle\!\langle 0|)|1\rangle\geq 1-g(\varepsilon)>0

for ε\varepsilon small enough and hence

⟨1|(ℳε​(ρ2,ε)−ρ2,ε)|1⟩=⟨1|ℳε​(ρ2,ε)|1⟩≥ε⁡(1−g⁡(ε))>0\displaystyle\langle 1|(\mathcal{M}_{\varepsilon}(\rho_{2,\varepsilon})-\rho_{2,\varepsilon})|1\rangle=\langle 1|\mathcal{M}_{\varepsilon}(\rho_{2,\varepsilon})|1\rangle\geq\varepsilon(1-g(\varepsilon))>0

which is a contradiction to the fixed point equation (3.11). Hence, we have shown that the approximate fixed point equation (3.9) cannot be fixed in the sense of (3.4) and (3.5) by only changing the the channel 𝒩2\mathcal{N}_{2} but not the state ρ2,ε.\rho_{2,\varepsilon}. On the other hand, for this particular example (3.9) can be fixed by doing the reverse, i.e. only changing the state to σ=|2⟩⟨2|≈ερ2,ε\sigma=|2\rangle\!\langle 2|\approx^{\varepsilon}\rho_{2,\varepsilon} but leaving the channel invariant ℳ=𝒩2.\mathcal{M}=\mathcal{N}_{2}.

Building both examples above on top of each other gives an example of an approximate fixed point equation which can only be fixed by both varying state and channel. More, precisely, we take as Hilbert space ℋ=ℋ1⊕ℋ2=ℂ5\mathcal{H}=\mathcal{H}_{1}\oplus\mathcal{H}_{2}=\mathbb{C}^{5} and for ε>0\varepsilon>0 the state

ρε=12​(ρ1⊕ρ2,ε)\displaystyle\rho_{\varepsilon}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\rho_{1}\oplus\rho_{2,\varepsilon}\right)

and channel

𝒩ε=𝒩1,ε⊕𝒩2\displaystyle\mathcal{N}_{\varepsilon}=\mathcal{N}_{1,\varepsilon}\oplus\mathcal{N}_{2}

This pair satisfies the approximate fixed point equation 𝒩ε(ρε)≈ερε\mathcal{N}_{\varepsilon}(\rho_{\varepsilon})\approx^{\varepsilon}\rho_{\varepsilon} but, by the above arguments, cannot be fixed by soley changing either state or channel.1212 12 Here, for a more detailed argument, denote by π1\pi_{1} and π2\pi_{2} the orthogonal projections on ℋ\mathcal{H} onto the subspaces ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} and ℋ2\mathcal{H}_{2} and note that for every σε∈ℱ⁡(𝒩ε)\sigma_{\varepsilon}\in{\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{N}_{\varepsilon}) we have necessarily σε=π1​σε​π1+π2​σε​π2.\sigma_{\varepsilon}=\pi_{1}\sigma_{\varepsilon}\pi_{1}+\pi_{2}\sigma_{\varepsilon}\pi_{2}. Therefore, π1​σε​π1∈ℱ⁡(𝒩1,ε)=span⁡{|1⟩​⟨1|}\pi_{1}\sigma_{\varepsilon}\pi_{1}\in{\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{N}_{1,\varepsilon})={\rm{span}}\{|1\rangle\!\langle 1|\} and hence ‖σε−ρε‖1≥‖π1​σε​π1−12​ρ1‖1≥12.\|\sigma_{\varepsilon}-\rho_{\varepsilon}\|_{1}\geq\|\pi_{1}\sigma_{\varepsilon}\pi_{1}-\frac{1}{2}\rho_{1}\|_{1}\geq\frac{1}{2}. On the other hand, any channel ℳε\mathcal{M}_{\varepsilon} having ρε\rho_{\varepsilon} as fixed point must be far from 𝒩ε\mathcal{N}_{\varepsilon} by exactly the same argument as for 𝒩2\mathcal{N}_{2} and ρ2,ε.\rho_{2,\varepsilon}.

Lastly, we want to point out that the difficulty of the problem outlined above lies in the fact that we demand certain structures (meaning membership of the sets 𝒮\mathcal{S} and 𝒞\mathcal{C}) to be preserved, e.g. that the new σ\sigma and ℳ\mathcal{M} satisfying ℳ⁡(σ)=σ\mathcal{M}(\sigma)=\sigma are a state and a channel respectively. To illustrate this, let VV be some dd-dimensional, normed and complex vector space, ε≥0,\varepsilon\geq 0, v∈Vv\in V with ‖v‖=1\|v\|=1 and A:V→VA:V\to V some linear map such that ‖A​v−v‖≤ε.\|Av-v\|\leq\varepsilon. We would like to fix this approximate fixed point equation by changing AA to BB while only demanding that BB must be linear as well. For that consider the following construction: Let (vi)i=1d\left(v_{i}\right)_{i=1}^{d} be a basis of VV with v1=v.v_{1}=v. We can now define BB simply on each basis vector and then extend linearly. Taking hence

B​v1=vandB​vi=A​vifor all i=2,⋯,d\displaystyle Bv_{1}=v\quad\quad\text{and}\quad\quad Bv_{i}=Av_{i}\quad\text{for all $i=2,\cdots,d$}

and then extending linearly, gives a well-defined linear map B:V→VB:V\to V satisfying the fixed point equation B​v=vBv=v and furthermore

‖B−A‖\displaystyle\left\|B-A\right\| =max‖w‖=1⁡‖(B−A)​w‖=max‖w‖=1⁡‖∑i=1dωi​(B−A)​vi‖\displaystyle=\max_{\|w\|=1}\left\|(B-A)w\right\|=\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}\|w\|=1\end{subarray}}\left\|\sum_{i=1}^{d}\omega_{i}(B-A)v_{i}\right\|
=max‖w‖=1⁡|ω1|​‖v−A​v‖≤cd​ε.\displaystyle=\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}\|w\|=1\end{subarray}}|\omega_{1}|\left\|v-Av\right\|\leq c_{d}\,\varepsilon. (3.12)

Here, (ωi)i=1d⊆ℂ\left(\omega_{i}\right)_{i=1}^{d}\subseteq\mathbb{C} denote the coefficients of the vector ww in the given basis and cd≥0c_{d}\geq 0 is some constant whose precise form may depend on the dimension d,d, the norm on VV and the choice of basis (vi)i=1d.\left(v_{i}\right)_{i=1}^{d}. For example, if the norm ∥⋅∥\|\,\cdot\,\| is induced by a scalar product on V,V, we can pick the basis to be orthonormal with respect to this scalar product and cd=1c_{d}=1 follows. For general norms the existence of such finite cdc_{d} follows by equivalence of all norms in finite dimensions. This shows that fixing approximate fixed point equations becomes a lot easier when only demanding to preserve linearity of the map when changing AA to BB. In particular here, unlike in Example 3.3 where also positivity of the map was supposed to be preserved, it suffices to only change the map AA to BB but leave the the vector vv invariant. In the sections below we see that for fixing approximate fixed points equations in terms of quantum states and channels more sophisticated techniques are necessary compared to the purely linear case.

4 Fixability for closed sets

In this section we first state Proposition 4.1 which provides for the finite dimensional case that approximate fixed point equations are always fixable in the sense of Definition 3.1 as long as the sets 𝒮⊆𝔖⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{S}\subseteq\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}) and 𝒞⊆CPTP⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{C}\subseteq{\rm{CPTP}}(\mathcal{H}) are closed and contain a fixed point pair. The proof relies on a compactness argument and hence we merely prove existence of approximation functions ff and gg satisfying the conditions in Defintion 3.1 but do not provide any specific form they need to satisfy.

We then review some of the theory of quantum Markov chains and their approximate analogs. We see that they can be defined by a certain (approximate) fixed point equation which they need to satisfy. Applying Proposition 4.1 to fix this particular approximate fixed point equation enables us to solve an open problem in the robustness theory of quantum Markov chains. In particular, we show that for every approximate Markov chain there is an exact quantum Markov chain close to it (Proposition 4.2). Here, the approximation error in mentioned closeness is measured in terms of a function f⁡(dA​B​C,ε)f(d_{ABC},\varepsilon) depending necessarily on the intrinsic dimension of the problem captured in dA​B​Cd_{ABC} and the error parameter ε≥0\varepsilon\geq 0 of the approximate fixed point equation and which decays as ε→0.\varepsilon\to 0.

Proposition 4.1 (Fixability for closed sets 𝒮\mathcal{S} and 𝒞\mathcal{C})

Let ℋ\mathcal{H} be a finite dimensional Hilbert space. Further, let 𝒮⊆𝔖⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{S}\subseteq\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}) and 𝒞⊆CPTP⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{C}\subseteq{\rm{CPTP}}(\mathcal{H}) be closed and such that there exist σ⋆∈𝒮\sigma_{\star}\in\mathcal{S} and ℳ⋆∈𝒞\mathcal{M}_{\star}\in\mathcal{C} satisfying the fixed point equation:

ℳ⋆​(σ⋆)=σ⋆.\displaystyle\mathcal{M}_{\star}(\sigma_{\star})=\sigma_{\star}. (4.1)

Then, there exist functions f,g:ℝ+→ℝ+f,g:\mathbbm{R}_{+}\to\mathbbm{R}_{+} such that

limε→0f⁡(ε)=limε→0g⁡(ε)=0\displaystyle\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}f(\varepsilon)=\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}g(\varepsilon)=0 (4.2)

and the following holds: For all ρ∈𝒮\rho\in\mathcal{S}, 𝒩∈𝒞\mathcal{N}\in\mathcal{C} and ε≥0\varepsilon\geq 0 with

𝒩(ρ)≈ερ,\displaystyle\mathcal{N}(\rho)\approx^{\varepsilon}\rho, (4.3)

there exist σ∈𝒮\sigma\in\mathcal{S} and ℳ∈𝒞\mathcal{M}\in\mathcal{C} with

σ≈f⁡(ε)ρandℳ≈g⁡(ε)𝒩,\displaystyle\sigma\approx^{f(\varepsilon)}\rho\quad\quad\text{and}\quad\quad\mathcal{M}\approx^{g(\varepsilon)}\mathcal{N}, (4.4)

such that the exact fixed point equation

ℳ⁡(σ)=σ\displaystyle\mathcal{M}(\sigma)=\sigma (4.5)

holds. In other words, all approximate fixed point equations are fixable for the pair (𝒮,𝒞)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C}) in the sense of Definition 3.1.

Note that the approximation functions ff and gg in Proposition 4.1 can implicitly depend on the dimension of the underlying Hilbert space, as remarked below Definition 3.1. We defer the proof of Proposition 4.1 in Subsection 4.2 and first discuss its application to the robustness theory of quantum Markov chains.

4.1 Application to the robustness of quantum Markov chains

We review some basic definitions and well-known facts regarding quantum Markov chains and their approximate analogs (see [Sut18] for a nice overview of all the mentioned results): We consider tripartite Hilbert spaces ℋA​B​C=ℋA⊗ℋB⊗ℋC\mathcal{H}_{ABC}=\mathcal{H}_{A}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{B}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{C} with finite dimensions dA≔dim(ℋA)d_{A}\coloneqq\dim(\mathcal{H}_{A}), dB≔dim(ℋB)=dBd_{B}\coloneqq\dim(\mathcal{H}_{B})=d_{B} and dC≔dim(ℋC)d_{C}\coloneqq\dim(\mathcal{H}_{C}). For a state ρA​B​C\rho_{ABC} on ℋA​B​C\mathcal{H}_{ABC} we can define the conditional mutual information

I(A:C|B)ρ≔S(ρA​B)+S(ρB​C)−S(ρA​B​C)−S(ρB)\displaystyle I(A:C|B)_{\rho}\coloneqq S(\rho_{AB})+S(\rho_{BC})-S(\rho_{ABC})-S(\rho_{B}) (4.6)

where we denoted the von Neumann entropy of a state σ\sigma by S⁡(σ)≔−Tr⁡(σ​log⁡(σ))S(\sigma)\coloneqq-\mathrm{Tr}(\sigma\log(\sigma)) and denoted the reduced states of ρA​B​C\rho_{ABC} by ρA​B≔TrC​(ρA​B​C)\rho_{AB}\coloneqq\mathrm{Tr}_{C}(\rho_{ABC}) and analogously for the other combinations. Note that the conditional mutual information is always non-negative, I(A:C|B)ρ≥0,I(A:C|B)_{\rho}\geq 0, which is due to the strong subadditivity of the von Neumann entropy [LR73].

A state ρA​B​C\rho_{ABC} is a (short) quantum Markov chain (QMC) if it satisfies strong subadditivity with equality, i.e.

I(A:C|B)ρ=0.\displaystyle I(A:C|B)_{\rho}=0. (4.7)

This entropic characterisation is equivalent to the existence of a recovery channel [Pet03], i.e. a completely positive and trace preserving linear map ℛB→B​C:ℬ⁡(ℋB)→ℬ⁡(ℋB​C)\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}:{\mathcal{B}}(\mathcal{H}_{B})\to{\mathcal{B}}(\mathcal{H}_{BC}) such that

(idA⊗ℛB→B​C)​(ρA​B)=ρA​B​C.\displaystyle({\rm{id}}_{A}\otimes\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC})(\rho_{AB})=\rho_{ABC}. (4.8)

Intuitively this means that system CC can be recovered exclusively by focusing on system BB while ignoring A.A. Note that a quantum Markov chain is hence characterised by satisfying a certain fixed point equation

𝒩⁡(ρA​B​C)=ρA​B​C\displaystyle\mathcal{N}(\rho_{ABC})=\rho_{ABC} (4.9)

for 𝒩\mathcal{N} being a channel of the specific form 𝒩=(idA⊗ℛB→B​C)∘TrC.\mathcal{N}=({\rm{id}}_{A}\otimes\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC})\circ\mathrm{Tr}_{C}. In [HJPW04] the authors realised that this implies an interesting structure of ρA​B​C\rho_{ABC}: There exists an orthogonal sum decomposition

ℋB=⨁j=1nℋbjL⊗ℋbjL\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{B}=\bigoplus_{j=1}^{n}\mathcal{H}_{b^{L}_{j}}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{b^{L}_{j}}

with n∈[dB]n\in[d_{B}] and Hilbert spaces (ℋbjL)j=1n(\mathcal{H}_{b^{L}_{j}})_{j=1}^{n} and (ℋbjR)j=1n(\mathcal{H}_{b^{R}_{j}})_{j=1}^{n} and such that

ρA​B​C=⨁j=1nqj​ρA​bjL⊗ρbjR​C\displaystyle\rho_{ABC}=\bigoplus_{j=1}^{n}q_{j}\,\rho_{Ab^{L}_{j}}\otimes\rho_{b^{R}_{j}C} (4.10)

for some probability distribution (qj)j=1n\left(q_{j}\right)_{j=1}^{n} and states ρA​bjL\rho_{Ab^{L}_{j}} on ℋA​bjL=ℋA⊗ℋbjL\mathcal{H}_{Ab^{L}_{j}}=\mathcal{H}_{A}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{b_{j}^{L}} and ρbjR​C\rho_{b^{R}_{j}C} on ℋbjR​C=ℋbjR⊗ℋC\mathcal{H}_{b^{R}_{j}C}=\mathcal{H}_{b_{j}^{R}}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{C} for all j∈[n].j\in[n]. An essential component in the proof of [HJPW04] is the Koashi-Imoto theorem [KI02] which implies a comparable orthogonal sum structure for one channel and multiple states, which are all fixed points of the channel. On the other hand, it is also easy to see that (4.10) implies (4.7) or (4.8), which gives that (4.7), (4.8) and (4.10) are all equivalent characterisations of quantum Markov chains.

It is important to note that the above is a sensible quantum generalisation of (classical) Markov chains: A probability distribution PX​Y​ZP_{XYZ} on some classical alphabet 𝒳×𝒴×𝒵{\cal X}\times\mathcal{Y}\times\mathcal{Z} is called (short) Markov chain (MC) if

PX​Y​Z=PX​Y​PZ|Y,\displaystyle P_{XYZ}=P_{XY}P_{Z|Y}, (4.11)

with PX​YP_{XY} denoting the marginal distribution of XX and YY and PZ|YP_{Z|Y} the conditional distribution of ZZ given Y.Y. Note that (4.11) can be seen as classical analog of (4.8) as the full distribution PX​Y​ZP_{XYZ} can be recovered by application of a classical channel which only acts on Y.Y.1313 13 More precisely, we can define the stochastic matrix T∈ℝ+|𝒵|​|𝒴|×|𝒴|T\in\mathbbm{R}_{+}^{|\mathcal{Z}||\mathcal{Y}|\times|\mathcal{Y}|} by denoting w=(z,y)w=(z,y) and Tw​y′:=δy​y′​PZ|Y​(z|y′).T_{w\,y^{\prime}}:=\delta_{yy^{\prime}}P_{Z|Y}(z|y^{\prime}). Equation (4.11) can then by written as the recovery relation (idX⊗T)​(PX​Y)=PX​Y​Z.({\rm{id}}_{X}\otimes T)(P_{XY})=P_{XYZ}. Similarly to the quantum case discussed above, (4.11) is equivalent to the conditional mutual information satisfying

I(X:Z|Y)P=0,\displaystyle I(X:Z|Y)_{P}=0, (4.12)

where I(X:Z|Y)PI(X:Z|Y)_{P} is defined analogously to (4.6) with von Neumann entropies replaced by the corresponding Shannon entropies.

An interesting question is whether the equivalences above are robust against small errors, i.e. when the statements (4.7)-(4.10) in the quantum case, and (4.11) and (4.12) in the classical case, does not hold exactly but only holds up to a small error ε≥0.\varepsilon\geq 0. Classically, this is the case as we have a very strong robustness theory of Markov chains due to the equality [HHHO]

I(X:Z|Y)P=minQX​Y​Z​MCD(PX​Y​Z∥QX​Y​Z)=D(PX​Y​Z∥PX​YPZ|Y),\displaystyle I(X:Z|Y)_{P}=\min_{Q_{XYZ}\ \text{MC}}D(P_{XYZ}\|Q_{XYZ})=D(P_{XYZ}\|P_{XY}P_{Z|Y}), (4.13)

where we have denoted the Kullback-Leibler divergence of two distributions P=(Pi)i=1mP=\left(P_{i}\right)_{i=1}^{m} and Q=(Qi)i=1mQ=\left(Q_{i}\right)_{i=1}^{m} by D(P∥Q)≔∑i=1mPilog(PiQi)D(P\|Q)\coloneqq\sum_{i=1}^{m}P_{i}\log(\frac{P_{i}}{Q_{i}}) if Pi=0P_{i}=0 for all i∈[m]i\in[m] for which Qi=0Q_{i}=0, and D(P∥Q)=∞D(P\|Q)=\infty otherwise. This can be combined with Pinsker’s inequality [CK11, Chapter I.3.] giving

minQX​Y​Z​MC12‖PX​Y​Z−QX​Z​Y‖1≤I(X:Z|Y)P2.\displaystyle\min_{Q_{XYZ}\ \text{MC}}\,\frac{1}{2}\left\|P_{XYZ}-Q_{XZY}\right\|_{1}\leq\sqrt{\frac{I(X:Z|Y)_{P}}{2}}. (4.14)

Therefore, (4.13) and (4.14) show that if the conditional mutual information of a distribution PX​Y​ZP_{XYZ} is small, it is close to a Markov chain, and hence can be written approximately in the form (4.11).

In the quantum case, the robustness theory of quantum Markov chains is far more involved: For an error parameter ε≥0\varepsilon\geq 0 we call a state ρA​B​C\rho_{ABC} an approximate quantum Markov chain if

I(A:C|B)ρ≤ε.\displaystyle I(A:C|B)_{\rho}\leq\varepsilon. (4.15)

In [FR15]1414 14 Note that in [FR15] the authors consider logarithms base 2 and not base ee as in this thesis, which is why they state (4.16) with a different prefactor in the error parameter. it was shown, and then extended in [BaHOS15, Wil15, SFR16, SBT17, JRS+18, Sut18], that this implies the existence of a recovery channel ℛB→B​C\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC} such that (4.8) holds up to ε\sqrt{\varepsilon} error, i.e. precisely

(idA⊗ℛB→B​C)(ρA​B)≈ερA​B​C.\displaystyle({\rm{id}}_{A}\otimes\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC})(\rho_{AB})\approx^{\sqrt{\varepsilon}}\rho_{ABC}. (4.16)

On the other hand, as argued in [FR15] using the Alicki-Fannes inequality [AF04], approximate recovery of the form (4.16) implies, up to changes in the error parameters, smallness of the conditional mutual information (4.15). Using the same argument as around (4.9), an approximate quantum Markov chain is hence characterised by satisfying a certain approximate fixed point equation.

In the quantum case, upper bounding the distance of a tripartite state to the set of quantum Markov chains in terms of some decaying function in the conditional mutual information similarly to (4.14) is, however, still an open problem. This is an interesting question as a positive answer would imply that an approximate quantum Markov chain can also, up to error terms, be written in an orthogonal sum decomposition of the form (4.10). It is, however, known that a possible answer in the quantum case must be far more complicated than in the classical case as concrete counterexamples of the quantum analogs of (4.13) and (4.14) have been found in [ILW08, CSW12, Sut18]. In particular, it has been shown that any possible upper bound of the trace distance to the closest quantum Markov chain in terms of some decaying function in the conditional mutual information must necessarily be dimension dependent.

Applying our result on fixability of approximate fixed point equations for closed sets 𝒮\mathcal{S} and 𝒞\mathcal{C}, Proposition 4.1, we are able to close this gap to some extent: In the proposition below we see that any approximate quantum Markov chain is close to an exact one, in the sense that if the conditional mutual information approaches zero, the corresponding state approaches the set of quantum Markov chains. The upper bound on the minimal distance to the set of quantum Markov chains is, as discussed above, dimension dependent. Moreover, as the proof relies on the compactness argument from Proposition 4.1, we can only show existence of such an approximation function but are not able to show that it must be of a specific form.

Proposition 4.2 (Robustness of quantum Markov chains)

There exists a function f:ℕ×ℝ+→ℝ+f:\mathbb{N}\times\mathbbm{R}_{+}\to\mathbbm{R}_{+} such that for all d∈ℕd\in\mathbb{N} we have

limε→0f⁡(d,ε)=0\displaystyle\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}f(d,\varepsilon)=0 (4.17)

and for all ℋA​B​C=ℋA⊗ℋB⊗ℋC\mathcal{H}_{ABC}=\mathcal{H}_{A}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{B}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{C} being a tripartite Hilbert space with finite dimensions dA≔dim(ℋA),d_{A}\coloneqq\dim(\mathcal{H}_{A}), dB≔dim(ℋB),d_{B}\coloneqq\dim(\mathcal{H}_{B}), dC≔dim(ℋC),d_{C}\coloneqq\dim(\mathcal{H}_{C}), and dA​B​C≔dim(ℋA​B​C)=dA​dB​dCd_{ABC}\coloneqq\dim(\mathcal{H}_{ABC})=d_{A}d_{B}d_{C} and tripartite states ρA​B​C∈𝔖⁡(ℋA​B​C)\rho_{ABC}\in\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}_{ABC}) such that

I(A:C|B)ρ≤ε\displaystyle I(A:C|B)_{\rho}\leq\varepsilon (4.18)

for some ε≥0\varepsilon\geq 0 there exists a quantum Markov chain σA​B​C\sigma_{ABC} such that

σA​B​C≈f⁡(dA​B​C,ε)ρA​B​C,\displaystyle\sigma_{ABC}\approx^{f(d_{ABC},\varepsilon)}\rho_{ABC}, (4.19)

In particular, ρA​B​C\rho_{ABC} can be written approximately in an orthogonal sum decomposition of the form (4.10).

Proof. By assumption and the results mentioned around (4.16), there exists a recovery channel ℛB→B​C\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC} such that

ρA​B​C≈ε(idA⊗ℛB→B​C)(ρA​B)=(idA⊗ℛB→B​C)∘TrC(ρA​B​C).\displaystyle\rho_{ABC}\approx^{\sqrt{\varepsilon}}({\rm{id}}_{A}\otimes\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC})(\rho_{AB})=({\rm{id}}_{A}\otimes\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC})\circ\mathrm{Tr}_{C}(\rho_{ABC}). (4.20)

We define the sets 𝒮≔𝔖⁡(ℋA​B​C)\mathcal{S}\coloneqq\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}_{ABC}) and as set of channels

𝒞≔{Φ∈CPTP(ℋA​B​C)|Φ=(idA⊗ℛB→B​C′)∘TrC,ℛB→B​C′ channel }.\displaystyle\mathcal{C}\coloneqq\left\{\Phi\in{\rm{CPTP}}(\mathcal{H}_{ABC})\,\Big|\,\Phi=({\rm{id}}_{A}\otimes\mathcal{R}^{\prime}_{B\to BC})\circ\mathrm{Tr}_{C},\ \,\mathcal{R}^{\prime}_{B\to BC}\,\text{ channel }\right\}. (4.21)

Note that 𝒮\mathcal{S} and 𝒞\mathcal{C} are closed and furthermore the corresponding set of fixed point pairs is non-empty as it precisely consists of the quantum Markov chains on ℋA​B​C\mathcal{H}_{ABC} and their respective recovery channels. Hence, by Proposition 4.1 there exist an approximation function1515 15 The approximation function in Proposition 4.1 does only implicitly depend on the dimension of the underlying Hilbert space. As we want to proof a result for all finite dimensional tripartite Hilbert spaces, we make this dimension dependence explicit in the following. f1:ℕ×ℝ+→ℝ+f_{1}:\mathbb{N}\times\mathbbm{R}_{+}\to\mathbbm{R}_{+} such that

limε→0f1​(dA​B​C,ε)=0,\displaystyle\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}f_{1}(d_{ABC},\varepsilon)=0,

a state σA​B​C\sigma_{ABC} on ℋA​B​C\mathcal{H}_{ABC} satisfying

σA​B​C≈f1​(dA​B​C,ε)ρA​B​C,\displaystyle\sigma_{ABC}\approx^{f_{1}(d_{ABC},\varepsilon)}\rho_{ABC},

and a recovery channel ℛB→B​C′\mathcal{R}^{\prime}_{B\to BC} such that

(idA⊗ℛB→B​C′)∘TrC​(σA​B​C)=(idA⊗ℛB→B​C′)​(σA​B)=σA​B​C.\displaystyle({\rm{id}}_{A}\otimes\mathcal{R}^{\prime}_{B\to BC})\circ\mathrm{Tr}_{C}(\sigma_{ABC})=({\rm{id}}_{A}\otimes\mathcal{R}^{\prime}_{B\to BC})(\sigma_{AB})=\sigma_{ABC}. (4.22)

Hence, σA​B​C\sigma_{ABC} is by the results stated around (4.8) a quantum Markov chain and we can take f⁡(dA​B​C,ε)≔f1​(dA​B​C,ε),f(d_{ABC},\varepsilon)\coloneqq f_{1}(d_{ABC},\sqrt{\varepsilon}), which finishes the proof.  

It would be desirable to obtain better control on the approximation function ff in Propositon 4.2. In particular, similarly to the definition of rapid fixability of approximate fixed points (cf. Defintion 3.2), we could hope for a bound of the form

minσA​B​C​QMC⁡12​‖ρA​B​C−σA​B​C‖1≤?c​dAbA​dBbB​dCbC​εa\displaystyle\min_{\sigma_{ABC}\ \text{QMC}}\,\frac{1}{2}\left\|\rho_{ABC}-\sigma_{ABC}\right\|_{1}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle?}}{{\leq}}c\,d^{\,b_{A}}_{A}d^{\,b_{B}}_{B}d^{\,b_{C}}_{C}\,\varepsilon^{a} (4.23)

for tripartite states ρA​B​C\rho_{ABC} satisfying

I(A:C|B)ρ≤ε\displaystyle I(A:C|B)_{\rho}\leq\varepsilon (4.24)

and some constants a>0a>0 and c,bA,bB,bC≥0c,b_{A},b_{B},b_{C}\geq 0 all independent of the dimensions dA,dB,dCd_{A},d_{B},d_{C} and the state ρA​B​C.\rho_{ABC}. As used in the proof of Proposition 4.2, we know by [FR15] that (4.24) implies the existence of a channel

𝒩∈𝒞={Φ∈CPTP(ℋA​B​C)|Φ=(idA⊗ℛB→B​C′)∘TrC,ℛB→B​C′ channel }.\displaystyle\mathcal{N}\in\mathcal{C}=\left\{\Phi\in{\rm{CPTP}}(\mathcal{H}_{ABC})\,\Big|\,\Phi=({\rm{id}}_{A}\otimes\mathcal{R}^{\prime}_{B\to BC})\circ\mathrm{Tr}_{C},\ \,\mathcal{R}^{\prime}_{B\to BC}\,\text{ channel }\right\}. (4.25)

such that

𝒩(ρA​B​C)≈ερA​B​C.\displaystyle\mathcal{N}(\rho_{ABC})\approx^{\sqrt{\varepsilon}}\rho_{ABC}.

Hence, (4.23) could be established by proving rapid fixability of approximate fixed points for the sets 𝒮=𝔖⁡(ℋA​B​C)\mathcal{S}=\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}_{ABC}) and 𝒞\mathcal{C} as above. However, unfortunately, this is impossible by Corollary 7.3 below. In particular, here, already for the case of system CC being trivial, i.e. ℋC=ℂ\mathcal{H}_{C}=\mathbb{C} for which the above reduces to the pair 𝒮=𝔖⁡(ℋA​B)\mathcal{S}=\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}_{AB}) and 𝒞=idA⊗CPTP⁡(ℋB),\mathcal{C}={\rm{id}}_{A}\otimes{\rm{CPTP}}(\mathcal{H}_{B}), rapid fixability of approximate fixed points is ruled out.

Note, however, that this does not exclude the possibility of the bound (4.23). The reason is that for proving (4.23) we only need to find

σA​B​C≈c​dAbA​dBbB​dCbC​εaρA​B​C\displaystyle\sigma_{ABC}\approx^{c\,d^{b_{A}}_{A}d^{b_{B}}_{B}d^{b_{C}}_{C}\,\varepsilon^{a}}\rho_{ABC} (4.26)

and a channel ℳ\mathcal{M} in the set denoted in (4.25), which crucially is allowed to be far from 𝒩,\mathcal{N}, such that

ℳ⁡(σA​B​C)=σA​B​C\displaystyle\mathcal{M}(\sigma_{ABC})=\sigma_{ABC} (4.27)

(cf. (4.9)).1616 16 Note that following the proof in [HJPW04], one can show that the knowledge of explicit approximation functions ff and gg satisfying Definition 3.1 for the pair 𝒮=𝔖⁡(ℋA​B)\mathcal{S}=\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}_{AB}) and 𝒞=idA⊗CPTP⁡(ℋB)\mathcal{C}={\rm{id}}_{A}\otimes{\rm{CPTP}}(\mathcal{H}_{B}) gives an explicit bound on minσA​B​C​QMC⁡12​‖ρA​B​C−σA​B​C‖1\min_{\sigma_{ABC}\ \text{QMC}}\,\frac{1}{2}\left\|\rho_{ABC}-\sigma_{ABC}\right\|_{1} in terms of ff and g.g. For that specific proof technique it is important to also have control on the function gg which measures the distance of the original and the new channel in Definition 3.1. Therefore, by the impossibility statement Corollary 7.3, proving (4.23) with that line of arguing is in fact excluded.

4.2 Proof of Proposition 4.1

We finish the section by giving a proof of Proposition 4.1:

Proof of Proposition 4.1. Define the function

F:𝒮×𝒞\displaystyle F:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{C} →ℝ+\displaystyle\to\mathbbm{R}_{+}
(ρ,𝒩)\displaystyle(\rho,\mathcal{N}) ↦12​‖𝒩⁡(ρ)−ρ‖1.\displaystyle\mapsto\frac{1}{2}\left\|\mathcal{N}(\rho)-\rho\right\|_{1}.

Firstly, note that FF is continuous. Moreover, the preimage F−1​({0})F^{-1}(\{0\}) is exactly the set of pairs of states and channels in 𝒮×𝒞\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{C} which satisfy an exact fixed point equation and is non-empty by assumption.

Now, since the set 𝒮×𝒞\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{C} is closed and hence compact, we see in the following

∀δ>0​∃ε>0​ s.t​∀(ρ,𝒩)∈𝒮×𝒞​ with​F​(ρ,𝒩)≤ε​ we have ​dist​((ρ,𝒩),F−1​({0}))≤δ,\displaystyle\forall\delta>0\,\exists\varepsilon>0\,\text{ s.t}\ \forall(\rho,\mathcal{N})\in\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{C}\text{ with}\ F(\rho,\mathcal{N})\leq\varepsilon\ \text{ we have }{\rm{dist}}((\rho,\mathcal{N}),F^{-1}(\{0\}))\leq\delta, (4.28)

where

dist⁡((ρ,𝒩),F−1​({0}))=min(σ,ℳ)∈F−1​({0})⁡(12​‖ρ−σ‖1+12​‖𝒩−ℳ‖⋄).{\rm{dist}}((\rho,\mathcal{N}),F^{-1}(\{0\}))=\min_{(\sigma,\mathcal{M})\in F^{-1}(\{0\})}\left(\frac{1}{2}\left\|\rho-\sigma\right\|_{1}+\frac{1}{2}\left\|\mathcal{N}-\mathcal{M}\right\|_{\diamond}\right).

To prove that (4.28) holds, we assume the opposite to arrive at a contradiction: In that case there exists δ>0\delta>0 such that for all n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} there exists (ρn,𝒩n)∈𝒮×𝒞(\rho_{n},\mathcal{N}_{n})\in\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{C} with F⁡(ρn,𝒩n)≤1nF(\rho_{n},\mathcal{N}_{n})\leq\frac{1}{n} and dist⁡((ρ,𝒩),F−1​({0}))>δ.{\rm{dist}}((\rho,\mathcal{N}),F^{-1}(\{0\}))>\delta. But, by compactness of 𝒮×𝒞,\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{C}, the sequence ((ρn,𝒩n))n∈ℕ\left((\rho_{n},\mathcal{N}_{n})\right)_{n\in\mathbb{N}} is, up to taking a subsequence, convergent. This already gives a contradiction as by continuity of FF the limit of named subsequence must lie in F−1​({0})F^{-1}(\{0\}).

Define now for ε≥0\varepsilon\geq 0

δ⋆​(ε)=sup(ρ,𝒩)∈F−1​([0,ε])dist⁡((ρ,𝒩),F−1​({0})).\displaystyle\delta_{\star}(\varepsilon)=\sup_{(\rho,\mathcal{N})\in F^{-1}([0,\varepsilon])}{\rm{dist}}((\rho,\mathcal{N}),F^{-1}(\{0\})).

Since ∅≠F−1​({0})⊆F−1​([0,ε]),\emptyset\neq F^{-1}(\{0\})\subseteq F^{-1}([0,\varepsilon]), we have δ⋆​(ε)≥0.\delta_{\star}(\varepsilon)\geq 0. Furthermore, we can show that

limε→0δ⋆​(ε)=0.\displaystyle\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}\delta_{\star}(\varepsilon)=0. (4.29)

To see this, let δ′>0\delta^{\prime}>0 and use that by (4.28) there exists an ε′>0\varepsilon^{\prime}>0 such that for all (ρ,𝒩)∈F−1​([0,ε′])(\rho,\mathcal{N})\in F^{-1}([0,\varepsilon^{\prime}]) we have dist⁡((ρ,𝒩),F−1​({0}))≤δ′{\rm{dist}}((\rho,\mathcal{N}),F^{-1}(\{0\}))\leq\delta^{\prime} and therefore

δ⋆​(ε)≤δ⋆​(ε′)≤δ′.\displaystyle\delta_{\star}(\varepsilon)\leq\delta_{\star}(\varepsilon^{\prime})\leq\delta^{\prime}.

for all 0≤ε≤ε′,0\leq\varepsilon\leq\varepsilon^{\prime}, where the first inequality follows since by definition ε↦δ⋆​(ε)\varepsilon\mapsto\delta_{\star}(\varepsilon) is monotonically increasing. As δ′>0\delta^{\prime}>0 was arbitrary, this shows (4.29).

Furthermore, simply by definition of δ⋆​(ε)\delta_{\star}(\varepsilon), we have for all (ρ,𝒩)∈𝒮×𝒞(\rho,\mathcal{N})\in\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{C} and ε≥0\varepsilon\geq 0 such that 𝒩(ρ)≈ερ\mathcal{N}(\rho)\approx^{\varepsilon}\rho that there exists a fixed point pair, i.e. (σ,ℳ)∈F−1​({0})(\sigma,\mathcal{M})\in F^{-1}(\{0\}) such that

12​‖ρ−σ‖1+12​‖𝒩−ℳ‖⋄≤δ⋆​(ε).\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left\|\rho-\sigma\right\|_{1}+\frac{1}{2}\left\|\mathcal{N}-\mathcal{M}\right\|_{\diamond}\leq\delta_{\star}(\varepsilon).

We can hence pick f⁡(ε)=g⁡(ε)=δ⋆​(ε)f(\varepsilon)=g(\varepsilon)=\delta_{\star}(\varepsilon) which finishes the proof.  

5 Rapid fixability for general quantum and classical channels

In this section we show rapid fixability of approximate fixed points in the sense of Definition 3.2 for the following:

  1. 1.

    general quantum states and quantum channels, i.e. for the choice 𝒮=𝔖⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{S}=\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}) and 𝒞=CPTP⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{C}={\rm{CPTP}}(\mathcal{H}) (Theorem 5.1),

  2. 2.

    classical states and classical channels, i.e. for the choice 𝒮=Prob⁡(𝒳)\mathcal{S}={\rm{Prob}}({\cal X}) and 𝒞=Stoch⁡(𝒳)\mathcal{C}={\rm{Stoch}}({\cal X}) (Theorem 5.2).

Here, we explicitly construct for ρ∈𝒮\rho\in\mathcal{S} and 𝒩∈𝒞\mathcal{N}\in\mathcal{C} and ε≥0\varepsilon\geq 0 satisfying the approximate fixed point equation

𝒩(ρ)≈ερ,\displaystyle\mathcal{N}(\rho)\approx^{\varepsilon}\rho, (5.1)

a state σ∈𝒮\sigma\in\mathcal{S} and a channel ℳ∈𝒞\mathcal{M}\in\mathcal{C} close to the original ones such that

ℳ⁡(σ)=σ.\displaystyle\mathcal{M}(\sigma)=\sigma. (5.2)

The aim is to have good control on the approximation errors in σ≈ρ\sigma\approx\rho and ℳ≈𝒩\mathcal{M}\approx\mathcal{N} and hence provide explicit forms of the approximation functions ff and gg in Definitions 3.1 and 3.2.

Both these results follow the same lines of proof. The key insight is to compose the original channel 𝒩\mathcal{N} with a particular choice of generalised depolarising channel given by

Φ=(1−ε)​id+ε​Tr​(⋅)​ρ.\displaystyle\Phi=(1-\sqrt{\varepsilon})\,{\rm{id}}+\sqrt{\varepsilon}\,\mathrm{Tr}(\,\cdot\,)\rho.

The main technical tool for proving Theorem 5.1 and 5.2 is then given by Lemma 5.5 below. Here, it is shown that the resulting channel ℳ=Φ∘𝒩\mathcal{M}=\Phi\circ\mathcal{N} has a unique fixed point state σ,\sigma, which is close to ρ.\rho. In particular we show that σ≈ερ.\sigma\approx^{\sqrt{\varepsilon}}\rho.

The results in this section hold true for general separable, possibly infinite dimensional Hilbert spaces or, in the classical case, for general countable classical alphabets 𝒳{\cal X}. In the following we first state the above mentioned results for the quantum case and then for the classical case:

Theorem 5.1 (Fixability for general quantum channels)

Let ρ\rho be state and 𝒩\mathcal{N} be a channel on some separable Hilbert space ℋ\mathcal{H} such that for ε≥0\varepsilon\geq 0 we have

𝒩(ρ)≈ερ.\displaystyle\mathcal{N}(\rho)\approx^{\varepsilon}\rho. (5.3)

Then, there exists a state σ\sigma and a channel ℳ\mathcal{M} satisfying

σ≈ερ,ℳ≈ε𝒩\displaystyle\sigma\approx^{\sqrt{\varepsilon}}\rho,\quad\quad\mathcal{M}\approx^{\sqrt{\varepsilon}}\mathcal{N} (5.4)

and

ℳ⁡(σ)=σ.\displaystyle\mathcal{M}(\sigma)=\sigma. (5.5)
Theorem 5.2 (Fixability for classical channels)

Let PP be a probability distribution and TT be a stochastic mapping on some countable classical alphabet 𝒳{\cal X} satisfying for some ε≥0\varepsilon\geq 0

TP≈εP.\displaystyle TP\approx^{\varepsilon}P. (5.6)

Then, there exists a SS stochastic mapping and a probability distribution QQ such that

Q≈εP,S≈εT\displaystyle Q\approx^{\sqrt{\varepsilon}}P,\quad\quad S\approx^{\sqrt{\varepsilon}}T (5.7)

and

S​Q=Q.\displaystyle SQ=Q. (5.8)
Remark 5.3

Note that Theorems 5.1 and 5.2 can be seen as improved versions of the results which appeared in the thesis of the first author [Sal23, Theorem 3.2.1 and 3.2.2]. In particular the approximations functions provided by Theorems 5.1 and 5.2, i.e. f⁡(d,ε)=g⁡(d,ε)=εf(d,\varepsilon)=g(d,\varepsilon)=\sqrt{\varepsilon} are unlike the ones in the older versions in [Sal23] not dimension dependent. Furthermore, the proofs outlined here are conceptually a lot simpler and shorter. In particular they do not rely on the iterative procedure called pp-iteration defined and analysed in [Sal23].

Remark 5.4 (Optimality of approximation functions in Theorems 5.1 and 5.2)

The scaling of the approximation functions in Theorems 5.1 and 5.2 is essentially optimal: For all 0<ε≤10<\varepsilon\leq 1 we can find a state ρε\rho_{\varepsilon} and a channel 𝒩ε\mathcal{N}_{\varepsilon} with 𝒩ε(ρε)≈ερε\mathcal{N}_{\varepsilon}(\rho_{\varepsilon})\approx^{\varepsilon}\rho_{\varepsilon} but for every new state σε\sigma_{\varepsilon} and new channel1717 17 The statement in fact also holds true when only requiring ℳε\mathcal{M}_{\varepsilon} to be a positive linear map. ℳε\mathcal{M}_{\varepsilon} which satisy

σε≈f⁡(ε)ρε,ℳε≈g⁡(ε)𝒩ε\displaystyle\sigma_{\varepsilon}\approx^{f(\varepsilon)}\rho_{\varepsilon},\quad\quad\mathcal{M}_{\varepsilon}\approx^{g(\varepsilon)}\mathcal{N}_{\varepsilon} (5.9)

and

ℳε​(σε)=σε\displaystyle\mathcal{M}_{\varepsilon}(\sigma_{\varepsilon})=\sigma_{\varepsilon} (5.10)

we have the lower bound on the approximation functions

max⁡{f⁡(ε),g⁡(ε)}=Ω⁡(ε),\displaystyle\max\{f(\varepsilon),g(\varepsilon)\}=\Omega\left(\sqrt{\varepsilon}\right), (5.11)

i.e. max⁡{f⁡(ε),g⁡(ε)}≥c​ε\max\{f(\varepsilon),g(\varepsilon)\}\geq c\sqrt{\varepsilon} for some c>0c>0 independent of 0<ε≤10<\varepsilon\leq 1.1818 18 Putting differently this means that we have the worst case bound
supρ,𝒩​ s.t. 𝒩(ρ)≈ερinfσ,ℳ​ s.t. ℳ⁡(σ)=σmax⁡{‖ρ−σ‖1,‖𝒩−ℳ‖⋄}=Ω⁡(ε).\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}\rho,\mathcal{N}\text{ s.t. }\\ \mathcal{N}(\rho)\approx^{\varepsilon}\rho\end{subarray}}\inf_{\begin{subarray}{c}\sigma,\mathcal{M}\text{ s.t. }\\ \mathcal{M}(\sigma)=\sigma\end{subarray}}\max\{\|\rho-\sigma\|_{1},\|\mathcal{N}-\mathcal{M}\|_{\diamond}\}=\Omega(\sqrt{\varepsilon}). The state ρε\rho_{\varepsilon} and 𝒩ε\mathcal{N}_{\varepsilon} can in fact taken to be classical, which hence also shows optimality of the scaling in Theorem 5.2 in the classical case. Note that this necessary ε\sqrt{\varepsilon}-scaling of the approximation functions in the case of general states and channels is in sharp contrast to the ε\varepsilon-scaling which was observed in (3.12) when only demanding that linearity of the map 𝒩\mathcal{N} is preserved when changing to ℳ.\mathcal{M}.

In the following we explicitly construct named state ρε\rho_{\varepsilon} and channel 𝒩ε\mathcal{N}_{\varepsilon} on the Hilbert space ℋ=ℂ3\mathcal{H}=\mathbb{C}^{3} with orthonormal basis {|0⟩,|1⟩,|2⟩}\{|0\rangle,|1\rangle,|2\rangle\}.1919 19 The example can then be embedded into any separable Hilbert space ℋ\mathcal{H} with dim(ℋ)≥3\dim(\mathcal{H})\geq 3. Consider

ρε=ε​|0⟩​⟨0|+(1−ε)|2⟩​⟨2|.\displaystyle\rho_{\varepsilon}=\sqrt{\varepsilon}|0\rangle\!\langle 0|+(1-\sqrt{\varepsilon})|2\rangle\!\langle 2|.

and furthermore the stochastic matrix

Tε=(1−εε0ε1−ε0001)\displaystyle T_{\varepsilon}=\begin{pmatrix}1-\sqrt{\varepsilon}&\sqrt{\varepsilon}&0\\ \sqrt{\varepsilon}&1-\sqrt{\varepsilon}&0\\ 0&0&1\end{pmatrix}

with corresponding (classical) channel 𝒩ε≡𝒩Tε\mathcal{N}_{\varepsilon}\equiv\mathcal{N}_{T_{\varepsilon}} where we used the notation (2.7). Note that we have the approximate fixed point equation
