6 Rapid fixability for strict subsets of states and channels

In this section we prove for finite dimensional quantum systems rapid fixability of approximate fixed points in the sense of Definition 3.2 for a variety of choices 𝒮\mathcal{S} and 𝒞.\mathcal{C}. In particular, here we focus on 𝒮=𝔖⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{S}=\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}) the full set of quantum states and

  1. 1.

    𝒞\mathcal{C} being the set of unitary channels (Theorem 6.10),

  2. 2.

    𝒞\mathcal{C} being the set of mixed-unitary channels (Theorem 6.11),

  3. 3.

    𝒞\mathcal{C} being the set of unital channels (Theorem 6.13).

Furthermore, in Theorem 6.17 we show rapid fixiability of approximate fixed points for

  1. 4.

    𝒮\mathcal{S} being the set of pure states on some bipartite Hilbert space ℋA​B=ℋA⊗ℋB\mathcal{H}_{AB}=\mathcal{H}_{A}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{B} and 𝒞\mathcal{C} being the set of local channels of the form idA⊗𝒩B{\rm{id}}_{A}\otimes\mathcal{N}_{B} with 𝒩B∈CPTP⁡(ℋB).\mathcal{N}_{B}\in{\rm{CPTP}}(\mathcal{H}_{B}).

All these results rely on similar proof techniques, which is why we present them together in this section. For 𝒮\mathcal{S} and 𝒞\mathcal{C} being one of the choices above and an approximate fixed point equation

𝒩(ρ)≈ερ\displaystyle\mathcal{N}(\rho)\approx^{\varepsilon}\rho (6.1)

with ε≥0\varepsilon\geq 0 and ρ∈𝒮\rho\in\mathcal{S} and 𝒩∈𝒞,\mathcal{N}\in\mathcal{C}, we explicitly construct a fixed point pair σ∈𝒮\sigma\in\mathcal{S} and ℳ∈𝒞\mathcal{M}\in\mathcal{C} approximating the original state and channel. The focus lies on bounding the approximation errors in σ≈ρ\sigma\approx\rho and ℳ≈𝒩\mathcal{M}\approx\mathcal{N} and by that providing explicit forms of the approximation functions ff and gg from Definitions 3.1 and 3.2.

Notably, in the results of this section, the corresponding new state σ\sigma only depends on the original state ρ\rho and the approximation error ε\varepsilon but not on the channel 𝒩.\mathcal{N}. For the results 1-3 the choice of σ\sigma relies on spectral clustering techniques which we outline in Section 6.1 below. Here, spectral points of ρ,\rho, which are close to each other, get clustered together in such a way that the resulting state has significant spectral gaps between different eigenvalues. From the approximate fixed point equation (6.1) and a standard matrix analytic result for continuity of spectral subspaces under spectral gaps (see Lemma 6.1 below), we then see that the resulting spectral projections are in some sense approximate fixed points of the channel 𝒩\mathcal{N} as well. It then remains to fix named approximate fixed point equations for the spectral projections by changing the channel 𝒩\mathcal{N} to ℳ.\mathcal{M}. For that we establish in Section 6.2 a plethora of results, which we call rotation lemmas and which are concerned with the question of how to rotate two or more close-by subspaces onto each other.

For the result 4, instead of spectral clustering techniques, we define the new state by setting small Schmidt coefficients of the original pure state to zero. By that, similarly as due to the spectral gaps mentioned above, we find approximate fixed point equations for each the remaining Schmidt vectors. Using again a rotation lemma then enables us to find a close-by channel which has the new state as a fixed point.

The size of the spectral gaps or, in the case of result 4, the size of the neglected Schmidt-coefficients is parametrised by some

δ≫ε\displaystyle\delta\gg\varepsilon (6.2)

and relates to the approximation error of the state in σ≈ρ.\sigma\approx\rho. Choosing a smaller δ\delta leads to a better approximation of the state but worse approximation of the channel in ℳ≈𝒩\mathcal{M}\approx\mathcal{N} as the error in the above-mentioned approximate fixed point equations for the remaining spectral projections and Schmidt vectors becomes larger. The last step of all of the proofs in this section is then given by an optimisation over δ\delta in this trade-off to guarantee good approximation of both state and channel.

In the remainder of this section we first discuss named spectral clustering technique, then the rotation lemmas and conclude with the precise statements and proofs of the results 1  - 4.

6.1 Spectral clustering

In the following we discuss a technique to separate the spectrum of a quantum state into (spectral) clusters, such that spectral points within a cluster are close to each other whereas different clusters are far from another. This technique is then used for proving Theorems 6.10, 6.11 and 6.13.

Before discussing the spectral clustering technique, let us recall some well-known facts about the continuity of spectral points and spectral projections of self-adjoint operators on some dd-dimensional Hilbert space: For A1,A2A_{1},A_{2} being self-adjoint we have by [Bha97, Equation (IV.62)]2121 21 In fact in [Bha97, Equation (IV.62)] the inequality (6.3) is stated for all unitarily invariant norms. the inequality

‖spec→​(A1)−spec→​(A2)‖1≤‖A1−A2‖1,\displaystyle\left\|\overrightarrow{{\rm{spec}}}(A_{1})-\overrightarrow{{\rm{spec}}}(A_{2})\right\|_{1}\leq\left\|A_{1}-A_{2}\right\|_{1}, (6.3)

where we denoted by spec→​(Ai)\overrightarrow{{\rm{spec}}}(A_{i}) the vector containing the ordered spectral points of AiA_{i}. This can be seen as a continuity statement of the spectral points of self-adjoint operators.

Such a continuity statement does, however, not hold for the respective spectral projections. To see this consider as an example the family of operators defined for ε>0\varepsilon>0 by

A1(ε)≔(1+ε)2|0⟩⟨0|+(1−ε)2|1⟩⟨1|,A2(ε)≔(1+ε)2|+⟩⟨+|+(1−ε)2|−⟩⟨−|\displaystyle A_{1}(\varepsilon)\coloneqq\frac{(1+\varepsilon)}{2}|0\rangle\!\langle 0|+\frac{(1-\varepsilon)}{2}|1\rangle\!\langle 1|,\quad\quad A_{2}(\varepsilon)\coloneqq\frac{(1+\varepsilon)}{2}|+\rangle\!\langle+|+\frac{(1-\varepsilon)}{2}|-\rangle\!\langle-|

where {|0⟩,|1⟩}\{|0\rangle,|1\rangle\} denotes some ortonormal set, |+⟩≔(|0⟩+|1⟩)/2|+\rangle\coloneqq\left(|0\rangle+|1\rangle\right)/\sqrt{2} and |−⟩≔(|0⟩−|1⟩)/2.|-\rangle\coloneqq\left(|0\rangle-|1\rangle\right)/\sqrt{2}. It is easy to see that A1​(ε)A_{1}(\varepsilon) and A2​(ε)A_{2}(\varepsilon) are close as

‖A1​(ε)−A2​(ε)‖≤ε,\displaystyle\left\|A_{1}(\varepsilon)-A_{2}(\varepsilon)\right\|\leq\varepsilon,

whereas the corresponding spectral projections are far apart, i.e.

‖|0⟩⟨0|−|+⟩⟨+|‖=12,‖|1⟩⟨1|−|−⟩⟨−|‖=12.\displaystyle\left\||0\rangle\!\langle 0|\,-\,|+\rangle\!\langle+|\right\|=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},\quad\quad\left\||1\rangle\!\langle 1|\,-\,|-\rangle\!\langle-|\right\|=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.

Assuming, however, gaps in the spectrum of A1A_{1} and A2,A_{2}, it is well-known that some form continuity of spectral projections can be recovered. This is stated as Theorem VII.3.1 in [Bha97], which we recall in the following lemma.

Lemma 6.1 (Theorem VII.3.1 in [Bha97])

Let A1,A2A_{1},A_{2} be two self-adjoint operators on a dd-dimensional Hilbert space ℋ\mathcal{H} with spectral decompositions

A1=∑i=1dλi​|φi⟩​⟨φi|andA2=∑i=1dμi​|ψi⟩​⟨ψi|.\displaystyle A_{1}=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\lambda_{i}|\varphi_{i}\rangle\!\langle\varphi_{i}|\quad\text{and}\quad A_{2}=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\mu_{i}|\psi_{i}\rangle\!\langle\psi_{i}|. (6.4)

Let J⊆ℝJ\subseteq\mathbbm{R} be an interval separating parts of the spectrum of A1A_{1} and A2A_{2} respectively, i.e.

dist⁡(J∩spec⁡(Ai),Jc∩spec⁡(Ai))≥δ\displaystyle{\rm{dist}}(J\cap{{\rm{spec}}(A_{i})},J^{c}\cap{{\rm{spec}}(A_{i})})\geq\delta

for i=1,2i=1,2 and some δ>0.\delta>0. Then for the spectral projections of A1A_{1} and A2A_{2} given by

PA1​(J)≔∑i​ s.t. ​λi∈J|φi⟩​⟨φi|andPA2​(J)≔∑i​ s.t. ​μi∈J|ψi⟩​⟨ψi|\displaystyle P_{A_{1}}(J)\coloneqq\sum_{i\text{ s.t. }\lambda_{i}\in J}|\varphi_{i}\rangle\!\langle\varphi_{i}|\quad\text{and}\quad P_{A_{2}}(J)\coloneqq\sum_{i\text{ s.t. }\mu_{i}\in J}|\psi_{i}\rangle\!\langle\psi_{i}| (6.5)

we have2222 22 Note again that in [Bha97, Theorem VII.3.1] the inequality (6.6) is stated for all unitarily invariant norms but we only need it for the operator norm in the following.

‖PA1​(J)−PA2​(J)‖≤2​‖A1−A2‖δ.\displaystyle\left\|P_{A_{1}}(J)-P_{A_{2}}(J)\right\|\leq\frac{2\|A_{1}-A_{2}\|}{\delta}. (6.6)

Proof. The lemma follows by noting

‖PA1​(J)−PA2​(J)‖≤‖(𝟙−PA2​(J))​PA1​(J)‖+‖PA2​(J)​(𝟙−PA1​(J))‖≤2​‖A1−A2‖δ.\displaystyle\left\|P_{A_{1}}(J)-P_{A_{2}}(J)\right\|\leq\left\|(\mathbbm{1}-P_{A_{2}}(J))P_{A_{1}}(J)\right\|+\left\|P_{A_{2}}(J)(\mathbbm{1}-P_{A_{1}}(J))\right\|\leq\frac{2\|A_{1}-A_{2}\|}{\delta}.

where the last inequality is true due to Theorem VII.3.1 in [Bha97].  

The spectral clustering technique defined below is a way to ensure the existence of spectral gaps larger than δ\delta between two respective spectral clusters. We can hence combine it with Lemma 6.1 to provide continuity bounds for the spectral projections of the respective clusters.
Let us now introduce the spectral clustering technique: We write a state ρ\rho on a dd-dimensional Hilbert space ℋ\mathcal{H} in spectral decomposition

ρ=∑i=1mλi​πi,\displaystyle\rho=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_{i}\pi_{i},

with m∈[d]m\in[d], spectral points λ1>λ2>⋯>λn≥0\lambda_{1}>\lambda_{2}>\cdots>\lambda_{n}\geq 0 and (πi)i=1m\left(\pi_{i}\right)_{i=1}^{m} non-zero orthogonal projections summing to 𝟙\mathbbm{1}. For δ≥0\delta\geq 0 fixed, the idea is to cluster the spectral points in a way that each point of a cluster is δ\delta-close to the next one in the cluster and different clusters are separated from each other with distance strictly larger than δ.\delta. For that, to define the first cluster, let k1∈[d]k_{1}\in[d] be the smallest number such that

λk1−λk1+1>δ.\displaystyle\lambda_{k_{1}}-\lambda_{k_{1}+1}>\delta.

The first cluster is then defined as I1≔[k1]I_{1}\coloneqq[k_{1}] and consequently we have

λi−λi+1≤δ for all i∈I1.\displaystyle\lambda_{i}-\lambda_{i+1}\leq\delta\quad\text{ for all $i\in I_{1}$.}

By iterating the above, we obtain k1<k2<k3<⋯<kn∈[m−1]k_{1}<k_{2}<k_{3}<\cdots<k_{n}\in[m-1] such that klk_{l} is the lt​hl^{th} smallest number with

λkl−λkl+1>δ\displaystyle\lambda_{k_{l}}-\lambda_{k_{l}+1}>\delta (6.7)

and moreover knk_{n} is additionally also the largest number such that (6.7) occurs. The lt​hl^{th} cluster is then defined to be Il≔{kl−1+1,⋯,kl}I_{l}\coloneqq\{k_{l-1}+1,\cdots,k_{l}\} and by definition we have

λi−λi+1\displaystyle\lambda_{i}-\lambda_{i+1} ≤δ for all i∈Il and\displaystyle\leq\delta\quad\text{ for all $i\in I_{l}$ and}
|λi−λj|\displaystyle|\lambda_{i}-\lambda_{j}| >δ for all i∈Il,j∈Il′ with l≠l′.\displaystyle>\delta\quad\text{ for all $i\in I_{l},j\in I_{l^{\prime}}$ with $l\neq l^{\prime}.$} (6.8)

We then define for each cluster the corresponding spectral projection

El≔∑i∈Ilπi=∑i=kl−1+1klπi\displaystyle E_{l}\coloneqq\sum_{i\in I_{l}}\pi_{i}=\sum_{i=k_{l-1}+1}^{k_{l}}\pi_{i} (6.9)

and denote the average spectral point by

μl≔1Tr⁡(El)​∑i∈Ilλi​Tr​(πi)\displaystyle\mu_{l}\coloneqq\frac{1}{\mathrm{Tr}(E_{l})}\sum_{i\in I_{l}}\lambda_{i}\mathrm{Tr}(\pi_{i}) (6.10)

With that we can define a new quantum state

σ≔∑l=1nμl​El.\displaystyle\sigma\coloneqq\sum_{l=1}^{n}\mu_{l}E_{l}. (6.11)

Note that σ\sigma indeed defines a quantum state as positive semi-definiteness is immediate from the definition and normalisation follows by

Tr⁡(σ)=∑l=1mμl​Tr​(El)=∑l=1m∑i∈Ilλi​Tr​(πi)=Tr⁡(ρ)=1.\displaystyle\mathrm{Tr}(\sigma)=\sum_{l=1}^{m}\mu_{l}\mathrm{Tr}(E_{l})=\sum_{l=1}^{m}\sum_{i\in I_{l}}\lambda_{i}\mathrm{Tr}(\pi_{i})=\mathrm{Tr}(\rho)=1.

The following lemma shows that for δ\delta small, σ\sigma is a good approximation of ρ.\rho.

Lemma 6.2

Let ρ\rho be a state on dd-dimensional Hilbert space ℋ\mathcal{H} and δ≥0.\delta\geq 0. Denote by σ\sigma the state defined through the spectral clustering for ρ\rho and δ\delta as outlined above, i.e. (6.11). Then we have

12​‖ρ−σ‖1≤d2​δ2.\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left\|\rho-\sigma\right\|_{1}\leq\frac{d^{2}\delta}{2}. (6.12)

Proof. Note that by construction of the clustering (6.8), the averages μl\mu_{l} satisfy for all l∈[n]l\in[n] and i∈Ili\in I_{l}

|λi−μl|≤∑j∈IlTr⁡(πj)Tr⁡(El)​|λi−λj|≤∑j∈IlTr⁡(πj)Tr⁡(El)​|Il|​δ=|Il|​δ.\displaystyle|\lambda_{i}-\mu_{l}|\leq\sum_{j\in I_{l}}\frac{\mathrm{Tr}(\pi_{j})}{\mathrm{Tr}(E_{l})}|\lambda_{i}-\lambda_{j}|\leq\sum_{j\in I_{l}}\frac{\mathrm{Tr}(\pi_{j})}{\mathrm{Tr}(E_{l})}|I_{l}|\delta=|I_{l}|\delta.

By that we see

12​‖ρ−σ‖1\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left\|\rho-\sigma\right\|_{1} =12​‖∑l=1m∑i∈Il(λi−μl)​πi‖1≤12​∑l=1m∑i∈IlTr⁡(πi)​|λi−μl|\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\left\|\sum_{l=1}^{m}\sum_{i\in I_{l}}(\lambda_{i}-\mu_{l})\pi_{i}\right\|_{1}\leq\frac{1}{2}\sum_{l=1}^{m}\sum_{i\in I_{l}}\mathrm{Tr}(\pi_{i})|\lambda_{i}-\mu_{l}|
≤δ2​∑l=1m∑i∈IlTr⁡(πi)​|Il|≤d2​δ2,\displaystyle\leq\frac{\delta}{2}\sum_{l=1}^{m}\sum_{i\in I_{l}}\mathrm{Tr}(\pi_{i})|I_{l}|\leq\frac{d^{2}\delta}{2},

where we have used that ∑l=1n∑i∈IlTr⁡(πi)=d.\sum_{l=1}^{n}\sum_{i\in I_{l}}\mathrm{Tr}(\pi_{i})=d.  

6.2 Rotation lemmas

In this section we state and prove the rotation lemmas mentioned above, which are a main ingredient in the proofs of Theorems 6.10, 6.11, 6.13 and 6.17. All of the rotation lemmas are concerned with providing an unitary close to the identity which rotates nearby subspaces onto each other. To be more precise we find unitaries U≈𝟙U\approx\mathbbm{1} which in the case of

  1. 1.

    (|vi⟩)i=1n\left(|v_{i}\rangle\right)_{i=1}^{n} and (|wi⟩)i=1n\left(|w_{i}\rangle\right)_{i=1}^{n} being orthonormal systems with |vi⟩≈|wi⟩|v_{i}\rangle\approx|w_{i}\rangle satisfy U⁡|vi⟩=|wi⟩U|v_{i}\rangle=|w_{i}\rangle (Lemma 6.5),

  2. 2.

    (|ψi⟩)i=1n\left(|\psi_{i}\rangle\right)_{i=1}^{n} being an orthonormal system and FF being an orthogonal projection with F⁡|ψi⟩≈|ψi⟩F|\psi_{i}\rangle\approx|\psi_{i}\rangle satisfy U​|ψi⟩∈ran⁡(F)U|\psi_{i}\rangle\in\operatorname{ran}(F) (Lemma 6.6),

  3. 3.

    (Ei)i=1n\left(E_{i}\right)_{i=1}^{n} and (Fi)i=1n\left(F_{i}\right)_{i=1}^{n} being orthogonal projections with Ei≈FiE_{i}\approx F_{i} satisfy U​Ei​U∗=FiUE_{i}U^{*}=F_{i} (Lemma 6.7).

We first state and prove Lemmas 6.3 and 6.4, which are at the core of the proofs of the results mentioned above and then continue to show the rotation lemmas.

Lemma 6.3

Let AA be a linear operator and EE be a projection on some finite dimensional Hilbert space ℋ\mathcal{H} satisfying

‖A−E‖<1.\displaystyle\|A-E\|<1. (6.13)

Then dim(ran⁡(A))≥dim(ran⁡(E)).\dim(\operatorname{ran}(A))\geq\dim(\operatorname{ran}(E)). In particular, this gives by symmetry for EE and FF being projections, satisfying

‖E−F‖<1,\displaystyle\|E-F\|<1, (6.14)

that dim(ran⁡(E))=dim(ran⁡(F)).\dim(\operatorname{ran}(E))=\dim(\operatorname{ran}(F)).

Proof. We write dE=dim(ran⁡(E)).d_{E}=\dim(\operatorname{ran}(E)). Assume for contradiction dim(ran​(E))>dim(ran​(A))\dim(\text{ran}(E))>\dim(\text{ran}(A)) and take (φi)i=1dE\left(\varphi_{i}\right)_{i=1}^{d_{E}} to be a basis of ran​(E)\text{ran}(E). As (A​φi)i=1dE\left(A\varphi_{i}\right)_{i=1}^{d_{E}} cannot be linearly independent, there exists (λi)i=1dE≠0∈ℂdE(\lambda_{i})_{i=1}^{d_{E}}\neq 0\in\mathbb{C}^{d_{E}} such that for φ=∑i=1dEλi​φi≠0∈ℋ\varphi=\sum_{i=1}^{d_{E}}\lambda_{i}\varphi_{i}\neq 0\in\mathcal{H} we have A​ϕ=0A\phi=0. But this gives

‖E−A‖≥‖(E−A)​φ‖‖φ‖=‖E​φ‖‖φ‖=‖φ‖‖φ‖=1\displaystyle\|E-A\|\geq\frac{\|(E-A)\varphi\|}{\|\varphi\|}=\frac{\|E\varphi\|}{\|\varphi\|}=\frac{\|\varphi\|}{\|\varphi\|}=1

contradicting the assumption of the lemma and therefore giving dim(ran​(E))≤dim(ran​(A)).\dim(\text{ran}(E))\leq\dim(\text{ran}(A)).  

Lemma 6.4

Let EE and FF be orthogonal projections on some finite dimensional Hilbert space ℋ\mathcal{H} satisfying

‖E−F‖≤ε\displaystyle\|E-F\|\leq\varepsilon

for some 0≤ε<10\leq\varepsilon<1. Then there exists an unitary UU with ‖U−𝟙‖≤2​ε\|U-\mathbbm{1}\|\leq 2\varepsilon and

U​E​U∗=F.\displaystyle UEU^{*}=F. (6.15)

Proof. By assumption and Lemma 6.3 we have dim(ran⁡(E))=dim(ran⁡(F))\dim(\operatorname{ran}(E))=\dim(\operatorname{ran}(F)) and we write in the following dE=dim(ran⁡(E)).d_{E}=\dim(\operatorname{ran}(E)). Define now

A≔F​E+(𝟙−F)​(𝟙−E)\displaystyle A\coloneqq FE+(\mathbbm{1}-F)(\mathbbm{1}-E)

and note that

‖A−𝟙‖=‖(F−E)​E−(F−E)​(𝟙−E)‖=‖F−E‖≤ε,\displaystyle\|A-\mathbbm{1}\|=\|(F-E)E-(F-E)(\mathbbm{1}-E)\|=\|F-E\|\leq\varepsilon, (6.16)

where for the second equality we have used that 𝟙−2​E\mathbbm{1}-2E is unitary. By singular value decomposition (SVD) we can write

A=∑i=1dEai​|vi⟩​⟨wi|+∑i=dE+1dai​|vi⟩​⟨wi|\displaystyle A=\sum_{i=1}^{d_{E}}a_{i}|v_{i}\rangle\!\langle w_{i}|+\sum_{i=d_{E}+1}^{d}a_{i}|v_{i}\rangle\!\langle w_{i}| (6.17)

with ai≥0a_{i}\geq 0 being the singular values of AA and (|vi⟩)i=1dE\left(|v_{i}\rangle\right)_{i=1}^{d_{E}} and (|wi⟩)i=1dE\left(|w_{i}\rangle\right)_{i=1}^{d_{E}} being orthonormal bases of ran​(F)\text{ran}(F) and ran​(E)\text{ran}(E) respectively and (|vi⟩)i=dE+1d\left(|v_{i}\rangle\right)_{i=d_{E}+1}^{d} and (|wi⟩)i=dE+1d\left(|w_{i}\rangle\right)_{i=d_{E}+1}^{d} being orthonormal bases of ran​(𝟙−F)\text{ran}(\mathbbm{1}-F) and ran​(𝟙−E)\text{ran}(\mathbbm{1}-E) respectively. That the SVD of AA has this form follows by block diagonality of AA or equivalently by considering SVDs of F​EFE and (𝟙−F)​(𝟙−E)(\mathbbm{1}-F)(\mathbbm{1}-E) individually leading to the first and second summand in (6.17).

Denoting the smallest singular value of AA by ai′a_{i^{\prime}} we find

ε≥‖A−𝟙‖\displaystyle\varepsilon\geq\|A-\mathbbm{1}\| ≥‖ai′​|vi′⟩−|wi′⟩‖=ai′2+1−2​ai′​ℜ⁡⟨vi′,wi′⟩≥ai′2+1−2​ai′\displaystyle\geq\|a_{i^{\prime}}|v_{i^{\prime}}\rangle-|w_{i^{\prime}}\rangle\|=\sqrt{a^{2}_{i^{\prime}}+1-2a_{i^{\prime}}\Re\langle v_{i^{\prime}},w_{i^{\prime}}\rangle}\geq\sqrt{a^{2}_{i^{\prime}}+1-2a_{i^{\prime}}}
=1−ai′=maxi=1,…,d⁡|1−ai|,\displaystyle=1-a_{i^{\prime}}=\max_{i=1,\dots,d}|1-a_{i}|,

where we have used in the second line that ai≤1a_{i}\leq 1 for all i=1,…,di=1,\dots,d which holds since A∗​A=E​F​E+(𝟙−E)​(𝟙−F)​(𝟙−E)≤𝟙.A^{*}A=EFE+(\mathbbm{1}-E)(\mathbbm{1}-F)(\mathbbm{1}-E)\leq\mathbbm{1}. Define now the unitary

U=∑i=1d|vi⟩​⟨wi|.\displaystyle U=\sum_{i=1}^{d}|v_{i}\rangle\!\langle w_{i}|.

By the above we have

‖U−𝟙‖≤‖U−A‖+‖A−𝟙‖=maxi=1,…,d⁡|ai−1|+|A−𝟙|≤2​ε.\displaystyle\|U-\mathbbm{1}\|\leq\|U-A\|+\|A-\mathbbm{1}\|=\max_{i=1,\dots,d}|a_{i}-1|+\|A-\mathbbm{1}\|\leq 2\varepsilon. (6.18)

Moreover, by construction we have U​E​U∗=FUEU^{*}=F.  

We now state and prove the the rotations lemmas mentioned in points 1-3 above.

Lemma 6.5

Let (|vi⟩)i=1n\left(|v_{i}\rangle\right)_{i=1}^{n} and (|wi⟩)i=1n\left(|w_{i}\rangle\right)_{i=1}^{n} be orthonormal systems on some finite dimensional Hilbert space ℋ\mathcal{H} such that

‖|vi⟩−|wi⟩‖≤ε\displaystyle\||v_{i}\rangle-|w_{i}\rangle\|\leq\varepsilon

for some ε≥0\varepsilon\geq 0. Then there exists an unitary UU such that ‖U−𝟙‖≤5​n​ε\|U-\mathbbm{1}\|\leq 5\sqrt{n}\,\varepsilon and

U⁡|vi⟩=|wi⟩\displaystyle U|v_{i}\rangle=|w_{i}\rangle (6.19)

for all i∈[n].i\in[n].

Proof. Define the orthogonal projections E=∑i=1n|vi⟩​⟨vi|E=\sum_{i=1}^{n}|v_{i}\rangle\!\langle v_{i}| and F=∑i=1n|wi⟩​⟨wi|F=\sum_{i=1}^{n}|w_{i}\rangle\!\langle w_{i}| and note that they satisfy

‖E−F‖≤‖∑i=1n(|vi⟩−|wi⟩)​⟨vi|‖+‖∑i=1n(|vi⟩−|wi⟩)​⟨wi|‖≤2​ε​n,\displaystyle\left\|E-F\right\|\leq\left\|\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(|v_{i}\rangle-|w_{i}\rangle\right)\!\langle v_{i}|\right\|+\left\|\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(|v_{i}\rangle-|w_{i}\rangle\right)\!\langle w_{i}|\right\|\leq 2\varepsilon\sqrt{n}, (6.20)

where we used the triangle inequality, the ∗*-invariance of the operator norm and for the last inequality

‖∑i=1n(|vi⟩−|wi⟩)​⟨vi|‖≤sup‖ψ‖=1∑i=1n‖|vi⟩−|wi⟩‖​|⟨vi,ψ⟩|≤ε​n​sup‖ψ‖=1∑i=1n|⟨vi,ψ⟩|2≤ε​n,\displaystyle\left\|\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(|v_{i}\rangle-|w_{i}\rangle\right)\!\langle v_{i}|\right\|\leq\sup_{\|\psi\|=1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left\||v_{i}\rangle-|w_{i}\rangle\right\||\langle v_{i},\psi\rangle|\leq\varepsilon\sqrt{n}\sup_{\|\psi\|=1}\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n}|\langle v_{i},\psi\rangle|^{2}}\leq\varepsilon\sqrt{n},

which follows by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality and similarly for the second term in (6.20). Hence, by Lemma 6.4 there exists an unitary U1U_{1} such that ‖U1−𝟙‖≤4​ε​n\|U_{1}-\mathbbm{1}\|\leq 4\varepsilon\sqrt{n} and

U1​E​U1∗=F.\displaystyle U_{1}EU_{1}^{*}=F.

Furthermore, we define the partial isometry

U2=∑i=1n|wi⟩​⟨vi|\displaystyle U_{2}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}|w_{i}\rangle\!\langle v_{i}|

with support ran⁡(E)\operatorname{ran}(E) and image ran⁡(F).\operatorname{ran}(F). Clearly U2​|vi⟩=|wi⟩U_{2}|v_{i}\rangle=|w_{i}\rangle. Moreover,

‖U2−E‖\displaystyle\|U_{2}-E\| =sup‖ψ‖=1‖(U2−E)​|ψ⟩‖≤sup‖ψ‖=1∑i=1n‖|wi⟩−|vi⟩‖​|⟨vi,ψ⟩|≤ε​n.\displaystyle=\sup_{\|\psi\|=1}\|(U_{2}-E)|\psi\rangle\|\leq\sup_{\|\psi\|=1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left\||w_{i}\rangle-|v_{i}\rangle\right\||\langle v_{i},\psi\rangle|\leq\varepsilon\sqrt{n}.

We can now define

U=U2⊕U1​(𝟙−E),\displaystyle U=U_{2}\oplus U_{1}(\mathbbm{1}-E),

which is unitary since U1​(𝟙−E)U_{1}(\mathbbm{1}-E) is a partial isometry with support ran⁡(𝟙−E)\operatorname{ran}(\mathbbm{1}-E) and image ran⁡(𝟙−F).\operatorname{ran}(\mathbbm{1}-F). Furthermore, it satisfies U⁡|vi⟩=|wi⟩U|v_{i}\rangle=|w_{i}\rangle and

‖U−𝟙|≤‖U2−E‖+‖U1−𝟙‖≤5εn.\displaystyle\left\|U-\mathbbm{1}\right|\leq\left\|U_{2}-E\right\|+\left\|U_{1}-\mathbbm{1}\right\|\leq 5\varepsilon\sqrt{n}.

 

Lemma 6.6

Let (|ψi⟩)i=1n\left(|\psi_{i}\rangle\right)_{i=1}^{n} be an orthonormal system and FF be some orthogonal projection on some finite dimensional Hilbert space ℋ\mathcal{H} satisfying

∑l=1n‖(𝟙−F)​|ψi⟩‖2≤ε.\displaystyle\sqrt{\sum_{l=1}^{n}\left\|(\mathbbm{1}-F)|\psi_{i}\rangle\right\|^{2}}\leq\varepsilon. (6.21)

for some 0≤ε<10\leq\varepsilon<1 and all i∈[n].i\in[n]. Then there exists an unitary UU such that ‖U−𝟙‖≤2​ε\|U-\mathbbm{1}\|\leq 2\,\varepsilon and

F​U​|ψi⟩=U⁡|ψi⟩\displaystyle FU|\psi_{i}\rangle=U|\psi_{i}\rangle (6.22)

for all i∈[n].i\in[n]. In particular if

F|ψi⟩≈ε|ψi⟩\displaystyle F|\psi_{i}\rangle\approx^{\varepsilon}|\psi_{i}\rangle (6.23)

for some 0≤ε<1/n,0\leq\varepsilon<1/\sqrt{n}, then there exists an unitary UU such that ‖U−𝟙‖≤2​n​ε\|U-\mathbbm{1}\|\leq 2\sqrt{n}\,\varepsilon satisfying (6.22).

Proof. We define the orthogonal projection E=∑i=1n|ψi⟩​⟨ψi|E=\sum_{i=1}^{n}|\psi_{i}\rangle\!\langle\psi_{i}|. Note that we have by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality and assumption (6.21)

‖E−F​E‖\displaystyle\|E-FE\| =‖(𝟙−F)​E‖≤sup‖ψ‖=1∑i=1n‖(𝟙−F)​|ψi⟩‖​|⟨ψi,ψ⟩|\displaystyle=\|(\mathbbm{1}-F)E\|\leq\sup_{\|\psi\|=1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\|(\mathbbm{1}-F)|\psi_{i}\rangle\|\,|\langle\psi_{i},\psi\rangle|
≤ε​sup‖ψ‖=1∑i=1n|⟨ψi,ψ⟩|2≤ε<1.\displaystyle\leq\varepsilon\sup_{\|\psi\|=1}\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n}|\langle\psi_{i},\psi\rangle|^{2}}\leq\varepsilon<1.

Using now Lemma 6.3 we see dim(ran⁡(F​E))≥dim(E)\dim(\operatorname{ran}(FE))\geq\dim(E) and since the opposite inequality holds trivially we have dim(ran⁡(F​E))=dim(E).\dim(\operatorname{ran}(FE))=\dim(E). Let now F′F^{\prime} be the orthogonal projection onto ran​(F​E)\text{ran}(FE) and note that it satisfies F′=F′​FF^{\prime}=F^{\prime}F and hence F′​E=F′​F​E=F​EF^{\prime}E=F^{\prime}FE=FE. Since, as established dim(ran⁡(F′))=dim(ran⁡(F​E))=dim(ran⁡(E))\dim(\operatorname{ran}(F^{\prime}))=\dim(\operatorname{ran}(FE))=\dim(\operatorname{ran}(E)), F′F^{\prime} and EE are unitarily equivalent and hence also

‖F′​(𝟙−E)‖=‖(𝟙−E)​F′‖=‖(𝟙−F′)​E‖=‖(𝟙−F)​E‖≤ε.\displaystyle\|F^{\prime}(\mathbbm{1}-E)\|=\|(\mathbbm{1}-E)F^{\prime}\|=\|(\mathbbm{1}-F^{\prime})E\|=\|(\mathbbm{1}-F)E\|\leq\varepsilon.

Therefore, using orthogonality, we have

‖E−F′‖=‖(𝟙−F′)​E+F′​(E−𝟙)‖=max⁡{‖F′​(𝟙−E)‖,‖(𝟙−F′)​E‖}≤ε.\displaystyle\|E-F^{\prime}\|=\|(\mathbbm{1}-F^{\prime})E+F^{\prime}(E-\mathbbm{1})\|=\max\Big\{\|F^{\prime}(\mathbbm{1}-E)\|,\|(\mathbbm{1}-F^{\prime})E\|\Big\}\leq\varepsilon.

Hence, using now Lemma 6.4 again, there exists an unitary UU satisfying ‖U−𝟙‖≤2​ε\|U-\mathbbm{1}\|\leq 2\varepsilon and U​E​U∗=F′UEU^{*}=F^{\prime}, which gives

F​U​|ψi⟩=F​U​E​|ψi⟩=F​F′​U​|ψi⟩=F′​U​|ψi⟩=U​E​|ψi⟩=U⁡|ψi⟩.\displaystyle FU|\psi_{i}\rangle=FUE|\psi_{i}\rangle=FF^{\prime}U|\psi_{i}\rangle=F^{\prime}U|\psi_{i}\rangle=UE|\psi_{i}\rangle=U|\psi_{i}\rangle.

For the statement under the assumption (6.23), we simply use that in this case

∑l=1n‖(𝟙−F)​|ψi⟩‖2≤∑l=1nε2=n​ε<1\displaystyle\sqrt{\sum_{l=1}^{n}\left\|(\mathbbm{1}-F)|\psi_{i}\rangle\right\|^{2}}\leq\sqrt{\sum_{l=1}^{n}\varepsilon^{2}}=\sqrt{n}\varepsilon<1

and apply the first part of the lemma.  

Lemma 6.7

Let (El)l=1n\left(E_{l}\right)_{l=1}^{n} and (Fl)l=1n\left(F_{l}\right)_{l=1}^{n} be families of orthogonal projections on some dd-dimensional Hilbert space ℋ\mathcal{H} with n∈[d]n\in[d] satisfying ∑l=1nEl≤𝟙\sum_{l=1}^{n}E_{l}\leq\mathbbm{1}, ∑l=1nFl≤𝟙\sum_{l=1}^{n}F_{l}\leq\mathbbm{1} and

‖El−Fl‖≤ε\displaystyle\|E_{l}-F_{l}\|\leq\varepsilon

for some 0≤ε<10\leq\varepsilon<1 and all l∈[n]l\in[n]. Then there exists an unitary UU with ‖U−𝟙‖≤6​ε​n.\|U-\mathbbm{1}\|\leq 6\varepsilon\sqrt{n}. and

U​El​U∗=Fl\displaystyle UE_{l}U^{*}=F_{l} (6.24)

for all l∈[n].l\in[n].

Proof. Using for each l∈[n]l\in[n] the Lemma 6.4 individually, we find unitaries UlU_{l} with ‖Ul−𝟙‖≤2​ε\|U_{l}-\mathbbm{1}\|\leq 2\varepsilon and

Ul​El​Ul∗=Fl.\displaystyle U_{l}E_{l}U_{l}^{*}=F_{l}.

We can now define the partial isometries Vl=Ul​ElV_{l}=U_{l}E_{l} with support ran⁡(El)\operatorname{ran}(E_{l}) and image ran⁡(Fl)\operatorname{ran}(F_{l}), which by the above satisfy ‖Vl−El‖≤2​ε.\|V_{l}-E_{l}\|\leq 2\varepsilon. We denote E=∑l=1nElE=\sum_{l=1}^{n}E_{l} and F=∑l=1nFlF=\sum_{l=1}^{n}F_{l} and define

V=⨁l=1nUl,\displaystyle V=\bigoplus_{l=1}^{n}U_{l},

which by construction is also a partial isometry with support ran⁡(E)\operatorname{ran}(E) and image ran⁡(F)\operatorname{ran}(F). Furthermore, note that we have

‖V−E‖\displaystyle\|V-E\| ≤sup‖ψ‖=1∑l=1n‖(Ul−El)​ψ‖≤2​ε​sup‖ψ‖=1∑l=1n‖El​ψ‖\displaystyle\leq\sup_{\|\psi\|=1}\sum_{l=1}^{n}\left\|(U_{l}-E_{l})\psi\right\|\leq 2\varepsilon\sup_{\|\psi\|=1}\sum_{l=1}^{n}\left\|E_{l}\psi\right\|
≤2​ε​n​sup‖ψ‖=1∑l=1n‖El​ψ‖2≤2​ε​n,\displaystyle\leq 2\varepsilon\sqrt{n}\sup_{\|\psi\|=1}\sqrt{\sum_{l=1}^{n}\left\|E_{l}\psi\right\|^{2}}\leq 2\varepsilon\sqrt{n},

where for the second line we used the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality and then Pythagorean identity. This gives

‖(𝟙−F)−(𝟙−E)‖=‖F−E‖=‖V​E​V∗−E‖≤2​‖V−E‖≤4​ε​n.\displaystyle\left\|(\mathbbm{1}-F)-(\mathbbm{1}-E)\right\|=\left\|F-E\right\|=\left\|VEV^{*}-E\right\|\leq 2\|V-E\|\leq 4\varepsilon\sqrt{n}.

Hence, applying Lemma 6.4 again for 𝟙−E\mathbbm{1}-E and 𝟙−F,\mathbbm{1}-F, we find another unitary U⟂U_{\perp} which satisfies

‖U⟂−𝟙‖≤4​ε​n\displaystyle\|U_{\perp}-\mathbbm{1}\|\leq 4\varepsilon\sqrt{n}

and U⟂​(𝟙−E)​U⟂∗=𝟙−F.U_{\perp}(\mathbbm{1}-E)U_{\perp}^{*}=\mathbbm{1}-F. Analogously to the above we define the partial isometry V⟂=U⟂​(𝟙−E)V_{\perp}=U_{\perp}(\mathbbm{1}-E), which has support ran⁡(𝟙−E)\operatorname{ran}(\mathbbm{1}-E) and image ran⁡(𝟙−F)\operatorname{ran}(\mathbbm{1}-F), and then finally the unitary

U=V⊕V⟂.\displaystyle U=V\oplus V_{\perp}.

Note that by construction, UU satisfies U​El​U∗=FlUE_{l}U^{*}=F_{l} for all l∈[n]l\in[n] and furthermore

‖U−𝟙‖≤‖V−E‖+‖(U⟂−𝟙)​(𝟙−E)‖≤6​ε​n.\displaystyle\left\|U-\mathbbm{1}\right\|\leq\left\|V-E\right\|+\|(U_{\perp}-\mathbbm{1})(\mathbbm{1}-E)\|\leq 6\varepsilon\sqrt{n}.

 

Another useful observation which is used in the proofs of the results below is that two channels with Stinespring isometries being close to each other in operator norm, are close to each other in diamond norm. This fact is stated and proved in the following lemma for later convenience.

Lemma 6.8

Let V:ℋA→ℋB⊗ℋEV:\mathcal{H}_{A}\to\mathcal{H}_{B}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{E} and W:ℋA→ℋB⊗ℋEW:\mathcal{H}_{A}\to\mathcal{H}_{B}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{E} be isometries on Hilbert spaces satisfying

‖V−W‖≤ε\displaystyle\|V-W\|\leq\varepsilon (6.25)

for ε≥0\varepsilon\geq 0. Then, defining the quantum channels 𝒩=TrE​(V⁡(⋅)​V∗)\mathcal{N}=\mathrm{Tr}_{E}(V(\,\cdot\,)V^{*}) and ℳ=TrE​(W⁡(⋅)​W∗)\mathcal{M}=\mathrm{Tr}_{E}(W(\,\cdot\,)W^{*}), we have

12​‖𝒩−ℳ‖⋄≤ε.\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left\|\mathcal{N}-\mathcal{M}\right\|_{\diamond}\leq\varepsilon. (6.26)

Proof. Using the definition of the diamond norm, monotonicity of the trace norm under under the partial trace and Hölder’s inequality we find

‖𝒩−ℳ‖⋄\displaystyle\left\|\mathcal{N}-\mathcal{M}\right\|_{\diamond} =supd∈ℕ,x∈𝒯⁡(ℋ⊗ℂd)​‖x‖1=1‖TrE​(V​x​V∗)−TrE​(W​x​W∗)‖1\displaystyle=\sup_{d\in\mathbb{N},x\in\mathcal{T}(\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathbb{C}^{d})\,\|x\|_{1}=1}\left\|\mathrm{Tr}_{E}(VxV^{*})-\mathrm{Tr}_{E}(WxW^{*})\right\|_{1}
≤supd∈ℕ,x∈𝒯⁡(ℋ⊗ℂd)​‖x‖1=1‖V​x​V∗−W​x​W∗‖1\displaystyle\leq\sup_{d\in\mathbb{N},x\in\mathcal{T}(\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathbb{C}^{d})\,\|x\|_{1}=1}\left\|VxV^{*}-WxW^{*}\right\|_{1}
≤supd∈ℕ,x∈𝒯⁡(ℋ⊗ℂd)​‖x‖1=1‖(V−W)​x​V∗‖1+supd∈ℕ,x∈𝒯⁡(ℋ⊗ℂd)​‖x‖1=1‖W​x​(V∗−W∗)‖1\displaystyle\leq\sup_{d\in\mathbb{N},x\in\mathcal{T}(\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathbb{C}^{d})\,\|x\|_{1}=1}\left\|(V-W)xV^{*}\right\|_{1}+\sup_{d\in\mathbb{N},x\in\mathcal{T}(\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathbb{C}^{d})\,\|x\|_{1}=1}\left\|Wx(V^{*}-W^{*})\right\|_{1}
≤2​‖V−W‖≤2​ε,\displaystyle\leq 2\|V-W\|\leq 2\varepsilon,

where we dropped the identities idd{\rm{id}}_{d} for notational simplicity.  

6.3 Generalised depolarising trick

In this section we establish the generalised depolarising trick (Lemma 6.9 below), which is a useful tool for fixing approximate fixed point equations in the sense of Definitions 3.1 and 3.2 and is employed in the proof of Theorem 6.13.

We consider two states σ\sigma and σ′\sigma^{\prime} which satisfy the operator inequality

σ′≤(1+p)​σ\displaystyle\sigma^{\prime}\leq(1+p)\sigma (6.27)

for some p∈[0,1].p\in[0,1]. The main observation is then that we can find a generalised depolarising channel of the form

Φ=(1−p)​id+p​Tr​(⋅)​ω\displaystyle\Phi=(1-p){\rm{id}}+p\mathrm{Tr}(\,\cdot\,)\,\omega (6.28)

for some state ω,\omega, which ‘pulls back’ σ′\sigma^{\prime} onto σ,\sigma, i.e. Φ⁡(σ′)=σ.\Phi(\sigma^{\prime})=\sigma. Furthermore, by the explicit form of (6.28) it is immediate to see that Φ≈pid.\Phi\approx^{p}{\rm{id}}. In the context of an approximate fixed point equation 𝒩⁡(σ)≈σ\mathcal{N}(\sigma)\approx\sigma we can take σ′=𝒩⁡(σ).\sigma^{\prime}=\mathcal{N}(\sigma). Hence, if (6.27) is satisfied we can define ℳ=Φ∘𝒩\mathcal{M}=\Phi\circ\mathcal{N} which has σ\sigma as an exact fixed point and is close to 𝒩,\mathcal{N}, i.e. ℳ≈p𝒩.\mathcal{M}\approx^{p}\mathcal{N}. For an illustration of the generalised depolarising trick consider Figure 1.

We now state and prove the generalised depolarising trick in the following lemma. In fact, we not just only prove it for single states σ′\sigma^{\prime} and σ\sigma but for families, as this the context in which it is employed in the proof of Theorem 6.13 below.

Lemma 6.9 (Generalised depolarising trick)

Let (σi)i=1n\left(\sigma_{i}\right)_{i=1}^{n} and (σi′)i=1n\left(\sigma^{\prime}_{i}\right)_{i=1}^{n} be families of states on a separable Hilbert space ℋ\mathcal{H} satisfying

σi′≤(1+p)​σi\displaystyle\sigma^{\prime}_{i}\leq(1+p)\sigma_{i} (6.29)

for some p∈[0,1]p\in[0,1] and all i∈[n].i\in[n]. Furthermore, assume that σi′\sigma^{\prime}_{i} and σj′\sigma^{\prime}_{j} have orthogonal support for i≠j.i\neq j. Then there exists a channel

Φ≈pid\displaystyle\Phi\approx^{p}{\rm{id}} (6.30)

such that

Φ⁡(σi′)=σi,\displaystyle\Phi(\sigma^{\prime}_{i})=\sigma_{i}, (6.31)

for all i∈[n].i\in[n].

Proof. Without loss of generality assume p>0p>0 as otherwise σi′=σi\sigma^{\prime}_{i}=\sigma_{i} holds true immediately. Note that by assumption σi−(1−p)​σi′≥0\sigma_{i}-(1-p)\sigma^{\prime}_{i}\geq 0, which follows trivially for p=1p=1 and otherwise by

σi−(1−p)​σi′=(1−p)​(11−p​σi−σi′)≥(1−p)​((1+p)​σi−σi′)≥0.\displaystyle\sigma_{i}-(1-p)\sigma_{i}^{\prime}=(1-p)\left(\frac{1}{1-p}\sigma_{i}-\sigma_{i}^{\prime}\right)\geq(1-p)\Big((1+p)\sigma_{i}-\sigma_{i}^{\prime}\Big)\geq 0.

Hence, we can define the normalised state

ωi≔σi−(1−p)​σi′p.\omega_{i}\coloneqq\frac{\sigma_{i}-(1-p)\sigma_{i}^{\prime}}{p}.

Furthermore, since σi′\sigma^{\prime}_{i} and σj′\sigma^{\prime}_{j} have orthogonal support for i≠ji\neq j, there exists a family of orthogonal projections (πi)i=1n\left(\pi_{i}\right)_{i=1}^{n} such that ∑i=1nπi=𝟙\sum_{i=1}^{n}\pi_{i}=\mathbbm{1} and

πi​σj′​πi=δi​j​σj′,\displaystyle\pi_{i}\sigma_{j}^{\prime}\pi_{i}=\delta_{ij}\sigma^{\prime}_{j},

with δi​j\delta_{ij} denoting the Kronecker delta. With that we can now define the quantum channel

Φ⁡(⋅)≔(1−p)​id+p​∑i=1nTr⁡(πi​(⋅)​πi)​ωi.\displaystyle\Phi(\,\cdot\,)\coloneqq(1-p){\rm{id}}+p\sum_{i=1}^{n}\,\mathrm{Tr}(\pi_{i}(\,\cdot\,)\pi_{i})\,\omega_{i}.

Note, by the triangle inequality and the fact that every quantum channel has diamond norm equal to 1, we see

12​‖Φ−id‖⋄≤p2​(‖id‖⋄+‖∑i=1nTr⁡(πi​(⋅)​πi)​ωi‖⋄)=p.\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left\|\Phi-{\rm{id}}\right\|_{\diamond}\leq\frac{p}{2}\left(\left\|{\rm{id}}\right\|_{\diamond}+\left\|\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathrm{Tr}(\pi_{i}(\,\cdot\,)\pi_{i})\,\omega_{i}\right\|_{\diamond}\right)=p.

Moreover, by definition we have for all i∈[n]i\in[n]

Φ⁡(σi′)=(1−p)​σi′+p​∑j=1nTr⁡(πj​σi′​πj)​ωj=(1−p)​σi′+σi−(1−p)​σi′=σi,\displaystyle\Phi(\sigma_{i}^{\prime})=(1-p)\sigma_{i}^{\prime}+p\sum_{j=1}^{n}\mathrm{Tr}\left(\pi_{j}\sigma^{\prime}_{i}\pi_{j}\right)\omega_{j}=(1-p)\sigma_{i}^{\prime}+\sigma_{i}-(1-p)\sigma_{i}^{\prime}=\sigma_{i},

which finishes the proof.  

6.4 Unitary channels

Theorem 6.10 below shows rapid fixiability of approximate fixed point equations in the sense of Definition 3.2 for 𝒮=𝔖⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{S}=\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}) and 𝒞\mathcal{C} being the set of unitary channels on ℋ:\mathcal{H}:

Theorem 6.10 (Fixability for unitary channels)

Let ρ\rho be a state and UU an unitary on a dd-dimensional Hilbert space ℋ\mathcal{H} such that for ε≥0\varepsilon\geq 0 we have

Then there exist a state σ\sigma and an unitary VV satisfying

σ≈4​d5/4​ερ,V≈4​d5/4​εU\displaystyle\sigma\approx^{4\,d^{5/4}\sqrt{\varepsilon}}\rho,\quad\quad V\approx^{4\,d^{5/4}\sqrt{\varepsilon}}U (6.33)

and

V​σ​V∗=σ.\displaystyle V\sigma V^{*}=\sigma. (6.34)

Furthermore, the state σ\sigma is independent of U.U.

The proof of Theorem 6.10 can be outlined as follows: First we use the technique discussed in Section 6.1 to find spectral clusters of the state ρ\rho separated by spectral gaps. Using Lemma 6.1, we know that the spectral projections of each of these clusters and their rotated versions under the unitary UU are close to each other due to the spectral gaps and the approximate fixed point equation (6.32). Therefore, by the rotation lemma 6.7, we can find an unitary close to the identity which rotates them back. The composition of this new unitary and the original unitary then defines the new unitary channel. Furthermore, we take as the new state the one defined through spectral clustering in (6.11). Both new state and channel are close to the original ones and furthermore satisfy an exact fixed point equation.

Proof of Theorem 6.10. We employ the spectral clustering technique outlined in Section 6.1 for ρ\rho and δ≥0\delta\geq 0 to be determined later. In particular the spectrum of ρ\rho is separated into nn clusters such that spectral points from different clusters are at least δ\delta far from each other.
We denote the spectral projections of the llth spectral cluster defined in (6.9) by ElE_{l} and the rotated projection by

Fl=U​El​U∗.\displaystyle F_{l}=UE_{l}U^{*}. (6.35)

By construction, in particular the seperation of spectral points established in (6.8), together with Lemma 6.1 we have for all l∈[n]l\in[n]

‖El−Fl‖≤2​‖ρ−U​ρ​U∗‖δ≤2​‖ρ−U​ρ​U∗‖1δ≤4​εδ.\displaystyle\left\|E_{l}-F_{l}\right\|\leq\frac{2\|\rho-U\rho U^{*}\|}{\delta}\leq\frac{2\|\rho-U\rho U^{*}\|_{1}}{\delta}\leq\frac{4\varepsilon}{\delta}.

Using now Lemma 6.7 we see that there exists an unitary U′U^{\prime} such that ‖U′−𝟙‖≤24​ε​n/δ\|U^{\prime}-\mathbbm{1}\|\leq 24\varepsilon\sqrt{n}/\delta and for all l∈[n]l\in[n]

U′​Fl​U′⁣∗=El.\displaystyle U^{\prime}F_{l}U^{\prime*}=E_{l}.

Moreover, define V=U′​UV=U^{\prime}U which satisfies

‖V−U‖=‖U′−𝟙‖≤24​ε​nδ≤24​ε​dδ.\displaystyle\left\|V-U\right\|=\|U^{\prime}-\mathbbm{1}\|\leq\frac{24\varepsilon\sqrt{n}}{\delta}\leq\frac{24\varepsilon\sqrt{d}}{\delta}.

Considering the state defined in (6.11), i.e.

σ=∑l=1nμl​El\displaystyle\sigma=\sum_{l=1}^{n}\mu_{l}E_{l}

where μl\mu_{l} is the average of the spectral point of the llth cluster defined in (6.10), we see that σ\sigma is a fixed point of the unitary channel associated with VV:

V​σ​V∗=∑l=1nμl​U′​U​El​U∗​U′⁣∗=∑l=1nμl​U′​Fl​U′⁣∗=∑l=1nμl​El=σ.\displaystyle V\sigma V^{*}=\sum_{l=1}^{n}\mu_{l}\,U^{\prime}UE_{l}U^{*}U^{\prime*}=\sum_{l=1}^{n}\mu_{l}\,U^{\prime}F_{l}U^{\prime*}=\sum_{l=1}^{n}\mu_{l}E_{l}=\sigma.

Furthermore, by Lemma 6.2 we know

Picking now

gives

‖U−V‖\displaystyle\left\|U-V\right\| ≤4​d5/4​ε,\displaystyle\leq 4\,d^{5/4}\sqrt{\varepsilon},

which finishes the proof. Furthermore, note that the state σ\sigma solely depends on ρ\rho as outlined in Section 6.1 but not on the unitary U.U.

 

6.5 Mixed-unitary channels

In the following we consider 𝒞\mathcal{C} to be the set of mixed-unitary channels on some dd-dimensional Hilbert space ℋ\mathcal{H}. More precisely, this means

𝒞=conv⁡{𝒰}≔conv⁡{𝒰|𝒰⁡(⋅)=U⁡(⋅)​U∗​with U unitary},\displaystyle\mathcal{C}={\rm{conv}}\!\left\{\mathcal{U}\right\}\coloneqq{\rm{conv}}\left\{\mathcal{U}\,\Big|\,\mathcal{U}(\,\cdot\,)=U(\,\cdot\,)U^{*}\ \text{with $U$ unitary}\right\},

where conv{\rm{conv}} denotes taking the convex hull. From Proposition 4.9 in [Wat18], which is a consequence of Caratheodory’s theorem [Car11], we see that for every 𝒩∈conv​{𝒰}\mathcal{N}\in{\rm{conv}}\!\left\{\mathcal{U}\right\} there exists a probability vector (pi)i=1d4∈ℝd4\left(p_{i}\right)_{i=1}^{d^{4}}\in\mathbbm{R}^{d^{4}} and unitaries (Ui)i=1d4(U_{i})_{i=1}^{d^{4}} on ℋ\mathcal{H} such that

𝒩⁡(ρ)=∑i=1d4pi​Ui​ρ​Ui∗\displaystyle\mathcal{N}(\rho)=\sum_{i=1}^{d^{4}}p_{i}\,U_{i}\rho U_{i}^{*} (6.36)

for all states ρ.\rho.

Theorem 6.11 shows rapid fixiability of approximate fixed point equations in the sense of Definition 3.2 for 𝒮=𝔖⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{S}=\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}) and 𝒞=conv​{𝒰}:\mathcal{C}={\rm{conv}}\!\left\{\mathcal{U}\right\}:

Theorem 6.11 (Fixability for mixed-unitary channels)

Let ρ\rho be a state and 𝒩∈conv​{𝒰}\mathcal{N}\in{\rm{conv}}\!\left\{\mathcal{U}\right\} on a dd-dimensional Hilbert space ℋ\mathcal{H} such that for ε≥0\varepsilon\geq 0 we have

𝒩(ρ)≈ερ.\displaystyle\mathcal{N}(\rho)\approx^{\varepsilon}\rho. (6.37)

Then there exist a state σ\sigma and a channel ℳ∈conv​{𝒰}\mathcal{M}\in{\rm{conv}}\!\left\{\mathcal{U}\right\} satisfying

σ≈4​d2​ε1/5ρ,ℳ≈7​d2​ε1/5𝒩\displaystyle\sigma\approx^{4d^{2}\,\varepsilon^{1/5}}\rho,\quad\quad\mathcal{M}\approx^{7d^{2}\,\varepsilon^{1/5}}\mathcal{N} (6.38)

and

ℳ⁡(σ)=σ.\displaystyle\mathcal{M}(\sigma)=\sigma. (6.39)

The following lemma shows that if ρ\rho is an approximate fixed point of 𝒩∈conv​{𝒰}\mathcal{N}\in{\rm{conv}}\!\left\{\mathcal{U}\right\} of the form (6.36), then it is also an approximate fixed point of all unitary channels Ui​(⋅)​Ui∗U_{i}(\,\cdot\,)U_{i}^{*} provided that the corresponding probability is not too small, i.e. pi≫d​ε.p_{i}\gg d\varepsilon. We use this fact in the proof of Theorem 6.11 to apply Theorem 6.10 for each of those unitary channels individually. Importantly, as the state obtained in Theorem 6.10 is independent of the unitary, we can pick the same state σ\sigma working for all of those unitaries.

We now first state and prove Lemma 6.12 and then give the detailed proof of Theorem 6.11.

Let ρ\rho be quantum state and 𝒩∈conv​{𝒰}\mathcal{N}\in{\rm{conv}}\!\left\{\mathcal{U}\right\} be a mixed-unitary channel of the form (6.36) on a dd-dimensional Hilbert space ℋ\mathcal{H} such that for ε≥0\varepsilon\geq 0 we have

=pj​(‖ρ‖2−1‖ρ‖2​Tr​(ρ​Uj​ρ​Uj∗)).\displaystyle=p_{j}\left(\|\rho\|_{2}-\frac{1}{\|\rho\|_{2}}\mathrm{Tr}\left(\rho U_{j}\rho U_{j}^{*}\right)\right).

6.6 Unital channels

Theorem 6.13 below shows rapid fixiability of approximate fixed point equations in the sense of Definition 3.2 for 𝒮=𝔖⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{S}=\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}) and 𝒞\mathcal{C} being the set of unital channels, i.e. channels 𝒩\mathcal{N} satisfying 𝒩⁡(𝟙)=𝟙.\mathcal{N}(\mathbbm{1})=\mathbbm{1}.

Theorem 6.13 (Fixability for unital channels)

Let ρ\rho be a state and 𝒩\mathcal{N} a unital channel on some dd-dimensional Hilbert space ℋ\mathcal{H} such that for ε≥0\varepsilon\geq 0 we have

𝒩(ρ)≈ερ.\displaystyle\mathcal{N}(\rho)\approx^{\varepsilon}\rho. (6.45)

Then there exist a state σ\sigma and an unital channel ℳ\mathcal{M} satisfying

σ≈7​d5/3​ε1/6ρ,ℳ≈7​d5/3​ε1/6𝒩\displaystyle\sigma\approx^{7d^{5/3}\varepsilon^{1/6}}\rho,\quad\quad\mathcal{M}\approx^{7d^{5/3}\varepsilon^{1/6}}\mathcal{N} (6.46)

and

ℳ⁡(σ)=σ.\displaystyle\mathcal{M}(\sigma)=\sigma. (6.47)

On of the main ingredients of the proof of Theorem 6.13 is Lemma 6.14 below, which can be seen as an approximate version of a well-known result about fixed points of quantum channels (see e.g. [Wol12, Proposition 6.8] and [BCG+13, Lemma 1]). In particular, Lemma 6.14 shows that if a linear operator AA is an approximate fixed point of some channel 𝒩,\mathcal{N}, then so is its real- and imaginary- and their respective positive- and negative parts. Since in the case of Theorem 6.13 the channel 𝒩\mathcal{N} is unital and has therefore additionally to the approximate fixed point ρ\rho also the exact one 𝟙,\mathbbm{1}, we can employ Lemma 6.14 to find multiple additional approximate fixed points of 𝒩.\mathcal{N}. More precisely, in Lemma 6.15 we find by taking weighted differences of ρ\rho and 𝟙\mathbbm{1} and then their respective positive parts, that all spectral projections of ρ\rho are approximate fixed points of 𝒩\mathcal{N} as well. In the proof of Theorem 6.13 we then again employ the spectral clustering technique outlined in Section 6.1 and focus on the spectral projections of the corresponding spectral clusters. We can then fix the approximate fixed point equation for each of those projections using first the rotation lemma 6.6, but on Stinespring level involving the environment of the channel, and then the, what we call, generalised depolarising trick in Lemma 6.9. By that we obtain a new unital channel ℳ\mathcal{M} which is close to 𝒩\mathcal{N} and which has the spectral cluster state σ\sigma defined in (6.11) as an exact fixed point.

We now state and prove the mentioned Lemmas 6.14 and 6.15 and then give the proof of Theorem 6.13.

Lemma 6.14

Let AA be a linear operator on a separable Hilbert space and 𝒩\mathcal{N} a channel2323 23 For the lemma it suffices to assume that 𝒩\mathcal{N} is linear, positive and trace-preserving. such that for ε≥0\varepsilon\geq 0 we have

12​‖𝒩⁡(A)−A‖1≤ε\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left\|\mathcal{N}(A)-A\right\|_{1}\leq\varepsilon (6.48)

Then also we also have for the corresponding real and imaginary parts ℜ⁡(A)=(A+A∗)/2\Re(A)=(A+A^{*})/2 and ℑ⁡(A)=(A−A∗)/(2​i)\Im(A)=(A-A^{*})/(2i)

12​‖𝒩⁡(ℜ⁡(A))−ℜ⁡(A)‖1≤ε,12​‖𝒩⁡(ℑ⁡(A))−ℑ⁡(A)‖1≤ε,\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left\|\mathcal{N}(\Re(A))-\Re(A)\right\|_{1}\leq\varepsilon,\quad\quad\frac{1}{2}\left\|\mathcal{N}(\Im(A))-\Im(A)\right\|_{1}\leq\varepsilon, (6.49)

and furthermore for their positive- and negative parts

12​‖𝒩⁡([ℜ⁡(A)]+)−[ℜ⁡(A)]+‖1\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left\|\mathcal{N}([\Re(A)]_{+})-[\Re(A)]_{+}\right\|_{1} ≤32​ε+ε​Tr​([ℜ⁡(A)]+),\displaystyle\leq\frac{3}{2}\varepsilon+\sqrt{\varepsilon\mathrm{Tr}([\Re(A)]_{+})},
12​‖𝒩⁡([ℜ⁡(A)]−)−[ℜ⁡(A)]−‖1\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left\|\mathcal{N}([\Re(A)]_{-})-[\Re(A)]_{-}\right\|_{1} ≤32​ε+ε​Tr​([ℜ⁡(A)]−)\displaystyle\leq\frac{3}{2}\varepsilon+\sqrt{\varepsilon\mathrm{Tr}([\Re(A)]_{-})}
12​‖𝒩⁡([ℑ⁡(A)]+)−[ℑ⁡(A)]+‖1\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left\|\mathcal{N}([\Im(A)]_{+})-[\Im(A)]_{+}\right\|_{1} ≤32​ε+ε​Tr​([ℑ⁡(A)]+),\displaystyle\leq\frac{3}{2}\varepsilon+\sqrt{\varepsilon\mathrm{Tr}([\Im(A)]_{+})},
12​‖𝒩⁡([ℑ⁡(A)]−)−[ℑ⁡(A)]−‖1\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left\|\mathcal{N}([\Im(A)]_{-})-[\Im(A)]_{-}\right\|_{1} ≤32​ε+ε​Tr​([ℑ⁡(A)]−).\displaystyle\leq\frac{3}{2}\varepsilon+\sqrt{\varepsilon\mathrm{Tr}([\Im(A)]_{-})}. (6.50)

Proof. The proof uses similar arguments to the ones in [Wol12, Proposition 6.8] and [BCG+13, Lemma 1], which proved the result in the exact case ε=0.\varepsilon=0.

Since 𝒩\mathcal{N} is positive and in particular hermiticity preserving, i.e. 𝒩⁡(A∗)=𝒩​(A)∗\mathcal{N}(A^{*})=\mathcal{N}(A)^{*}, (6.49) immediately follows from (6.48) and the triangle inequality.

We now focus on proving (6.50). For that let XX be a self-adjoint trace class operator satisfying

12​‖𝒩⁡(X)−X‖1≤ε.\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left\|\mathcal{N}(X)-X\right\|_{1}\leq\varepsilon. (6.51)

Let π+\pi_{+} be the projection onto the orthogonal sum of the support of [X]+[X]_{+} and the kernel of XX and π−\pi_{-} the projection onto the support of [X]−[X]_{-}, such that we have π++π−=𝟙\pi_{+}+\pi_{-}=\mathbbm{1}. Using (6.51) and the variational expression of the trace distance (2.2) we have

Tr⁡(π+​(X−𝒩⁡(X)))≤12​‖𝒩⁡(X)−X‖1≤ε.\displaystyle\mathrm{Tr}\big(\pi_{+}\left(X-\mathcal{N}(X)\right)\big)\leq\frac{1}{2}\big\|\mathcal{N}(X)-X\big\|_{1}\leq\varepsilon.

Therefore, we have

Tr⁡([X]+)\displaystyle\mathrm{Tr}\big([X]_{+}\big) =Tr⁡(π+​X)≤Tr⁡(π+​𝒩​(X))+ε=Tr⁡(π+​𝒩​([X]+))−Tr⁡(π+​𝒩​([X]−))+ε\displaystyle=\mathrm{Tr}\big(\pi_{+}X\big)\leq\mathrm{Tr}\big(\pi_{+}\,\mathcal{N}(X)\big)+\varepsilon=\mathrm{Tr}\big(\pi_{+}\,\mathcal{N}([X]_{+})\big)-\mathrm{Tr}\big(\pi_{+}\,\mathcal{N}([X]_{-})\big)+\varepsilon
≤Tr⁡(π+​𝒩​([X]+))+ε≤Tr⁡([X]+)+ε.\displaystyle\leq\mathrm{Tr}\big(\pi_{+}\,\mathcal{N}([X]_{+})\big)+\varepsilon\leq\mathrm{Tr}\big([X]_{+}\big)+\varepsilon.

This shows Tr⁡(π+​𝒩​([X]−))≤ε\mathrm{Tr}\big(\pi_{+}\,\mathcal{N}([X]_{-}))\leq\varepsilon and by the same argument with positive- and negative parts interchanged also Tr⁡(π−​𝒩​([X]+)≤εCLOSE.\mathrm{Tr}\big(\pi_{-}\,\mathcal{N}([X]_{+})\leq\varepsilon. By Hölder’s inequality and positive semi-definiteness of 𝒩⁡([X]+)\mathcal{N}([X]_{+}) and 𝒩⁡([X]−)\mathcal{N}([X]_{-}) we see

‖π−​𝒩​([X]+)‖1\displaystyle\left\|\pi_{-}\mathcal{N}([X]_{+})\right\|_{1} ≤Tr⁡(π−​𝒩​([X]+))​Tr⁡([X]+)≤ε​Tr​([X]+)\displaystyle\leq\sqrt{\mathrm{Tr}\big(\pi_{-}\,\mathcal{N}([X]_{+})\big)}\sqrt{\mathrm{Tr}\big([X]_{+}\big)}\leq\sqrt{\varepsilon\mathrm{Tr}\big([X]_{+}\big)}
‖π+​𝒩​([X]−)‖1\displaystyle\left\|\pi_{+}\mathcal{N}([X]_{-})\right\|_{1} ≤ε​Tr​([X]−)\displaystyle\leq\sqrt{\varepsilon\mathrm{Tr}([X]_{-})}

This gives

‖𝒩⁡([X]+)−[X]+‖1\displaystyle\left\|\mathcal{N}([X]_{+})-[X]_{+}\right\|_{1} ≤‖π+​(𝒩⁡([X]+)−X)​π+‖1+‖π−​𝒩​([X]+)‖1+‖π−​𝒩​([X]+)​π+‖1\displaystyle\leq\left\|\pi_{+}(\mathcal{N}([X]_{+})-X)\pi_{+}\right\|_{1}+\left\|\pi_{-}\mathcal{N}([X]_{+})\right\|_{1}+\left\|\pi_{-}\mathcal{N}([X]_{+})\pi_{+}\right\|_{1}
≤‖π+(𝒩(X)−X)π+‖1+‖π+(𝒩([X]−)π+‖1+2ε​Tr​([X]+)\displaystyle\leq\left\|\pi_{+}(\mathcal{N}(X)-X)\pi_{+}\right\|_{1}+\left\|\pi_{+}(\mathcal{N}([X]_{-})\pi_{+}\right\|_{1}+2\sqrt{\varepsilon\mathrm{Tr}\big([X]_{+}\big)}
≤2​ε+Tr⁡(π+​𝒩​([X]−))+2​ε​Tr​([X]+)≤3​ε+2​ε​Tr​([X]+)\displaystyle\leq 2\varepsilon+\mathrm{Tr}(\pi_{+}\mathcal{N}([X]_{-}))+2\sqrt{\varepsilon\mathrm{Tr}\big([X]_{+}\big)}\leq 3\varepsilon+2\sqrt{\varepsilon\mathrm{Tr}\big([X]_{+}\big)}

By symmetry we also get

12​‖𝒩⁡([X]−)−[X]−‖1≤32​ε+ε​Tr​([X]−),\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left\|\mathcal{N}([X]_{-})-[X]_{-}\right\|_{1}\leq\frac{3}{2}\varepsilon+\sqrt{\varepsilon\mathrm{Tr}\big([X]_{-}\big)},

which finishes the proof  

Lemma 6.15

Let ρ\rho be a state and 𝒩\mathcal{N} an unital channel on some dd-dimensional Hilbert space ℋ\mathcal{H} such that for 0≤ε≤10\leq\varepsilon\leq 1 we have

𝒩(ρ)≈ερ.\displaystyle\mathcal{N}(\rho)\approx^{\varepsilon}\rho. (6.52)

Write ρ\rho in spectral decomposition

ρ=∑i=1mλi​πi\displaystyle\rho=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_{i}\pi_{i} (6.53)

with m∈[d],m\in[d], spectral points λ1>λ2>⋯>λm\lambda_{1}>\lambda_{2}>\cdots>\lambda_{m} and non-zero orthogonal projections (πi)i=1m\left(\pi_{i}\right)_{i=1}^{m} summing to 𝟙\mathbbm{1}. Then for all j∈[m−1]j\in[m-1] we have

12​‖𝒩⁡(∑i=1jπi)−∑i=1jπi‖1≤5​εδj\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left\|\mathcal{N}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{j}\pi_{i}\right)-\sum_{i=1}^{j}\pi_{i}\right\|_{1}\leq\frac{5\sqrt{\varepsilon}}{\delta_{j}} (6.54)

where δj=λj−λj+1>0.\delta_{j}=\lambda_{j}-\lambda_{j+1}>0.

Remark 6.16

Lemmas 6.14 and 6.15 provide a way to construct many new (approximate) fixed points of a quantum channel 𝒩\mathcal{N} from a few. By that, having only knowledge of the channel’s output on some input states, we might be able to determine the whole channel fully or at least partially. Let us illustrate this by considering the example of an unital channel 𝒩,\mathcal{N}, which we know to have an additional exact fixed point state ρ.\rho. Assume furthermore that the state ρ\rho has simple spectrum and hence can be written in spectral decomposition

ρ=∑i=1dλi​|ψi⟩​⟨ψi|\displaystyle\rho=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\lambda_{i}|\psi_{i}\rangle\!\langle\psi_{i}|

with spectral points λ1>λ2>⋯>λd\lambda_{1}>\lambda_{2}>\cdots>\lambda_{d} and an orthonormal basis (ψi)i=1d.\left(\psi_{i}\right)_{i=1}^{d}. From Lemma 6.15 we can deduce that also all of the spectral projections of ρ\rho are fixed points of 𝒩,\mathcal{N}, i.e.

𝒩⁡(|ψi⟩​⟨ψi|)=|ψi⟩​⟨ψi|\displaystyle\mathcal{N}(|\psi_{i}\rangle\!\langle\psi_{i}|)=|\psi_{i}\rangle\!\langle\psi_{i}|

for all i∈[d].i\in[d]. This gives for V:ℋ→ℋ⊗ℋEV:\mathcal{H}\to\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{E} being a Stinespring isometry of 𝒩\mathcal{N} that

V⁡|ψi⟩=|ψi⟩​|ϕi⟩\displaystyle V|\psi_{i}\rangle=|\psi_{i}\rangle|\phi_{i}\rangle

for some normalised vectors (|ϕi⟩)i=1d\left(|\phi_{i}\rangle\right)_{i=1}^{d} on the environment Hilbert space ℋE.\mathcal{H}_{E}. Therefore, for any linear operator AA which can be written in matrix components as A=∑i,j=1dai,j​|ψi⟩​⟨ψj|A=\sum_{i,j=1}^{d}a_{i,j}|\psi_{i}\rangle\!\langle\psi_{j}| we see that the channel’s output is given by

𝒩⁡(A)=∑i,j=1dai,j​⟨ϕj,ϕi⟩​|ψi⟩​⟨ψj|.\displaystyle\mathcal{N}(A)=\sum_{i,j=1}^{d}a_{i,j}\langle\phi_{j},\phi_{i}\rangle\,|\psi_{i}\rangle\!\langle\psi_{j}|.

Therefore, only from the two fixed points 𝟙\mathbbm{1} and ρ,\rho, we are able to determine the channel 𝒩\mathcal{N} uniquely up to knowledge of the complex numbers ⟨ϕj,ϕi⟩.\langle\phi_{j},\phi_{i}\rangle.

Proof of Lemma 6.15. Define

A1=ρ−λ2​𝟙\displaystyle A_{1}=\rho-\lambda_{2}\mathbbm{1}

and note that since 𝒩\mathcal{N} is unital we have

Therefore, using Lemma 6.14, we find for the positive part

where we have used Tr⁡([A1]+)≤Tr⁡(ρ)=1\mathrm{Tr}([A_{1}]_{+})\leq\mathrm{Tr}(\rho)=1 and ε≤1.\varepsilon\leq 1. Using the spectral decomposition (6.53), we can read off

[A1]+=(λ1−λ2)​π1=δ1​π1[A_{1}]_{+}=(\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{2})\pi_{1}=\delta_{1}\pi_{1}

Iterating the above procedure, we define for all j∈[m−1]j\in[m-1]

Aj=ρ−λj+1​𝟙=∑i=1m(λi−λj+1)​πi,\displaystyle A_{j}=\rho-\lambda_{j+1}\mathbbm{1}=\sum_{i=1}^{m}(\lambda_{i}-\lambda_{j+1})\pi_{i},

[Aj]+\displaystyle[A_{j}]_{+} =∑i=1j(λi−λj+1)​πi=∑i=1j−1(λi−λj)​πi+∑i=1j(λj−λj+1)​πi\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{j}(\lambda_{i}-\lambda_{j+1})\pi_{i}=\sum_{i=1}^{j-1}(\lambda_{i}-\lambda_{j})\pi_{i}+\sum_{i=1}^{j}(\lambda_{j}-\lambda_{j+1})\pi_{i}
=[Aj−1]++δj​∑i=1jπj.\displaystyle=[A_{j-1}]_{+}+\delta_{j}\sum_{i=1}^{j}\pi_{j}.

we see from (6.55) and the triangle inequality that

for all j∈[m−1].j\in[m-1].

6.7 Local channels and pure states

In the following we consider a bipartiate Hilbert space ℋA​B=ℋA⊗ℋB\mathcal{H}_{AB}=\mathcal{H}_{A}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{B} with ℋA\mathcal{H}_{A} and ℋB\mathcal{H}_{B} being Hilbert spaces of finite dimension dAd_{A} and dBd_{B} respectively. Theorem 6.17 below shows rapid fixability of approximate fixed points in the sense of Defintion 3.2 for 𝒮\mathcal{S} being the set of pure states on ℋA​B\mathcal{H}_{AB} and 𝒞=idA⊗CPTP⁡(ℋB).\mathcal{C}={\rm{id}}_{A}\otimes{\rm{CPTP}}(\mathcal{H}_{B}).

Theorem 6.17 (Fixability for local channels and pure states)

Let ℋA​B=ℋA⊗ℋB\mathcal{H}_{AB}=\mathcal{H}_{A}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{B} be a finite-dimensional, bipartite Hilbert space with dA≔dim(ℋA)d_{A}\coloneqq\dim(\mathcal{H}_{A}) and dB≔dim(ℋB)d_{B}\coloneqq\dim(\mathcal{H}_{B}). Let ρA​B=|Ψ⟩​⟨Ψ|A​B\rho_{AB}=|\Psi\rangle\!\langle\Psi|_{AB} be a pure state on ℋA​B\mathcal{H}_{AB} and 𝒩B∈CPTP⁡(ℋB)\mathcal{N}_{B}\in{\rm{CPTP}}(\mathcal{H}_{B}) such that for ε≥0\varepsilon\geq 0 we have

(idA⊗𝒩B)(ρA​B)≈ερA​B.\displaystyle({\rm{id}}_{A}\otimes\mathcal{N}_{B})(\rho_{AB})\approx^{\varepsilon}\rho_{AB}. (6.70)

Then there exist a pure state σA​B=|Φ⟩​⟨Φ|A​B\sigma_{AB}=|\Phi\rangle\!\langle\Phi|_{AB} and a channel ℳB∈CPTP⁡(ℋB)\mathcal{M}_{B}\in{\rm{CPTP}}(\mathcal{H}_{B}) such that

ρA​B≈7​d∗​ε1/3σA​B,ℳB≈7​d∗​ε1/3𝒩B,\displaystyle\rho_{AB}\approx^{7\sqrt{d_{*}}\,\varepsilon^{1/3}}\sigma_{AB},\quad\quad\mathcal{M}_{B}\approx^{7\sqrt{d_{*}}\,\varepsilon^{1/3}}\mathcal{N}_{B}, (6.71)

where d∗=min⁡{dA,dB},d_{*}=\min\{d_{A},d_{B}\}, and

(idA⊗ℳB)​(σA​B)=σA​B.\displaystyle({\rm{id}}_{A}\otimes\mathcal{M}_{B})(\sigma_{AB})=\sigma_{AB}. (6.72)

Furthermore, the state σA​B\sigma_{AB} is independent of 𝒩B.\mathcal{N}_{B}.

For the proof of Theorem 6.17 we express the state vector |Ψ⟩A​B|\Psi\rangle_{AB} in Schmidt decomposition as

|Ψ⟩A​B=∑i=1d∗μi​|ei⟩A​|fi⟩B.\displaystyle|\Psi\rangle_{AB}=\sum_{i=1}^{d_{*}}\sqrt{\mu_{i}}|e_{i}\rangle_{A}|f_{i}\rangle_{B}. (6.73)

The idea is then to define the new state vector |Φ⟩A​B|\Phi\rangle_{AB} approximating |Ψ⟩A​B|\Psi\rangle_{AB} by setting Schmidt coefficients in (6.73) below a certain threshold δ\delta equal to zero. Denoting by V:ℋB→ℋB⊗ℋEV:\mathcal{H}_{B}\to\mathcal{H}_{B}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{E} a Stinespring isometry of the channel 𝒩B,\mathcal{N}_{B}, we show for remainder of the Schmidt vectors |fi⟩B|f_{i}\rangle_{B} with large Schmidt coefficients that

for some fixed state vector |β⟩E|\beta\rangle_{E} on the environment Hilbert space ℋE\mathcal{H}_{E} independent of the index i.i. Hence, using the rotation lemma 6.5 we can find an unitary UU close to the identity on ℋB⊗ℋE\mathcal{H}_{B}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{E} such that its application onto the left hand side of (6.74) makes this an exact equality. Therefore, defining the channel ℳB\mathcal{M}_{B} with Stinespring isometry U​V,UV, we see that when applied onto the state |Φ⟩​⟨Φ|A​B|\Phi\rangle\!\langle\Phi|_{AB} no correlations between the system and environment are produced and the state is left invariant. Similarly as in the proof of Theorems 6.10, 6.11 and 6.13 we then optimise over the parameter δ\delta to obtain good approximation error for both state and channel.

7 Impossibility of rapid fixability for local channels

In the previous sections we have shown that for a variety of natural choices of 𝒮\mathcal{S} and 𝒞\mathcal{C}, approximate fixed point equations are rapidly fixable in the sense of Definition 3.2. In particular, Theorem 6.17 shows that rapid fixability is possible in the bipartite regime ℋA​B=ℋA⊗ℋB\mathcal{H}_{AB}=\mathcal{H}_{A}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{B} with 𝒮\mathcal{S} being the set of pure states on ℋA​B\mathcal{H}_{AB} and 𝒞=idA⊗CPTP⁡(ℋB).\mathcal{C}={\rm{id}}_{A}\otimes{\rm{CPTP}}(\mathcal{H}_{B}). In contrast, we show in this section that if one considers instead the full set of general mixed states, 𝒮=𝔖⁡(ℋA​B)\mathcal{S}=\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}_{AB}), rapid fixability of approximate fixed points is no longer possible for 𝒞=idA⊗CPTP⁡(ℋB).\mathcal{C}={\rm{id}}_{A}\otimes{\rm{CPTP}}(\mathcal{H}_{B}). We do this by providing a concrete counterexample. As a matter of fact, we also see that named impossibility already occurs in the classical bipartite regime, i.e. for 𝒮=Prob⁡(𝒳×𝒴)\mathcal{S}={\rm{Prob}}({\cal X}\times\mathcal{Y}) and 𝒞=idX⊗Stoch⁡(𝒴)\mathcal{C}={\rm{id}}_{X}\otimes{\rm{Stoch}}(\mathcal{Y}). Both of these results are stated in Corollary 7.3 below.

To prove Corollary 7.3, we first focus on the question of fixability of multiple approximate fixed points at once. Similarly to Definition 3.1, we say that for a dd-dimensional Hilbert space ℋ,\mathcal{H}, n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} and 𝒮⊆𝔖⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{S}\subseteq\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}) and 𝒞⊆CPTP⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{C}\subseteq{\rm{CPTP}}(\mathcal{H}), nn approximate fixed point equations are fixable at once for the pair 𝒮⊆𝔖\mathcal{S}\subseteq\mathfrak{S} and 𝒞⊆CPTP⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{C}\subseteq{\rm{CPTP}}(\mathcal{H}) if the following holds: There exist approximation functions f,g:ℕ×ℝ+→ℝ+f,g:\mathbb{N}\times\mathbbm{R}_{+}\to\mathbbm{R}_{+} such that

limε→0f⁡(d,ε)=limε→0g⁡(d,ε)=0,\displaystyle\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}f(d,\varepsilon)=\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}g(d,\varepsilon)=0, (7.1)

and for all ρ1,⋯,ρn∈𝒮,𝒩∈𝒞\rho_{1},\cdots,\rho_{n}\in\mathcal{S},\,\mathcal{N}\in\mathcal{C} and ε≥0\varepsilon\geq 0 such that 𝒩(ρi)≈ερi\mathcal{N}(\rho_{i})\approx^{\varepsilon}\rho_{i} for all i∈[n]i\in[n], we can find new states and a channel of the same structure:

σi∈𝒮andℳ∈𝒞,\displaystyle\sigma_{i}\in\mathcal{S}\quad\quad\text{and}\quad\quad\mathcal{M}\in\mathcal{C},\quad (7.2)

which are close to original ones, i.e.

σi≈f⁡(d,ε)ρiandℳ≈g⁡(d,ε)𝒩,\displaystyle\sigma_{i}\approx^{f(d,\varepsilon)}\rho_{i}\quad\quad\text{and}\quad\quad\mathcal{M}\approx^{g(d,\varepsilon)}\mathcal{N}, (7.3)

and which satisfy the fixed point equations

ℳ⁡(σi)=σi.\displaystyle\mathcal{M}(\sigma_{i})=\sigma_{i}. (7.4)

Importantly, here we demand that the new channel ℳ\mathcal{M} satisfies an exact fixed point equation for all states σi\sigma_{i} at the same time.

Furthermore, analogously to Definition 3.2 we say nn approximate fixed point equations are rapidly fixable at once if the functions ff and gg in the above satisfy

f⁡(d,ε)=c​db​εaandg⁡(d,ε)=c′​db′​εa′,\displaystyle f(d,\varepsilon)=c\,d^{b}\varepsilon^{a}\quad\quad\text{and}\quad\quad g(d,\varepsilon)=c^{\prime}d^{b^{\prime}}\varepsilon^{a^{\prime}}, (7.5)

for some a,a′>0a,a^{\prime}>0 (and typically a,a′≤1a,a^{\prime}\leq 1) and b′,b′,c,c′≥0b^{\prime},b^{\prime},c,c^{\prime}\geq 0 all independent of dd and ε.\varepsilon.

Theorem 7.1 below shows (via a concrete counterexample) that already in the classical case, i.e. for 𝒮=Prob⁡(𝒳)\mathcal{S}={\rm{Prob}}({\cal X}) and 𝒞=Stoch⁡(𝒳)\mathcal{C}={\rm{Stoch}}({\cal X}), rapid fixability of two approximate fixed points at once is in general impossible. Here, we find for every dimension dd, two probability vectors and a stochastic matrix which satisfy approximate fixed point equations with error parameter vanishing exponentially as d→∞d\to\infty, i.e. ε=12d.\varepsilon=\frac{1}{2^{d}}. However, for any two new probability vectors and a stochastic matrix, which fix named approximate fixed point equations at once, at least one needs to be at a constant distance from the corresponding original one.

Theorem 7.1 (No rapid fixing of 2 approximate fixed points in the classical case)

For every d∈ℕd\in\mathbb{N} there exist probability vectors P→1\vec{P}_{1} and P→2\vec{P}_{2} and a stochastic matrix TT on a classical alphabet 𝒳{\cal X} with |𝒳|=d|{\cal X}|=d such that

12​‖P→1−P→2‖1=1\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left\|\vec{P}_{1}-\vec{P}_{2}\right\|_{1}=1 (7.6)

and

12​‖T​P→1−P→1‖1≤12d,12​‖T​P→2−P→2‖1≤12d,\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left\|T\vec{P}_{1}-\vec{P}_{1}\right\|_{1}\leq\frac{1}{2^{d}},\quad\quad\frac{1}{2}\left\|T\vec{P}_{2}-\vec{P}_{2}\right\|_{1}\leq\frac{1}{2^{d}}, (7.7)

and which satisfy the following: For any pair of probability vectors Q→1\vec{Q}_{1} and Q→2\vec{Q}_{2} and any stochastic matrix SS such that

S​Q→1=Q→1andS​Q→2=Q→2,\displaystyle S\vec{Q}_{1}=\vec{Q}_{1}\quad\quad\text{and}\quad\quad S\vec{Q}_{2}=\vec{Q}_{2}, (7.8)

we either have

‖S−T‖≥14or12​‖Q→1−P→1‖1≥12or12​‖Q→2−P→2‖1≥12.\displaystyle\|S-T\|\geq\frac{1}{4}\quad\text{or}\quad\frac{1}{2}\left\|\vec{Q}_{1}-\vec{P}_{1}\right\|_{1}\geq\frac{1}{2}\quad\text{or}\quad\frac{1}{2}\left\|\vec{Q}_{2}-\vec{P}_{2}\right\|_{1}\geq\frac{1}{2}. (7.9)

This shows that two approximate fixed points are, in general, not rapidly fixable at once for the pair 𝒮=Prob⁡(𝒳)\mathcal{S}={\rm{Prob}}(\mathcal{{\cal X}}) and 𝒞=Stoch⁡(𝒳)\mathcal{\mathcal{C}}={\rm{Stoch}}(\mathcal{{\cal X}}) for classical alphabets of size |𝒳|=d.|{\cal X}|=d.

We can embed this counterexample into the quantum setting using the natural constructions (2.6) and (2.7). Hence, we find for every dimension dd, two states and a channel which satisfy approximate fixed point equations with error parameter vanishing exponentially in the dimension. Importantly, in the quantum setting we have a bigger set of possible states and channels to fix named approximate fixed point equation. Therefore, the impossibility statement of Theorem 7.1 does not immediately also give the corresponding impossibility statement in the quantum case. However, using a slight adjustment of the classical argument we are still able to show that for any new two states and a channel, which fix named approximate fixed point equations at once, at least one needs to be at a distance of order 𝒪⁡(1/d)\mathcal{O}(1/d) from the corresponding original one. Since, as mentioned, we have for the error parameter ε=12d\varepsilon=\frac{1}{2^{d}}, this shows that these two approximate fixed points are also not rapidly fixable in the quantum setting:

Theorem 7.2 (No rapid fixing of 2 approximate fixed points in quantum case)

For every d∈ℕd\in\mathbb{N} there exist states ρ1\rho_{1} and ρ2\rho_{2} and a channel 𝒩\mathcal{N} on a dd-dimensional Hilbert space ℋ\mathcal{H} such that

12​‖ρ1−ρ2‖1=1\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left\|\rho_{1}-\rho_{2}\right\|_{1}=1 (7.10)

and

12​‖𝒩⁡(ρ1)−ρ1‖1≤12d,12​‖𝒩⁡(ρ2)−ρ2‖1≤12d,\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left\|\mathcal{N}(\rho_{1})-\rho_{1}\right\|_{1}\leq\frac{1}{2^{d}},\quad\quad\frac{1}{2}\left\|\mathcal{N}(\rho_{2})-\rho_{2}\right\|_{1}\leq\frac{1}{2^{d}}, (7.11)

and which satisfy the following: For all states σ1\sigma_{1} and σ2\sigma_{2} and channels ℳ\mathcal{M} such that

ℳ⁡(σ1)=σ1andℳ⁡(σ2)=σ2\displaystyle\mathcal{M}(\sigma_{1})=\sigma_{1}\quad\quad\text{and}\quad\quad\mathcal{M}(\sigma_{2})=\sigma_{2} (7.12)

we either have

12​‖ℳ−𝒩‖⋄≥116​dor12​‖σ1−ρ1‖1≥12or12​‖σ2−ρ2‖1≥12.\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\|\mathcal{M}-\mathcal{N}\|_{\diamond}\geq\frac{1}{16d}\quad\text{or}\quad\frac{1}{2}\left\|\sigma_{1}-\rho_{1}\right\|_{1}\geq\frac{1}{2}\quad\text{or}\quad\frac{1}{2}\left\|\sigma_{2}-\rho_{2}\right\|_{1}\geq\frac{1}{2}. (7.13)

This shows two approximate fixed points are, in general, not rapidly fixable at once for the pair 𝒮=𝔖⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{S}=\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}) and 𝒞=CPTP⁡(ℋ).\mathcal{C}={\rm{CPTP}}(\mathcal{H}).

We can encode the counterexamples of Theorem 7.1 and Theorem 7.2 into the language of bipartite states. By that, we see the impossibility of rapidly fixing approximate fixed point equations in the bipartite setting with channels acting trivially on the first of the systems. We present this statement in the following corollary and prove it using the results from Theorems 7.1 and 7.2. We then continue to provide the proofs for Theorems 7.1 and 7.2.

Corollary 7.3

Approximate fixed point equations are in general not rapidly fixable in the sense of Defintion 3.2 for the following cases:

  1. 1.

    𝒮∈𝔖⁡(ℋA​B)\mathcal{S}\in\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}_{AB}) and 𝒞=idA⊗CPTP⁡(ℋB)\mathcal{C}={\rm{id}}_{A}\otimes{\rm{CPTP}}(\mathcal{H}_{B}), with ℋA​B=ℋA⊗ℋB\mathcal{H}_{AB}=\mathcal{H}_{A}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{B} being a bipartite Hilbert space, with dim(ℋA)≥2\dim(\mathcal{H}_{A})\geq 2

    𝒮=Prob⁡(𝒳×𝒴)\mathcal{S}={\rm{Prob}}(\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}) and 𝒞=idX⊗Stoch⁡(𝒴)\mathcal{C}={\rm{id}}_{X}\otimes{\rm{Stoch}}(\mathcal{Y}) for |𝒳|≥2.|\mathcal{X}|\geq 2.

In the following two lemmas we see that any stochastic matrix SS close to TT necessarily has an unique fixed point probability vector. From that Theorem 7.1 is easy to conclude since, for SS being close to TT, the fixed points Q→1\vec{Q}_{1} and Q→2\vec{Q}_{2} must be equal and hence far from the P→1\vec{P}_{1} and P→2\vec{P}_{2} respectively (cf. (7.9)) as they are orthogonal.

First we see in Lemma 7.4 that any stochastic matrix SS sufficiently close to TT which has a fixed point Q→≠P→2\vec{Q}\neq\vec{P}_{2} necessarily needs to have a positive flow from the entry dd to some entry j≠dj\neq d, with which we precisely mean

Sj​d>0.\displaystyle S_{j\,d}>0.

From that we conclude in Lemma 7.5 that SS has in fact a one-dimensional fixed point space using the Perron-Frobenius theorem for irreducible matrices [HJ85, Theorem 8.4.4]. This can be interpreted as a robustness result for the uniqueness of fixed points in a neighbourhood around T.T.

Lemma 7.4

Let SS be a stochastic matrix in dd dimensions satisfying

and therefore Qd−2=0Q_{d-2}=0 since Sd−1​d−2>0S_{d-1\,d-2}>0. By iterating this we find Qj=0Q_{j}=0 for all j∈[d−1]j\in[d-1] and since Q→\vec{Q} is a probability vector this already implies

Lemma 7.5 (Robustness of uniqueness of fixed point in classical case)

Let SS be a stochastic matrix in dd dimensions satisfying

‖S−T‖<14,\displaystyle\left\|S-T\right\|<\frac{1}{4}, (7.26)

with TT being the stochastic matrix defined in (7.21). Then ℱ⁡(S){\mathcal{F}}(S) is one-dimensional, i.e. SS has an unique fixed point probability vector.

Proof. Similarly to the argument in the proof of Lemma 7.4 we get that since

‖S−T‖=max⁡∑i=1dj∈[d]⁡|Si​j−Ti​j|<1/4\displaystyle\|S-T\|=\max_{j\in[d]}\sum_{i=1}^{d}|S_{ij}-T_{ij}|<1/4

we have

Sj​d>0.\displaystyle S_{j\,d}>0. (7.29)

From (7.27) and (7.29) we see that for every i,j∈[d]i,j\in[d] with i≠ji\neq j there exists a path connecting ii and jj and such that SS is componentwise positive along this path, with which we mean precisely the following:2525 25 To convince ourselves that for i,j∈[d]i,j\in[d] with i≠ji\neq j such a path exists, consider the following construction in different cases: Case 1) i<ji<j: Simply take the path i1=i,i_{1}=i, i2=i+1,⋯,in=ji_{2}=i+1,\cdots,i_{n}=j which is possible by (7.28). Case 2) i>j,i≠di>j,\ i\neq d: Take as path i1=i,i_{1}=i, i2=i−1,⋯in=ji_{2}=i-1,\cdots i_{n}=j which is possible by (7.27). Case 3) i=d>j:i=d>j: Let k∈[d−1]k\in[d-1] be such that Sk​d>0S_{kd}>0 which exists as argued in (7.29). For all i,j∈[d]i,j\in[d] there exists n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} and i2,i3,…,in−1∈[d]i_{2},i_{3},\dots,i_{n-1}\in[d] such that denoting i1≡ii_{1}\equiv i and in≡ji_{n}\equiv j we have for all l∈[n]l\in[n]
