In other words, SS is irreducible (cf. [HJ85, Theorem 6.2.24] for other characterisations of irreducible matrices). Therefore, we can apply the Perron-Frobenius theorem for irreducible matrices [HJ85, Theorem 8.4.4] giving that 11 is a simple eigenvalue of SS, i.e. ℱ⁡(S){\mathcal{F}}(S) is one-dimensional.  

We are now ready to apply Lemma 7.5 to give the proof of Theoerm 7.1.

Proof of Theorem 7.1. For every dimension d∈ℕd\in\mathbb{N} we pick the probability vectors P→1\vec{P}_{1}, P→2\vec{P}_{2} and the stochastic matrix TT as defined in (7.19), (7.20) and (7.21). Since P→1\vec{P}_{1} and P→2\vec{P}_{2} have orthogonal support we see

12​‖P→1−P→2‖1=1.\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left\|\vec{P}_{1}-\vec{P}_{2}\right\|_{1}=1. (7.30)

Moreover, from (7.22) and (7.23) we know

12​‖T​P→1−P→1‖1≤12d,12​‖T​P→2−P→2‖1=0.\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left\|T\vec{P}_{1}-\vec{P}_{1}\right\|_{1}\leq\frac{1}{2^{d}},\quad\quad\frac{1}{2}\left\|T\vec{P}_{2}-\vec{P}_{2}\right\|_{1}=0.

Hence, P→1\vec{P}_{1}, P→2\vec{P}_{2} and TT satisfy the assumptions of the theorem. To prove the final statement of the theorem (7.9), assume that SS is a stochastic matrix satisfying ‖S−T‖<14\|S-T\|<\frac{1}{4}. Then by Lemma 7.5, we see that if Q→1,Q→2\vec{Q}_{1},\vec{Q}_{2} are probability vectors and fixed points of S,S, we necessarily have Q→≔Q→1=Q→2.\vec{Q}\coloneqq\vec{Q}_{1}=\vec{Q}_{2}. Therefore, using (7.30) we have

1=12​‖P→1−P→2‖1≤12​‖P→1−Q→‖1+12​‖Q→−P→2‖1\displaystyle 1=\frac{1}{2}\left\|\vec{P}_{1}-\vec{P}_{2}\right\|_{1}\leq\frac{1}{2}\left\|\vec{P}_{1}-\vec{Q}\right\|_{1}+\frac{1}{2}\left\|\vec{Q}-\vec{P}_{2}\right\|_{1}

and hence either

12​‖P→1−Q→‖1≥12or‖P→2−Q→‖1≥12.\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left\|\vec{P}_{1}-\vec{Q}\right\|_{1}\geq\frac{1}{2}\quad\text{or}\quad\left\|\vec{P}_{2}-\vec{Q}\right\|_{1}\geq\frac{1}{2}.

 

To prove Theorem 7.2 for the quantum setting, we need to prove an analouge of the robustness result in Lemma 7.5 above. That is, embedding the stochastic matrix TT into the channel 𝒩T\mathcal{N}_{T} using the natural construction (2.7), also all quantum channels in a neighbourhood around 𝒩T\mathcal{N}_{T} have a unique fixed point state. Since the set of quantum channels around 𝒩T\mathcal{N}_{T} is obviously larger than the set of classical channels around 𝒩T\mathcal{N}_{T} (which corresponds to stochastic matrices around TT) the desired robustness result in the quantum setting does not immediately follow from Lemma 7.5. Therefore, we prove it independently in the next lemma. Here, the idea is that given a quantum channel ℳ\mathcal{M} close to 𝒩T,\mathcal{N}_{T}, which has two fixed points, it necessarily needs to have two orthogonal invariant subspaces in the sense of (2.12). But therefore also 𝒩T\mathcal{N}_{T} needs to leave named subspaces approximately invariant, which quickly leads to a contradiction given the precise form of the stochastic matrix T.T.

Lemma 7.6 (Robustness of uniqueness of fixed point in quantum case)

Let ℳ\mathcal{M} be a quantum channel on a dd-dimensional Hilbert space ℋ\mathcal{H} satisfying

12​‖ℳ−𝒩T‖⋄≤116​d,\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left\|\mathcal{M}-\mathcal{N}_{T}\right\|_{\diamond}\leq\frac{1}{16d}, (7.31)

with 𝒩T\mathcal{N}_{T} being the channel defined trough (2.7) and TT being the stochastic matrix defined in (7.21). Then ℱ⁡(ℳ){\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{M}) is one-dimensional, i.e. ℳ\mathcal{M} has an unique fixed point state.

Proof. Assume for contradiction dim(ℱ⁡(M))≥2.\dim({\mathcal{F}}(M))\geq 2. Then let A,B∈ℱ⁡(ℳ)A,B\in{\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{M}) be non-zero with A≠B.A\neq B. Without loss of generality we can assume that AA and BB are both self-adjoint, as otherwise we could simply take ℜ⁡(A)\Re(A) and ℑ⁡(A)\Im(A) which, by (2.11), are also fixed points. Moreover, taking hence [A−B]+[A-B]_{+} and [A−B]−[A-B]_{-} gives, again by (2.11), two non-zero, positive semi-definite operators which are fixed points of ℳ.\mathcal{M}. Therefore, by (2.12) we find two orthogonal invariant subspaces, i.e. the orthogonal projections π1\pi_{1} and π2\pi_{2} onto the supports of [A−B]+[A-B]_{+} and [A−B]−[A-B]_{-} respectively satisfy

Tr⁡((𝟙−π1)​ℳ​(π1))=Tr⁡((𝟙−π2)​ℳ​(π2))=0\displaystyle\mathrm{Tr}\left((\mathbbm{1}-\pi_{1})\mathcal{M}(\pi_{1})\right)=\mathrm{Tr}\left((\mathbbm{1}-\pi_{2})\mathcal{M}(\pi_{2})\right)=0

and furthermore by definition π1​π2=0.\pi_{1}\pi_{2}=0. Hence, by assumption (7.31) and the variational expression of the trace distance (2.2) we also have

Tr⁡((𝟙−π1)​𝒩T​(π1))\displaystyle\mathrm{Tr}\left((\mathbbm{1}-\pi_{1})\mathcal{N}_{T}(\pi_{1})\right) =Tr⁡((𝟙−π1)​(𝒩T​(π1)−ℳ⁡(π1)))\displaystyle=\mathrm{Tr}\left((\mathbbm{1}-\pi_{1})\left(\mathcal{N}_{T}(\pi_{1})-\mathcal{M}(\pi_{1})\right)\right)
≤Tr⁡(π1)2​‖𝒩T−ℳ‖⋄≤116\displaystyle\leq\frac{\mathrm{Tr}(\pi_{1})}{2}\left\|\mathcal{N}_{T}-\mathcal{M}\right\|_{\diamond}\leq\frac{1}{16} (7.32)

and similarly

Tr⁡((𝟙−π2)​𝒩T​(π2))≤116.\displaystyle\mathrm{Tr}\left((\mathbbm{1}-\pi_{2})\mathcal{N}_{T}(\pi_{2})\right)\leq\frac{1}{16}. (7.33)

Now note that this gives that either ⟨d|π1|d⟩<12\langle d|\pi_{1}|d\rangle<\frac{1}{2} or ⟨d|π2|d⟩<12\langle d|\pi_{2}|d\rangle<\frac{1}{2} as otherwise by definition of the stochastic matrix TT in (7.21)

Tr⁡((𝟙−π1)​𝒩T​(π1))≥Tr⁡(π2​𝒩T​(π1))≥Td​d​⟨d|π2​|d⟩​⟨d|​π1|d⟩≥14.\displaystyle\mathrm{Tr}\left((\mathbbm{1}-\pi_{1})\mathcal{N}_{T}(\pi_{1})\right)\geq\mathrm{Tr}\left(\pi_{2}\mathcal{N}_{T}(\pi_{1})\right)\geq T_{dd}\langle d|\pi_{2}|d\rangle\langle d|\pi_{1}|d\rangle\geq\frac{1}{4}.

Without loss of generality we hence assume

⟨d|π1|d⟩<1/2\displaystyle\langle d|\pi_{1}|d\rangle<1/2 (7.34)

This gives that there exists i∗∈[d−1]i_{*}\in[d-1] such that

⟨i∗|π1|i∗⟩≥12\displaystyle\langle i_{*}|\pi_{1}|i_{*}\rangle\geq\frac{1}{2} (7.35)

as otherwise ⟨j|(𝟙−π1)|j⟩>12\langle j|(\mathbbm{1}-\pi_{1})|j\rangle>\frac{1}{2} for all j∈[d]j\in[d] and hence

Tr⁡((𝟙−π1)​𝒩T​(π1))≥∑j=1dTj​j​⟨j|(𝟙−π1)|j⟩​⟨j​|π1|​j⟩>18​∑j=1d⟨j​|π1|​j⟩=Tr⁡(π1)8,\displaystyle\mathrm{Tr}\left((\mathbbm{1}-\pi_{1})\mathcal{N}_{T}(\pi_{1})\right)\geq\sum_{j=1}^{d}T_{jj}\langle j|(\mathbbm{1}-\pi_{1})|j\rangle\langle j|\pi_{1}|j\rangle>\frac{1}{8}\sum_{j=1}^{d}\langle j|\pi_{1}|j\rangle=\frac{\mathrm{Tr}(\pi_{1})}{8},

which is a contradiction to (7.32) since π1≠0\pi_{1}\neq 0. Note that since ⟨i∗|π1|i∗⟩≥1/2\langle i_{*}|\pi_{1}|i_{*}\rangle\geq 1/2 also ⟨i∗+1|π1|i∗+1⟩≥1/2\langle i_{*}+1|\pi_{1}|i_{*}+1\rangle\geq 1/2 as otherwise we have by definition of the stochastic matrix TT in (7.21)

Tr⁡((𝟙−π1)​𝒩T​(π1))≥Ti∗+1​i∗​⟨i∗+1|(𝟙−π1)|i∗+1⟩​⟨i∗​|π1|​i∗⟩>116,\displaystyle\mathrm{Tr}\left((\mathbbm{1}-\pi_{1})\mathcal{N}_{T}(\pi_{1})\right)\geq T_{i_{*}+1\,i_{*}}\langle i_{*}+1|(\mathbbm{1}-\pi_{1})|i_{*}+1\rangle\langle i_{*}|\pi_{1}|i_{*}\rangle>\frac{1}{16},

which is a contradiction to (7.32). However, by iterating this argument we see ⟨j|π1|j⟩≥1/2\langle j|\pi_{1}|j\rangle\geq 1/2 for all j∈{i∗,⋯,d},j\in\{i_{*},\cdots,d\}, which is a contradiction to (7.34). To conclude, we have shown that ℳ\mathcal{M} cannot have two orthogonal invariant subspaces, and therefore dim(ℱ⁡(ℳ))=1\dim({\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{M}))=1, as this would otherwise contradict assumption (7.32).

 

Proof of Theorem 7.2. The proof of Theorem 7.2 follows from exactly the same lines as the one of Theorem 7.1, with the usage of Lemma 7.6 instead of Lemma 7.5. We still give it here explicitly for completeness.

We use the natural embedding (2.6) and pick for every dimension d∈ℕd\in\mathbb{N} the states ρ1≔ρP→1\rho_{1}\coloneqq\rho_{\vec{P}_{1}} and ρ2≔ρP→2\rho_{2}\coloneqq\rho_{\vec{P}_{2}} with probability vectors P→1\vec{P}_{1} and P→2\vec{P}_{2} defined in (7.19) and (7.20). We again have by orthogonality

12​‖ρ1−ρ2‖1=1.\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left\|\rho_{1}-\rho_{2}\right\|_{1}=1. (7.36)

Furthermore, using the embedding (2.7), we pick as channel 𝒩≔𝒩T\mathcal{N}\coloneqq\mathcal{N}_{T} with TT being the stochastic matrix defined in (7.21) and see from (7.22) and (7.23) that

12​‖𝒩⁡(ρ1)−ρ1‖1=12​‖T​P→1−P→1‖1≤12d,12​‖𝒩⁡(ρ2)−ρ2‖1=0.\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left\|\mathcal{N}(\rho_{1})-\rho_{1}\right\|_{1}=\frac{1}{2}\left\|T\vec{P}_{1}-\vec{P}_{1}\right\|_{1}\leq\frac{1}{2^{d}},\quad\quad\frac{1}{2}\left\|\mathcal{N}(\rho_{2})-\rho_{2}\right\|_{1}=0.

Hence, ρ1\rho_{1}, ρ2\rho_{2} and 𝒩\mathcal{N} satisfy the assumptions of the theorem. To prove the final statement of the theorem, i.e. (7.13), assume that ℳ\mathcal{M} is a channel satisfying 12​‖ℳ−𝒩‖≤116​d\frac{1}{2}\|\mathcal{M}-\mathcal{N}\|\leq\frac{1}{16d}. Then by Lemma 7.6, we see that if σ1,σ2\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2} are states and fixed points of ℳ,\mathcal{M}, we necessarily have σ≔σ1=σ2.\sigma\coloneqq\sigma_{1}=\sigma_{2}. Therefore, using (7.36) we have

1=12​‖ρ1−ρ2‖1≤12​‖ρ1−σ‖1+12​‖σ−ρ2‖1\displaystyle 1=\frac{1}{2}\left\|\rho_{1}-\rho_{2}\right\|_{1}\leq\frac{1}{2}\left\|\rho_{1}-\sigma\right\|_{1}+\frac{1}{2}\left\|\sigma-\rho_{2}\right\|_{1}

and hence either

12​‖ρ1−σ‖1≥12or12​‖ρ2−σ‖1≥12.\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left\|\rho_{1}-\sigma\right\|_{1}\geq\frac{1}{2}\quad\text{or}\quad\frac{1}{2}\left\|\rho_{2}-\sigma\right\|_{1}\geq\frac{1}{2}.

 

8 Summary and open problems

We have defined the notion of fixability and rapid fixability of approximate fixed point equations of states and channels, which are, respectively, elements of the fixed sets 𝒮⊆𝔖⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{S}\subseteq\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}) and 𝒞⊆CPTP⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{C}\subseteq{\rm{CPTP}}(\mathcal{H}) (Definition 3.1 and 3.2). For finite dimensional Hilbert spaces and under the assumption that 𝒮\mathcal{S} and 𝒞\mathcal{C} are closed and contain a fixed point pair, we have shown that approximate fixed point equations are always fixable in the sense of Definition 3.1 (Proposition 4.1). We have applied this result to show that for any approximate quantum Markov chain ρA​B​C\rho_{ABC} there exists an exact quantum Markov chain close to ρA​B​C.\rho_{ABC}. Here, the provided upper bound on the distance between ρA​B​C\rho_{ABC} and σA​B​C\sigma_{ABC} necessarily depends on the dimensions of the systems and decays for vanishing conditional mutual information I(A:C|B)ρI(A:C|B)_{\rho} (Proposition 4.2).

Furthermore, we have established rapid fixability of approximate fixed point equations for the choices

  1. 1.

    𝒮=𝔖⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{S}=\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}) and 𝒞=CPTP⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{C}={\rm{CPTP}}(\mathcal{H}) (Theorem 5.1),

  2. 2.

    𝒮=Prob⁡(𝒳)\mathcal{S}={\rm{Prob}}({\cal X}) and 𝒞=Stoch⁡(𝒳)\mathcal{C}={\rm{Stoch}}({\cal X}) (Theorem 5.2),

  3. 3.

    𝒮=𝔖⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{S}=\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}) and 𝒞\mathcal{C} being the set of unitary channels (Theorem 6.10),

  4. 4.

    𝒮=𝔖⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{S}=\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}) and 𝒞\mathcal{C} being the set of mixed-unitary channels (Theorem 6.11),

  5. 5.

    𝒮=𝔖⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{S}=\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}) and 𝒞\mathcal{C} being the set of unital channels (Theorem 6.13),

  6. 6.

    𝒮\mathcal{S} being the set of pure states on a bipartite Hilbert space ℋA​B=ℋA⊗ℋB\mathcal{H}_{AB}=\mathcal{H}_{A}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{B} and 𝒞=idA⊗CPTP⁡(ℋB)\mathcal{C}={\rm{id}}_{A}\otimes{\rm{CPTP}}(\mathcal{H}_{B}) (Theorem 6.17).

Lastly, in Corollary 7.3 we have shown that approximate fixed point equations are not rapidly fixable for

  1. 1.

    𝒮=𝔖⁡(ℋA​B)\mathcal{S}=\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}_{AB}) and 𝒞=idA⊗CPTP⁡(ℋB),\mathcal{C}={\rm{id}}_{A}\otimes{\rm{CPTP}}(\mathcal{H}_{B}),

  2. 2.

    𝒮=Prob⁡(𝒳×𝒴)\mathcal{S}={\rm{Prob}}({\cal X}\times\mathcal{Y}) and 𝒞=idX⊗Stoch⁡(𝒴).\mathcal{C}={\rm{id}}_{X}\otimes{\rm{Stoch}}(\mathcal{Y}).

For the last result, we generalised the notion of rapid fixability to the situation of multiple approximate fixed point states of one specific channel. In this context, we show that these multiple approximate fixed point equations are not rapidly fixable at once, by providing an explicit counterexample (Theorems 7.1 and Theorem 7.2).

In the following we list some interesting open problems which can be subject to future research:

It would be interesting to obtain optimal bounds on the approximation functions ff and gg introduced in Definitions 3.1 and 3.2 for different choices of 𝒮\mathcal{S} and 𝒞.\mathcal{C}. Here, to establish optimality one needs to prove the corresponding lower bounds on the possible approximation functions. For that, we have already seen in Remark 5.4 that at least the scaling of max⁡{f,g}\max\{f,g\} for the cases (𝒮,𝒞)=(𝔖⁡(ℋ),CPTP⁡(ℋ))(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C})=(\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}),{\rm{CPTP}}(\mathcal{H})) and (𝒮,𝒞)=(Prob⁡(𝒳),Stoch⁡(𝒳))(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C})=({\rm{Prob}}({\cal X}),{\rm{Stoch}}({\cal X})) given in Theorems 5.1 and 5.2 is optimal. However, providing optimal bounds on both ff and gg individually, including the correct constants is still open. Furthermore, the constructions carried out for the above mentioned results on rapid fixability for all other choices of 𝒮\mathcal{S} and 𝒞\mathcal{C} led to bounds on the approximation functions which explicitly depend on the dimension of the underlying Hilbert space. It would be of great interest to determine when this dimension dependence is necessary.

Probably the most significant open problem, which lies outside the immediate scope of fixability of approximate fixed point equations, is to establish an improved version of Proposition 4.2, with an explicit control on the robustness of quantum Markov chains. As outlined at the end of Section 4 (in particular around (4.23)) it would be highly desirable to prove a bound for tripartite states ρA​B​C\rho_{ABC} of the form

minσA​B​C​QMC12‖ρA​B​C−σA​B​C‖1≤?cdAbAdBbBdCbCI(A:C|B)ρa,\displaystyle\min_{\sigma_{ABC}\ \text{QMC}}\,\frac{1}{2}\left\|\rho_{ABC}-\sigma_{ABC}\right\|_{1}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle?}}{{\leq}}c\,d^{\,b_{A}\,}_{A}d^{\,b_{B}\,}_{B}d^{\,b_{C}}_{C}\,I(A:C|B)^{a}_{\rho}, (8.1)

with constants a>0a>0 and bA,bB,bC,c≥0b_{A},b_{B},b_{C},c\geq 0 independent of the dimensions dA,dB,dCd_{A},d_{B},d_{C} and ρA​B​C.\rho_{ABC}.
